lemma_278.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(r\ge1\), let \(C_1,\dots,C_r\) be smooth projective geometrically connected curves over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(X\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension \(r\) over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, and let \(f:C_1\times_{\mathbb F_q}\cdots\times_{\mathbb F_q}C_r\to X\) be a proper surjective generically finite morphism. Writing \(F_X=(\mathrm{id}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(c)=c^q\), for the \(q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius of \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\), the operator \(F_X\) is semisimple on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) for every \(n\ge0\).
lemma_278.proof:
Throughout put k = \(\overline{\mathbb F}_q\) and \(\sigma:k\to k,\ c\mapsto c^q\), and for a smooth projective \(\mathbb F_q\)-scheme \(Z\) write \(F_Z=(\mathrm{id}_{Z_k}\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma)^*\) for the \(q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius automorphism of \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\). Set
\[
Y \;:=\; C_1\times_{\mathbb F_q}\cdots\times_{\mathbb F_q} C_r ,
\]
so that \(f:Y\to X\) is, by hypothesis, proper, surjective and generically finite.

We record three preliminary facts, prove them, and then assemble the argument.

=== Preliminary fact 1 (finite-dimensionality) ===
For every smooth projective variety \(Z\) over \(\mathbb F_q\) and every \(n\ge 0\), \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) is finite-dimensional over \(\mathbb Q_\ell\). Indeed, take \(K=\mathbb Q_\ell\in D^b_c(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) equipped with its natural arithmetic Frobenius isomorphism \(\psi:F_Z^*\mathbb Q_\ell\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell\); lemma_45_finite_frob (applied with \(\phi=\psi\)) gives finite-dimensionality of \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) and identifies the induced automorphism with the usual \(F_Z\). Thus the phrase "\(F_Z\) is semisimple" is meaningful (each group is a finite-dimensional \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-vector space on which \(F_Z\in\mathrm{GL}\) acts).

=== Preliminary fact 2 (vanishing above twice the dimension) ===
If \(Z\) is smooth projective of pure dimension \(d\) over \(\mathbb F_q\), then \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=0\) for all \(n>2d\).

Proof. By definition \(H^n(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=\bigl(\varprojlim_m H^n(Z_k,\mathbb Z/\ell^m\mathbb Z)\bigr)\otimes_{\mathbb Z_\ell}\mathbb Q_\ell\); it is therefore enough to prove \(H^n(Z_k,\mathbb Z/\ell^m\mathbb Z)=0\) for every \(m\ge 1\) and every \(n>2d\). Fix \(m\) and write \(\Lambda=\mathbb Z/\ell^m\mathbb Z\).

(a) Projective Noether normalization over the arbitrary field \(k\): the homogeneous coordinate ring \(A\) of a closed embedding \(Z_k\hookrightarrow\mathbb P^N_k\) is a finitely generated \(k\)-domain, and the Noether normalization lemma (valid over every field, since it uses only the "standard" prime-avoidance form and not a generic linear change of coordinates) provides homogeneous algebraically independent elements \(x_0,\dots,x_d\in A_+\) such that \(A\) is finite over \(k[x_0,\dots,x_d]\). The corresponding morphism \(\pi:Z_k\to\mathbb P^d_k\) is finite and surjective.

(b) Let \(D_+(x_i)\subset\mathbb P^d_k\) be the \(d+1\) standard affine opens and put \(U_i:=\pi^{-1}(D_+(x_i))\). A finite morphism is affine, so each \(U_i\) is affine; the \(U_i\) cover \(Z_k\); and because \(Z_k\) is separated, the intersection of any subfamily is again affine (an intersection of affine opens inside a separated scheme is affine). Every \(U_I:=\bigcap_{i\in I}U_i\) has dimension \(\le d\).

(c) Artin's vanishing theorem for the étale topos of an affine scheme (SGA 4, Exposé XVII, Th. 5.4): if \(U\) is affine of dimension \(\le d\) over the separably closed field \(k\) and \(\mathcal F\) is a torsion sheaf whose torsion is prime to \(\mathrm{char}(k)=p\), then \(H^n(U,\mathcal F)=0\) for \(n>d\). Since \(\ell\neq p\), the constant sheaf \(\Lambda\) qualifies, so \(H^q(U_I,\Lambda)=0\) for \(q>d\).

(d) The finite open covering \(\{U_0,\dots,U_d\}\) gives the Čech-to-derived spectral sequence (standard: SGA 4, Exposé VIII, Th. 3.1)
\[
E_1^{p,q}=\bigoplus_{\substack{I\subset\{0,\dots,d\}\\ |I|=p+1}} H^q(U_I,\Lambda)\;\Longrightarrow\; H^{p+q}(Z_k,\Lambda),\qquad 0\le p\le d .
\]
By (c) the only possibly non-zero terms have \(0\le q\le d\) and \(0\le p\le d\); hence \(E_1^{p,q}=0\) whenever \(p+q>2d\), and therefore \(H^n(Z_k,\Lambda)=0\) for \(n>2d\). This proves the claim. \(\square\)

=== Preliminary fact 3 (products of geometrically connected smooth projective varieties) ===
If \(V_1,\dots,V_s\) are smooth projective geometrically connected varieties over \(\mathbb F_q\), then \(V_1\times_{\mathbb F_q}\cdots\times_{\mathbb F_q}V_s\) is smooth projective geometrically connected.

Proof. Smoothness and projectivity of the product are standard and immediate. Since each \(V_i\) is smooth and connected over a field, it is regular; a connected locally Noetherian regular scheme is irreducible (regular local rings are domains, so the irreducible components of an open affine are open, and connectedness leaves only one); in particular each \(V_i\) is non-empty and integral.

It suffices to treat \(s=2\), and then to prove: for geometrically connected proper \(k_0\)-schemes \(V,W\) over a field \(k_0\), with \(W\) geometrically reduced, the product \(V\times_{k_0}W\) is connected (geometric connectedness then follows because geometric connectedness is preserved by arbitrary field extension: \((V_{K})_{K'}=V_{K'}\) is connected for every \(K'/k_0\), and similarly for \(W\)).

For a proper scheme \(T\) over a field \(k_0\), the Stein factorization \(T\to\mathrm{Spec}\,\Gamma(T,\mathcal O_T)\to\mathrm{Spec}\,k_0\) exhibits \(\mathrm{Spec}\,\Gamma(T,\mathcal O_T)\) as the finite \(k_0\)-scheme of connected components of \(T\) (the first map is proper with geometrically connected fibres, the second is finite, and \(\Gamma(T,\mathcal O_T)\) is a finite-dimensional \(k_0\)-algebra). Hence \(T\) is connected iff its only idempotents in \(\Gamma(T,\mathcal O_T)\) are \(0,1\).

Because \(V\) and \(W\) are geometrically connected, geometrically reduced and proper over \(k_0\), flat base change to \(\overline{k_0}\) gives \(\Gamma(V_{\overline{k_0}},\mathcal O)\otimes_{k_0}\overline{k_0}\cong\Gamma(V_{\overline{k_0}},\mathcal O)\), and \(\Gamma(V_{\overline{k_0}},\mathcal O)\) is a finite reduced \(\overline{k_0}\)-algebra, i.e. \(\overline{k_0}^{\,\pi_0}\); since \(V_{\overline{k_0}}\) is connected this is \(\overline{k_0}\). Thus \(\Gamma(V,\mathcal O_V)\) is a finite-dimensional \(k_0\)-algebra becoming \(\overline{k_0}\) after the faithfully flat extension \(\overline{k_0}/k_0\), so \(\Gamma(V,\mathcal O_V)=k_0\); likewise \(\Gamma(W,\mathcal O_W)=k_0\).

Now consider \(p:V\times_{k_0}W\to V\). It is proper, flat and of finite presentation, and its fibre over \(v\in V\) is \(W_{\kappa(v)}\), which is connected (indeed geometrically connected, as \(\kappa(v)\) is a field extension of \(k_0\)) and has \(\Gamma(W_{\kappa(v)},\mathcal O)=\kappa(v)\). By cohomology-and-base-change for \(p_*\mathcal O\) (\(h^0\) of the fibres is the constant function \(1\), and \(p\) is proper flat finitely presented), \(p_*\mathcal O\) is locally free of rank \(1\) and the natural map \(\mathcal O_V\to p_*\mathcal O\) is an isomorphism on every fibre, hence an isomorphism. Therefore
\[
\Gamma(V\times_{k_0}W,\mathcal O)=\Gamma(V,p_*\mathcal O)=\Gamma(V,\mathcal O_V)=k_0 ,
\]
so the only idempotents are \(0,1\), and \(V\times_{k_0}W\) is connected by the Stein-factorization criterion above. This proves fact 3. \(\square\)

In particular \(Y=C_1\times\cdots\times C_r\) is smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension \(\sum_i\dim C_i=r\), so it satisfies exactly the same kind of hypotheses as \(X\), and \(f:Y\to X\) is a proper surjective generically finite morphism between smooth projective geometrically connected varieties of the same pure dimension \(D=r\).

=== Step 1: semisimplicity for each curve factor ===
Fix \(i\in\{1,\dots,r\}\). For \(0\le n\le 2\), lemma_260 asserts that \(F_{C_i}\) acts semisimply on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}((C_i)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\). For \(n>2=2\dim C_i\), Preliminary fact 2 gives \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}((C_i)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=0\); the operator \(F_{C_i}\) on the zero space is semisimple (the empty set is a basis of eigenvectors, equivalently the minimal polynomial divides \(t-1\) vacuously). Hence \(F_{C_i}\) is semisimple on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}((C_i)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) for every \(n\ge 0\).

=== Step 2: semisimplicity for the product \(Y\) ===
We argue by induction on \(s\in\{1,\dots,r\}\) that for \(Y_s:=C_1\times\cdots\times C_s\) the operator \(F_{Y_s}\) is semisimple on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}((Y_s)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) for every \(n\ge0\).

Base \(s=1\): this is Step 1 with \(i=1\).

Inductive step: assume the claim for \(s-1\) (\(s\ge 2\)). By Preliminary fact 3, \(Y_{s-1}\) and \(C_s\) are smooth projective geometrically connected over \(\mathbb F_q\), and \(Y_s\cong Y_{s-1}\times_{\mathbb F_q}C_s\). By the induction hypothesis \(F_{Y_{s-1}}\) is semisimple on \(H^r((Y_{s-1})_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) for every \(r\ge0\), and by Step 1 \(F_{C_s}\) is semisimple on \(H^t((C_s)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) for every \(t\ge0\). Lemma_236, applied with \(X=Y_{s-1}\) and \(Y=C_s\), yields that \(F_{Y_s}\) (whose definition \((\mathrm{id}\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma)^*\) is precisely the one supplied by the lemma, since Frobenius on a fibre product is the product of the Frobenii by functoriality of base change) is semisimple on \(H^n((Y_s)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) for every \(n\ge0\). This completes the induction, and with \(s=r\) we obtain:
\[
\text{\(F_Y\) is semisimple on } H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\ \text{ for every } n\ge0. \tag{$\ast$}
\]

=== Step 3: descend semisimplicity along \(f:Y\to X\) ===
We check the hypotheses of lemma_263 for the morphism \(f:Y\to X\) (source \(=Y\), target \(=X\)):
\begin{itemize}
\item \(q=p^a\) is a prime power and \(\ell\neq p\): given.
\item \(Y\) and \(X\) are smooth projective geometrically connected varieties of pure dimension \(D\): for \(X\) this is hypothesis with \(D=r\); for \(Y\) this is Preliminary fact 3 with \(D=\sum_i\dim C_i=r\).
\item \(f\) is proper, surjective and generically finite: given.
\item \(k=\overline{\mathbb F_q}\) and \(F_Z=(\mathrm{id}_{Z_k}\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(c)=c^q\), for \(Z\in\{Y,X\}\): exactly the operators of the statement.
\end{itemize}
Fix \(n\) with \(0\le n\le 2D=2r\). By (\(\ast\)), \(F_Y\) acts semisimply on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\). Lemma_263 then implies that \(F_X\) acts semisimply on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\).

(For the reader's reassurance about the mechanism: lemma_263 is proved from lemma_242, which supplies the correspondence \(e=d^{-1}f^*\circ f_*\) that is an idempotent commuting with Frobenius and whose image is \(\operatorname{im}f^*\cong H^n(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) as a Frobenius module; lemma_237 then gives semisimplicity on the Frobenius-stable direct summand, and lemma_8 transfers it along the Frobenius-equivariant isomorphism. No additional input is needed here.)

=== Step 4: the degrees \(n>2r\) ===
If \(n>2r=2\dim X\), Preliminary fact 2 gives \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=0\). The zero operator on the zero \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-vector space is diagonalizable over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\) (the empty family is a basis consisting of eigenvectors; equivalently, the space is a direct sum of \(0\) eigenspaces), so \(F_X\) is semisimple on it.

=== Conclusion ===
Combining Step 3 (all \(0\le n\le 2r\)) with Step 4 (all \(n>2r\)), the operator \(F_X=(\mathrm{id}\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma)^*\) is semisimple on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) for every \(n\ge0\), which is precisely the assertion of the lemma. \(\blacksquare\)

lemma_279.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(f:X\to Y\) be a smooth projective morphism of smooth projective geometrically connected varieties over \(\mathbb F_q\) whose geometric fibres are connected of pure dimension \(r\ge0\), let \(y\in Y(\mathbb F_q)\) be a rational point and \(A:=f^{-1}(y)\), let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, and for a variety \(Z\) over \(\mathbb F_q\) write \(F_Z=(\mathrm{id}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(c)=c^q\), for the \(q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius of \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\). Let \(\Phi_{p,q}\) denote the automorphism of \(H^p_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,R^qf_*\mathbb Q_\ell)\) induced by the arithmetic Frobenius structure on \(R^qf_*\mathbb Q_\ell\). Suppose (i) \(F_Y\) is semisimple on \(H^p_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) for all \(p\ge0\); (ii) \(F_A\) is semisimple on \(H^q_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(A_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) for all \(q\ge0\); (iii) for all \(p,q\ge0\) there is a \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear isomorphism \(H^p_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,R^qf_*\mathbb Q_\ell)\simeq H^p_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}H^q_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(A_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) carrying \(\Phi_{p,q}\) to \(F_Y\otimes F_A\); and (iv) for every \(n\ge0\) there is an \(F_X\)-equivariant \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear isomorphism \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\simeq\bigoplus_{p+q=n}H^p_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,R^qf_*\mathbb Q_\ell)\), the summands carrying \(\Phi_{p,q}\). Then \(F_X\) is semisimple on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) for every \(n\ge0\).
lemma_279.proof:
Throughout, k = \overline{\mathbb F}_q and \sigma:k\to k, \sigma(c)=c^q; for a variety Z over \mathbb F_q we write F_Z=(\mathrm{id}_{Z_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^* for the q-power arithmetic Frobenius acting on H^m_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell). We abbreviate
  W_p := H^p_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell),  U_q := H^q_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(A_k,\mathbb Q_\ell),  V_{p,q} := H^p_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,R^qf_*\mathbb Q_\ell).
Note at the outset which properties of the operators \Phi_{p,q} the argument actually consumes: only (a) that each V_{p,q} is finite-dimensional over \mathbb Q_\ell and (b) that each \Phi_{p,q} is a \mathbb Q_\ell-linear AUTOMORPHISM of V_{p,q}. Both are formal consequences of hypothesis (iii) together with the constant-coefficient facts for Y and A proved in Step 1b below; no other property of \Phi_{p,q} (in particular no construction of the arithmetic Frobenius structure on R^qf_*\mathbb Q_\ell, and no naturality statement for it) is used anywhere.

STEP 1a (the fibre A is an \mathbb F_q-variety of the same kind as X and Y). The rational point y gives a section of the structure morphism i:\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_q\to Y. By definition A:=f^{-1}(y)=X\times_{Y,\,i}\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_q is the scheme-theoretic fibre of f over y. Since f is a smooth (resp. projective) morphism, base change along i shows that A\to\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_q is smooth (resp. projective); in particular A is smooth, proper (hence a proper variety) and of finite type over \mathbb F_q. Because y is \mathbb F_q-rational, the residue field \kappa(y) equals \mathbb F_q, so for a geometric geometric point \bar y over y the geometric fibre of f at \bar y is
  X_{\bar y}=X\times_{Y}\operatorname{Spec}\overline{\kappa(y)}=X\times_{Y}\operatorname{Spec}k = A\times_{\mathbb F_q}k = A_k.
By hypothesis the geometric fibres of f are connected and of pure dimension r; hence A_k is connected and of pure dimension r. A scheme of finite type over a field whose geometric fibre is connected is geometrically connected, so A is smooth projective geometrically connected over \mathbb F_q (of pure dimension r; the case r=0 gives A=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_q, which is harmless and is treated by the same argument). Thus X, Y and A are all proper varieties over the SAME ground field \mathbb F_q, and the operator F_A=(\mathrm{id}_{A_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^* is defined by exactly the same convention as F_X and F_Y. No extension \mathbb F_{q^m} is introduced anywhere in this proof.

STEP 1b (finite-dimensionality and invertibility of F_X, F_Y, F_A). For Z\in\{X,Y,A\}, Z is proper over \mathbb F_q and of finite type over the separably closed field k, so the constant sheaf \mathbb Q_\ell is an object of D^b_c(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell); it carries its natural arithmetic Frobenius isomorphism \psi:(F_Z^{\mathrm{sch}})^*\mathbb Q_\ell\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell, where F_Z^{\mathrm{sch}} is the q-power arithmetic Frobenius morphism of Z_k. Applying lemma_45_finite_frob (eoinm) over \mathbb F_q to the proper \mathbb F_q-scheme Z with K=\mathbb Q_\ell and \phi=\psi, we obtain that H^m_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) is finite-dimensional over \mathbb Q_\ell for every m\ge 0. Applying lemma_6a (eoinm) to the same Z and \sigma(c)=c^q, the two pullbacks
  F_Z=(\mathrm{id}_{Z_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*,  \qquad G_Z:=(\mathrm{id}_{Z_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma^{-1})^*\nare mutually inverse \mathbb Q_\ell-linear automorphisms of H^m_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) (finite-dimensionality having just been established). Hence, recording what we shall need:
  F_X\in\mathrm{GL}(H^n(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)) for every n\ge0,   F_Y|_{W_p}\in\mathrm{GL}(W_p) for every p\ge0,   F_A|_{U_q}\in\mathrm{GL}(U_q) for every q\ge0,\nwith W_p and U_q finite-dimensional. (We also note, for later reference, that the hypotheses of lemma_8 and lemma_225 require exactly this invertibility, and it is now on record.)

STEP 2 (the tensor-product operator is semisimple). Fix p,q\ge0 and set
  \Theta_{p,q}:=F_Y|_{W_p}\ \otimes\ F_A|_{U_q}\ \in\ \mathrm{GL}(W_p\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}U_q).
This is a well-defined automorphism: the tensor product of two \mathbb Q_\ell-linear automorphisms is an automorphism, and W_p\otimes U_q is finite-dimensional with \dim(W_p\otimes U_q)=\dim W_p\cdot\dim U_q<\infty. By hypothesis (i), F_Y is semisimple on W_p; by hypothesis (ii), F_A is semisimple on U_q. By lemma_5 (eoinm), applied to the finite-dimensional spaces W_p and U_q, semisimplicity over \mathbb Q_\ell is equivalent to diagonalisability of the base change to \overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell; hence (F_Y|_{W_p})_{\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell} and (F_A|_{U_q})_{\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell} are diagonalisable. Lemma_225 (eoinm), applied to the \mathbb Q_\ell-vector spaces W_p, U_q and the automorphisms F_Y|_{W_p}, F_A|_{U_q} whose base changes to \overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell are diagonalisable, gives that (\Theta_{p,q})_{\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell}= (F_Y|_{W_p})_{\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell}\otimes (F_A|_{U_q})_{\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell} is diagonalisable over \overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell. Applying lemma_5 again in the converse direction (W_p\otimes U_q is finite-dimensional by Step 1b) we conclude:
  (2.1) \Theta_{p,q}\in\mathrm{GL}(W_p\otimes U_q) is semisimple.

STEP 3 (each Leray piece V_{p,q} carries a semisimple automorphism \Phi_{p,q}; finite-dimensionality and invertibility). Fix p,q\ge0. Hypothesis (iii) supplies a \mathbb Q_\ell-linear isomorphism
  \beta_{p,q}:V_{p,q}\ \xrightarrow{\sim}\ W_p\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}U_q  \qquad\text{with}\qquad \beta_{p,q}\circ\Phi_{p,q}=\Theta_{p,q}\circ\beta_{p,q},\nwhere \Theta_{p,q} is the operator of Step 2. Two formal consequences, which replace any sheaf-theoretic finiteness argument:
  (3.1) V_{p,q} is finite-dimensional over \mathbb Q_\ell, since it is \mathbb Q_\ell-linearly isomorphic to W_p\otimes U_q, which is finite-dimensional by Step 1b;
  (3.2) \Phi_{p,q}=\beta_{p,q}^{-1}\circ\Theta_{p,q}\circ\beta_{p,q}\in\mathrm{GL}(V_{p,q}), since it is the conjugate of the automorphism \Theta_{p,q} by the isomorphism \beta_{p,q}.
Now \beta_{p,q} is an intertwining isomorphism between the automorphism \Phi_{p,q} of the finite-dimensional space V_{p,q} (by (3.1)) and the automorphism \Theta_{p,q} of W_p\otimes U_q (by (3.2) and Step 2). All hypotheses of lemma_8 (eoinm) are therefore satisfied, and lemma_8 together with (2.1) yields
  (3.3) \Phi_{p,q}\ \text{is semisimple on}\ V_{p,q}.

STEP 4 (the direct sum of the Leray pieces). Fix n\ge0 and let I_n:=\{(p,q)\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^2:p+q=n\}; this set has exactly n+1 elements, so the family \{(V_{p,q},\Phi_{p,q})\}_{(p,q)\in I_n} is a finite family of finite-dimensional \mathbb Q_\ell-vector spaces (3.1) equipped with invertible \mathbb Q_\ell-linear operators (3.2), each semisimple by (3.3). Put
  \Sigma_n:=\bigoplus_{(p,q)\in I_n}V_{p,q},\qquad \Phi_n:=\bigoplus_{(p,q)\in I_n}\Phi_{p,q}.
Then \Sigma_n is finite-dimensional, \Phi_n\in\mathrm{GL}(\Sigma_n) (a block-diagonal automorphism), and by lemma_9 (eoinm), applied to the finite family \{(V_{p,q},\Phi_{p,q})\}_{(p,q)\in I_n}, the block-diagonal operator \Phi_n is semisimple on \Sigma_n.

STEP 5 (transfer to X). Hypothesis (iv) supplies an F_X-equivariant \mathbb Q_\ell-linear isomorphism
  \alpha:H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\ \xrightarrow{\sim}\ \Sigma_n=\bigoplus_{p+q=n}H^p_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,R^qf_*\mathbb Q_\ell)\nunder which the summands carry \Phi_{p,q}; i.e. \alpha is an isomorphism of \mathbb Q_\ell-vector spaces satisfying
  \alpha\circ F_X=\Phi_n\circ\alpha .
(The left-hand operator F_X is the one of Step 1b; the right-hand operator is the block-diagonal operator of Step 4, whose blocks are the \Phi_{p,q} by (iv).) By Step 1b, F_X is an automorphism of the finite-dimensional space H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell); by Step 4, \Phi_n is an automorphism of the finite-dimensional space \Sigma_n and is semisimple. Hence all hypotheses of lemma_8 (eoinm) hold for \alpha, and lemma_8 gives that F_X is semisimple on H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell).

STEP 6 (conclusion). The integer n\ge0 was arbitrary, and in Steps 2-5 the only uses of p and q were through hypotheses (i)-(iii) for that fixed n, which hold for all p,q\ge0 by assumption. Therefore F_X=(\mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^* is semisimple on H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) for every n\ge0, which is exactly the required conclusion.

REMARKS ON THE USE OF HYPOTHESES. Hypotheses (iii) and (iv) are used exactly as stated and are not reproved. As announced, the only properties of the operators \Phi_{p,q} entering Steps 3-5 are the finite-dimensionality of V_{p,q} and the invertibility of \Phi_{p,q}, both obtained in (3.1)-(3.2) from (iii); in particular no naturality of \Phi_{p,q} with respect to pullback maps, and no comparison between the Frobenius structure on R^qf_*\mathbb Q_\ell and any Ext-realisation of the cohomological operator, is asserted or needed.

lemma_283.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(X\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension \(d\ge1\) over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(Y\subset X\) be an effective ample divisor defined over \(\mathbb F_q\) and smooth of pure dimension \(d-1\), let \(U=X\setminus Y\) with open immersion \(j:U\hookrightarrow X\) and closed immersion \(i:Y\hookrightarrow X\), let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\) and \(\ell\neq p\) prime. Then there is a long exact sequence of finite-dimensional \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-vector spaces \(\cdots\to H^n_c(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{i^*}H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{n+1}_c(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to\cdots\) whose middle map is the pullback \(i^*\), and in which every map commutes with the \(q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius automorphisms of the four terms.
lemma_283.proof:
PROOF. Fix $q=p^a$, $k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q$, $\sigma:k\to k$, $\sigma(c)=c^q$, and $\ell\neq p$. For an $\mathbb F_q$-scheme $Z$ of finite type write $Z_k:=Z\times_{\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_q}\operatorname{Spec}k$, let $\mathsf F_Z:=\operatorname{id}_Z\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma:Z_k\to Z_k$ be the $q$-power arithmetic Frobenius morphism, and write $F_Z:=\mathsf F_Z^{*}$ for the induced pullback on étale sheaves and on cohomology. The maps $i:Y\hookrightarrow X$ and $j:U\hookrightarrow X$ are defined over $\mathbb F_q$, and after base change to $k$ we write $i_k,j_k$ for the induced closed and open immersions.

STEP 0 (The Frobenius morphism is an isomorphism, and the two squares are cartesian).
(a) $\mathsf F_Z$ is an isomorphism of schemes with inverse $\operatorname{id}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma^{-1}$: on an affine open $\operatorname{Spec}B$ with $B$ an $\mathbb F_q$-algebra it is induced by the ring automorphism $B\otimes_{\mathbb F_q}k\to B\otimes_{\mathbb F_q}k$, $b\otimes c\mapsto b\otimes c^q$ (inverse uses $\sigma^{-1}$). Hence inverse image $\mathsf F_Z^{*}$ is an exact autoequivalence of the abelian category of étale sheaves of $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector spaces on $Z_k$. By lemma_6a the induced maps $F_Z$ on $H^i_{\text{ét}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ (for $Z=X,Y$) are invertible $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear operators.
(b) Since $Y$ (hence also $U$) is defined over $\mathbb F_q$, $\mathsf F_X$ carries $Y_k$ onto $Y_k$ and $U_k$ onto $U_k$, and $\mathsf F_X\circ i_k=i_k\circ\mathsf F_Y$, $\mathsf F_X\circ j_k=j_k\circ\mathsf F_U$. Scheme-theoretically: locally $X=\operatorname{Spec}A$ with $Y=V(I)$, $I\triangleleft A$; the inverse image of $I\cdot(A\otimes_{\mathbb F_q}k)$ under $a\otimes c\mapsto a\otimes c^q$ equals $I\cdot(A\otimes k)$, because if $\sum_i a_i\otimes c_i^{\,q}\in I(A\otimes k)$ then $\sum_i a_i\otimes c_i=\sum_i a_i\otimes(\sigma^{-1}(c_i))^{q}\in I(A\otimes k)$, using that $\sigma$ is an automorphism fixing $\mathbb F_q$. Thus the scheme-theoretic inverse image of $Y_k$ (resp. $U_k$) under $\mathsf F_X$ is $Y_k$ (resp. $U_k$), so both squares
  $U_k\xrightarrow{j_k}X_k$, $\ \downarrow\mathsf F_U\ \ \downarrow\mathsf F_X$; and $Y_k\xrightarrow{i_k}X_k$, $\ \downarrow\mathsf F_Y\ \ \downarrow\mathsf F_X$
are cartesian.

STEP 1 (Sheaves with Frobenius structure).
Let $\operatorname{Sh}(X_k)$ be the abelian category of étale sheaves of $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector spaces on $X_k$ and put $T:=\mathsf F_X^{*}$. An $F$-structure on $\mathcal G\in\operatorname{Sh}(X_k)$ is an isomorphism $\varphi:T\mathcal G\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathcal G$; since $T$ is an exact autoequivalence, the category of such pairs is abelian (kernels and cokernels are taken in $\operatorname{Sh}(X_k)$ and inherit the induced structure).
Because $T$ is an equivalence of abelian categories it preserves injectives: $\operatorname{Hom}(-,TI)\cong\operatorname{Hom}(T^{-1}(-),I)$ is exact in $-$ since $T^{-1}$ is exact and $I$ is injective. Hence for an injective resolution $\mathcal G\to\mathcal I^\bullet$, $T\mathcal G\to T\mathcal I^\bullet$ is an injective resolution, and applying $T$ degreewise gives a canonical isomorphism $T^{*}:H^n(X_k,\mathcal G)\xrightarrow{\sim}H^n(X_k,T\mathcal G)$. For $\varphi:T\mathcal G\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathcal G$ we define the Frobenius automorphism $F_\varphi:=H^n(\varphi)\circ T^{*}$ of $H^n(X_k,\mathcal G)$.
This agrees with the canonical automorphism $F_\phi$ supplied by lemma_45_finite_frob: under $H^n(X_k,K)=\operatorname{Ext}^n(\underline{\mathbb Q_\ell},K)$ that lemma sends $u$ to $\phi\circ\mathsf F_X^{*}(u)\circ\psi^{-1}$, whereas $H^n(\phi)\circ T^{*}$ sends $u$ to $\phi\circ\mathsf F_X^{*}(u)$ with source $\mathsf F_X^{*}\underline{\mathbb Q_\ell}$ identified with $\underline{\mathbb Q_\ell}$ through $\psi$; the two prescriptions are the same.

Define $j_!\underline{\mathbb Z_\ell}:=\varprojlim_m j_!\underline{\mathbb Z/\ell^m}$ and $j_!\mathbb Q_\ell:=(j_!\underline{\mathbb Z_\ell})\otimes_{\mathbb Z_\ell}\mathbb Q_\ell$. For an open immersion, extension by zero $j_!$ is exact and is characterised on geometric stalks by $(j_!\mathcal F)_{\bar x}=\mathcal F_{\bar x}$ for $\bar x\in U_k$ and $(j_!\mathcal F)_{\bar x}=0$ for $\bar x\in Y_k$; exactness then follows by checking stalks. In particular $j_!\mathbb Q_\ell$ is a sheaf concentrated in degree $0$ with these stalks.

We put $F$-structures on the three sheaves as follows.
(1) $\psi_X:T\underline{\mathbb Q_\ell}\xrightarrow{\sim}\underline{\mathbb Q_\ell}$, and similarly $\psi_Y:\mathsf F_Y^{*}\underline{\mathbb Q_\ell}\xrightarrow{\sim}\underline{\mathbb Q_\ell}$, $\psi_U:\mathsf F_U^{*}\underline{\mathbb Q_\ell}\xrightarrow{\sim}\underline{\mathbb Q_\ell}$, are the canonical isomorphisms: inverse image preserves the terminal sheaf, finite products and colimits, so $f^{-1}\underline{A}=\underline A$ for any morphism of topoi, and the resulting isomorphism of constant sheaves is the identity on every geometric stalk.
(2) For $j_!\mathbb Q_\ell$: the cartesian square of Step 0(b) gives a base-change isomorphism $\mathrm{bc}_j:Tj_!\mathbb Q_\ell=\mathsf F_X^{-1}j_!\mathbb Q_\ell\xrightarrow{\sim}j_!\mathsf F_U^{-1}\mathbb Q_\ell=j_!\mathsf F_U^{*}\mathbb Q_\ell$. Indeed, at a geometric point $\bar x\in X_k$ the left side has stalk $(j_!\mathbb Q_\ell)_{\overline{\mathsf F_X(\bar x)}}$, which is $\mathbb Q_\ell$ if $\mathsf F_X(\bar x)\in U_k$ and $0$ otherwise, while the right side has stalk $(\mathsf F_U^{*}\mathbb Q_\ell)_{\bar x'}=\mathbb Q_\ell$ if $\bar x\in U_k$ (i.e. $\bar x$ lifts to $U_k$) and $0$ otherwise; since $\mathsf F_X^{-1}(U_k)=U_k$ these conditions coincide and the canonical map is an isomorphism. Set $\phi_{j_!}:=j_!(\psi_U)\circ\mathrm{bc}_j:Tj_!\mathbb Q_\ell\xrightarrow{\sim}j_!\mathbb Q_\ell$.
(3) For $i_*\mathbb Q_\ell$: the cartesian square gives $\mathrm{bc}_i:Ti_*\mathbb Q_\ell\xrightarrow{\sim}i_*\mathsf F_Y^{*}\mathbb Q_\ell$, checked on stalks identically ($(i_*\mathcal G)_{\bar x}=\mathcal G_{\bar x}$ for $\bar x\in Y_k$, $0$ otherwise), and we set $\phi_{i_*}:=i_*(\psi_Y)\circ\mathrm{bc}_i$.

STEP 2 (Short exact sequence in the category of sheaves with $F$-structure).
The canonical maps give a sequence of sheaves
  $0\to j_!\mathbb Q_\ell\xrightarrow{\mathrm{can}}\underline{\mathbb Q_\ell}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{can}}i_*\mathbb Q_\ell\to0$.
Exactness is checked on geometric stalks: at $\bar x\in U_k$ it reads $0\to\mathbb Q_\ell\xrightarrow{\mathrm{id}}\mathbb Q_\ell\to0\to0$; at $\bar y\in Y_k$ it reads $0\to0\to\mathbb Q_\ell\xrightarrow{\mathrm{id}}\mathbb Q_\ell\to0$, where the middle stalk map is the identity because $i^{-1}i_*=\mathrm{id}$ and the adjunction map $\underline{\mathbb Q_\ell}\to i_*i^{-1}\underline{\mathbb Q_\ell}=i_*\mathbb Q_\ell$ has stalk $\mathrm{id}$ at points of $Y_k$. So the sequence is exact.
It is a short exact sequence in the abelian category of sheaves with $F$-structure, i.e. the two squares
  $Tj_!\mathbb Q_\ell\to T\underline{\mathbb Q_\ell}$, down-maps $\phi_{j_!},\psi_X$, bottom $\mathrm{can}$; and $T\underline{\mathbb Q_\ell}\to Ti_*\mathbb Q_\ell$, down-maps $\psi_X,\phi_{i_*}$, bottom $\mathrm{can}$,
commute. Stalkwise: if $\bar x\in U_k$ then $\mathsf F_X(\bar x)\in U_k$, all four stalks involved in the first square are $\mathbb Q_\ell$, and every map in it is the identity on stalks (each $\psi$ is the identity on stalks, $\mathrm{can}$ is the identity on stalks over $U_k$, and $\phi_{j_!}$ is $\psi_U$ composed with the stalk identification, hence also the identity); so both composites are $\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}$. If $\bar y\in Y_k$ then $(j_!\mathbb Q_\ell)_{\bar y}=0$ and $(Tj_!\mathbb Q_\ell)_{\bar y}=(j_!\mathbb Q_\ell)_{\overline{\mathsf F_X(\bar y)}}=0$ (as $\mathsf F_X(\bar y)\in Y_k$), so both composites are the zero map $0\to\mathbb Q_\ell$. For the second square, at $\bar y\in Y_k$ all four stalks are $\mathbb Q_\ell$ and all maps are identities, and at $\bar x\notin Y_k$ both $(i_*\mathbb Q_\ell)_{\bar x}$ and $(Ti_*\mathbb Q_\ell)_{\bar x}=(i_*\mathbb Q_\ell)_{\overline{\mathsf F_X(\bar x)}}$ vanish (as $\mathsf F_X(\bar x)\notin Y_k$), so both composites are the zero map $\mathbb Q_\ell\to0$. Hence both squares commute.

STEP 3 (Constructibility and finite-dimensionality).
For each $m\ge1$ the sheaf $j_!\underline{\mathbb Z/\ell^m}$ is constructible on $X_k$: by the closed/open dévissage criterion for constructible sheaves on a noetherian scheme (a sheaf of finite abelian groups on a noetherian scheme is constructible iff its pullbacks to a closed subscheme and to the complementary open are constructible), it suffices that $j^{*}j_!\underline{\mathbb Z/\ell^m}=\underline{\mathbb Z/\ell^m}$ on $U_k$ (constructible, $U_k$ noetherian) and $i^{*}j_!\underline{\mathbb Z/\ell^m}=0$ on $Y_k$ (constructible). Consequently $j_!\mathbb Q_\ell$ has constructible $\ell$-power-torsion reductions, so $j_!\mathbb Q_\ell\in D^b_c(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$, concentrated in degree $0$.
Since $X$ is projective, and $Y$ is a closed subscheme of $X$ hence projective, both are proper over $\mathbb F_q$; $U$ is of finite type. Applying lemma_45_finite_frob three times:
 - with $Z=X$, $K=\underline{\mathbb Q_\ell}$, $\phi=\psi_X$: $\dim_{\mathbb Q_\ell}H^n_{\text{ét}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)<\infty$;
 - with $Z=Y$, $K=\underline{\mathbb Q_\ell}$, $\phi=\psi_Y$: $\dim_{\mathbb Q_\ell}H^n_{\text{ét}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)<\infty$;
 - with $Z=X$, $K=j_!\mathbb Q_\ell$, $\phi=\phi_{j_!}$: $\dim_{\mathbb Q_\ell}H^n(X_k,j_!\mathbb Q_\ell)<\infty$.
Thus all four terms of the desired sequence are finite-dimensional $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector spaces.

STEP 4 (The long exact sequence, and identification of the terms).
Applying the cohomological functor $R\Gamma(X_k,-)$ to the short exact sequence of Step 2 (viewed in $\operatorname{Sh}(X_k)$) yields the long exact sequence
 $\cdots\to H^n(X_k,j_!\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^n(X_k,\underline{\mathbb Q_\ell})\to H^n(X_k,i_*\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\delta_n}H^{n+1}(X_k,j_!\mathbb Q_\ell)\to\cdots$ .
We identify the three terms.
(i) $H^n(X_k,i_*\mathbb Q_\ell)\cong H^n(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$: a closed immersion is affine, so $i_*$ is exact on étale sheaves, and $i^{-1}i_*=\mathrm{id}$ (the small étale site of $Y_k$ identifies with the category of étale $X_k$-schemes factoring through $Y_k$); hence $\Gamma(X_k,i_*\mathcal G)=\Gamma(Y_k,\mathcal G)$ functorially and, $i_*$ being exact and preserving injectives (it has the exact left adjoint $i^{-1}$ and is fully faithful), $R\Gamma(X_k,i_*\mathcal G)=R\Gamma(Y_k,\mathcal G)$.
(ii) $H^n(X_k,j_!\mathbb Q_\ell)=:H^n_c(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$: this is the definition of compactly supported cohomology using the compactification $X$ of $U$; it is independent of the compactification (any two compactifications $\bar U,\bar U'$ are dominated by the closure of $U$ in $\bar U\times_{\mathbb F_q}\bar U'$, and the resulting identifications are compatible).
(iii) Under (i), the map $H^n(X_k,\underline{\mathbb Q_\ell})\to H^n(X_k,i_*\mathbb Q_\ell)$ induced by $\mathrm{can}$ is the pullback $i^{*}$. Indeed, for any morphism $f:Z\to W$ and any sheaf $\mathcal G$ on $W$, the map $R\Gamma(W,\mathcal G)\to R\Gamma(Z,f^{-1}\mathcal G)$ induced by the adjunction map $\mathcal G\to f_*f^{-1}\mathcal G$ is, by definition, the pullback $f^{*}$; here $i^{-1}\underline{\mathbb Q_\ell}=\underline{\mathbb Q_\ell}$ and $\mathrm{can}$ corresponds to $\mathrm{id}$ under the adjunction bijection $\operatorname{Hom}(\underline{\mathbb Q_\ell},i_*\mathbb Q_\ell)\cong\operatorname{Hom}(i^{-1}\underline{\mathbb Q_\ell},\mathbb Q_\ell)$. So the middle map of the sequence is exactly $i^{*}$, as required.

STEP 5 (The Frobenius automorphisms on $H^n_c(U_k)$ and $H^n(Y_k)$).
We check that the structures of Step 1 give the standard arithmetic Frobenius on these two groups.
(a) $H^n_c(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$: the pullback on compactly supported cohomology for a morphism $f:(\bar V,j_V)\to(\bar W,j_W)$ of compactified $\mathbb F_q$-schemes is defined by the canonical morphism of sheaves $\bar f^{-1}j_{W,!}\mathcal F\to j_{V,!}f^{-1}\mathcal F$ (on stalks: the identity over $V$, the zero map off $V$), applied to $\mathcal F=\mathbb Q_\ell$; this yields $f^{*}:H^n_c(W_k)\to H^n_c(V_k)$. Taking $\bar f=\mathsf F_X$ and $f=\mathsf F_U$ (valid since $\mathsf F_X\circ j_k=j_k\circ\mathsf F_U$), this canonical morphism is precisely $\phi_{j_!}=j_!(\psi_U)\circ\mathrm{bc}_j$. Hence $F_{\phi_{j_!}}$ on $H^n(X_k,j_!\mathbb Q_\ell)=H^n_c(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ is exactly the pullback along the $q$-power Frobenius morphism $\mathsf F_U:U_k\to U_k$, i.e. the $q$-power arithmetic Frobenius automorphism of $H^n_c(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$; it is an automorphism because $\mathsf F_U$ is an isomorphism of schemes (Step 0(a)), equivalently because $\phi_{j_!}$ is an isomorphism of sheaves.
(b) $H^n(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$: the isomorphism of (i) identifies $F_{\phi_{i_*}}$ on $H^n(X_k,i_*\mathbb Q_\ell)$ with the automorphism of $H^n(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ induced by $\psi_Y:\mathsf F_Y^{*}\underline{\mathbb Q_\ell}\to\underline{\mathbb Q_\ell}$, because $\phi_{i_*}=i_*(\psi_Y)\circ\mathrm{bc}_i$ and $\mathrm{bc}_i$ is exactly the comparison used in the identification $R\Gamma(X_k,i_*\mathsf F_Y^{*}\mathcal G)=R\Gamma(Y_k,\mathsf F_Y^{*}\mathcal G)$. By the description in Step 1 this automorphism is $F_Y=(\mathrm{id}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^{*}$.

STEP 6 (Equivariance of the three maps).
We use the notation $F_{\psi_X},F_{\phi_{j_!}},F_{\phi_{i_*}}$ of Step 1, which by Steps 5 and (1) are the arithmetic Frobenius operators $F_X,F_{U,c},F_Y$.
(a) The middle map $\beta_n=i^{*}:H^n(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^n(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ commutes with Frobenius by lemma_214 applied to the morphism $i:Y\to X$ of schemes of finite type over $\mathbb F_q$: $i_k^{*}\circ F_X=F_Y\circ i_k^{*}$.
(b) The map $\alpha_n:H^n_c(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^n(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$, induced by $\mathrm{can}:j_!\mathbb Q_\ell\to\underline{\mathbb Q_\ell}$, commutes with Frobenius:
 $F_{\psi_X}\circ H^n(\mathrm{can})=H^n(\psi_X)\circ T^{*}\circ H^n(\mathrm{can})=H^n(\psi_X)\circ H^n(\mathrm{can})\circ T^{*}=H^n(\mathrm{can})\circ H^n(\phi_{j_!})\circ T^{*}=H^n(\mathrm{can})\circ F_{\phi_{j_!}}$,
where the middle equality is functoriality of $T^{*}$ (applying the exact functor $T$ to the chain map $\mathrm{can}$) and the second equality is the commutativity of the first square of Step 2.
(c) The connecting homomorphism $\delta_n$. Two standard properties of the derived-functor long exact sequence are needed, both immediate from the injective-resolution/snake-lemma construction: (N1) naturality in the short exact sequence: a morphism of short exact sequences $0\to A\to B\to C\to0\to0\to A'\to B'\to C'\to0$ induces $\delta'\circ H^n(f_C)=H^{n+1}(f_A)\circ\delta$; (N2) compatibility with an exact autoequivalence preserving injectives: if $\delta'$ is the connecting map of $0\to TA\to TB\to TC\to0$ then $\delta'\circ T^{*}_C=T^{*}_A\circ\delta$. Concretely, choosing a short exact sequence of injective resolutions $0\to K^\bullet\to J^\bullet\to I^\bullet\to0$ of $0\to A\to B\to C\to0$, $\delta$ is represented on cochains by "lift a cocycle $z\in I^n$ to $y\in J^n$ and take $dy\in K^{n+1}$"; applying $T$ degreewise gives the same formula for $\delta'$ (and $T I^\bullet,T J^\bullet,T K^\bullet$ are injective resolutions since $T$ preserves injectives), and a morphism of short exact sequences lifts to a morphism of such diagrams commuting with the same formula. Taking $A=j_!\mathbb Q_\ell$, $B=\underline{\mathbb Q_\ell}$, $C=i_*\mathbb Q_\ell$ and applying (N1) to the morphism $(\phi_{j_!},\psi_X,\phi_{i_*})$ from $0\to TA\to TB\to TC\to0$ to $0\to A\to B\to C\to0$ (a morphism of short exact sequences by Step 2), then (N2), gives
 $\delta_n\circ F_{\phi_{i_*}}=\delta_n\circ H^n(\phi_{i_*})\circ T^{*}=H^{n+1}(\phi_{j_!})\circ\delta'_n\circ T^{*}=H^{n+1}(\phi_{j_!})\circ T^{*}\circ\delta_n=F_{\phi_{j_!}}\circ\delta_n$,
which is precisely the claimed commutativity $\delta_n\circ F_Y=F_{U,c}\circ\delta_n$.
Since the sequence is the $n$-periodic concatenation of $\alpha_n,\beta_n,\delta_n$, all its maps commute with the Frobenius automorphisms of the four terms.

STEP 7 (Edge cases and unused hypotheses).
For $n<0$ all four groups are $0$ by convention, and the corresponding pieces of the sequence are trivially exact and equivariant. If $Y=\varnothing$ (which cannot occur here: $d\ge1$ and $Y$ ample effective would force $X=U$ both affine and projective, hence finite over $\mathbb F_q$), the same proof applies verbatim with $i_*\mathbb Q_\ell=0$ and $j_!\mathbb Q_\ell=\underline{\mathbb Q_\ell}$, and the sequence degenerates to the identity maps. The hypotheses that $X$ is geometrically connected, that $Y$ is smooth of pure dimension $d-1$, and that $Y$ is ample are not used in this lemma; only that $Y\subset X$ is a closed subscheme defined over $\mathbb F_q$ (which gives properness of $Y$, needed for finite-dimensionality, and the cartesian Frobenius squares of Step 0).

Assembling Steps 3, 4, 5 and 6 gives the asserted long exact sequence of finite-dimensional $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector spaces with middle map $i^{*}$, in which every map commutes with the $q$-power arithmetic Frobenius automorphisms. $\blacksquare$

lemma_288.statement: Let \(k\) be an algebraically closed field, let \(\ell\) be a prime different from the characteristic of \(k\), let \(U\) be an affine scheme of finite type over \(k\) of Krull dimension \(n\), and let \(K\) be an object of the derived category \(D^b_c(U_{\mathrm{\acute et}},\mathbb Q_\ell)\) of constructible \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-complexes on the \(\mathrm{\acute etale}\) site of \(U\) whose cohomology sheaves satisfy \(\mathcal H^q(K)=0\) for \(q>0\). Then \(H^q(R\Gamma(U_{\mathrm{\acute et}},K))=0\) for every integer \(q>n\).
lemma_288.proof:
Proof. We write \(H^q(U,\mathcal F)\) for \(H^q(R\Gamma(U_{\acute et},\mathcal F))\).

If \(U\) is empty, then \(R\Gamma(U,K)=0\) and the assertion is trivial. Assume \(U\) is non-empty.

1. Artin vanishing for constructible \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-sheaves. We use the standard Artin vanishing theorem (SGA 4, Expose XVI, Theoreme 3.7, together with the usual \(\ell\)-adic formalism). Theorem (AV). Let \(k_0\) be a separably closed field, let \(X\) be an affine noetherian scheme of finite type over \(k_0\) of Krull dimension \(d\), and let \(\ell\) be a prime different from \(\operatorname{char}(k_0)\). If \(\mathcal F\) is a constructible \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-sheaf on \(X_{\acute et}\), then \(H^q(X_{\acute et},\mathcal F)=0\) for all \(q>d\).

For completeness, if one starts from the torsion version for constructible \(\mathbb Z/m\mathbb Z\)-sheaves with \(m\) invertible on \(k_0\), the \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-version follows by choosing a constructible \(\mathbb Z_\ell\)-lattice \(L\) in \(\mathcal F\), using \(R\Gamma(X,\mathcal F)\simeq R\Gamma(X,L)\otimes^L_{\mathbb Z_\ell}\mathbb Q_\ell\), applying torsion Artin vanishing to \(L/\ell^mL\), and using the finiteness theorem for constructible torsion sheaves to make the Milnor sequence \(0\to R^1\varprojlim_m H^{q-1}(X,L/\ell^mL)\to H^q(X,L)\to \varprojlim_m H^q(X,L/\ell^mL)\to 0\) have vanishing derived-limit term. This standard input is the only geometric fact used below.

Now verify the hypotheses: \(k\) is algebraically closed, hence separably closed; \(U\) is affine of finite type over \(k\), hence affine noetherian of finite type over a separably closed field; and \(\ell\neq\operatorname{char}(k)\). For every integer \(r\), \(\mathcal H^r(K)\) is a constructible \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-sheaf because \(K\in D^b_c(U_{\acute et},\mathbb Q_\ell)\). Therefore AV gives
\[
H^q(U,\mathcal H^r(K))=0\quad\text{for all }q>n.
\]

2. Devissage from complexes to sheaves. Since \(K\) is bounded, there exists an integer \(a\) such that \(\mathcal H^q(K)=0\) for \(q<a\). The hypothesis \(\mathcal H^q(K)=0\) for \(q>0\) allows us to choose \(a\le 0\). If \(K=0\), the conclusion is immediate. For \(r\in\mathbb Z\), put \(K_r=\tau^{\le r}K\). Then \(K_r\in D^b_c(U_{\acute et},\mathbb Q_\ell)\), \(K_{a-1}=0\), and \(K_0=K\).

For each \(r\) there is a canonical truncation triangle
\[
K_{r-1}\longrightarrow K_r\longrightarrow (\mathcal H^r K)[-r]\longrightarrow K_{r-1}[1].
\]
Applying the triangulated functor \(R\Gamma(U,-)\) gives a triangle
\[
R\Gamma(U,K_{r-1})\longrightarrow R\Gamma(U,K_r)\longrightarrow R\Gamma(U,(\mathcal H^rK)[-r])\longrightarrow R\Gamma(U,K_{r-1})[1].
\]
Its long exact cohomology sequence contains
\[
H^m(R\Gamma(U,K_{r-1}))\to H^m(R\Gamma(U,K_r))\to H^m(R\Gamma(U,(\mathcal H^rK)[-r]))\to H^{m+1}(R\Gamma(U,K_{r-1})).
\]

We prove by induction on \(r\) from \(a\) to \(0\) that
\[
P(r):\quad H^m(R\Gamma(U,K_r))=0\quad\text{for all integers }m>n.
\]
Base case: for \(r=a-1\), \(K_{a-1}=0\), so \(P(a-1)\) holds.
Induction step: assume \(P(r-1)\) for some \(r\) with \(a\le r\le 0\). Let \(m>n\). By \(P(r-1)\), the first and fourth terms in the displayed exact sequence vanish. Hence \(H^m(R\Gamma(U,K_r))\) is isomorphic to \(H^m(R\Gamma(U,(\mathcal H^rK)[-r]))\). But by the definition of the shift,
\[
H^m(R\Gamma(U,(\mathcal H^rK)[-r]))=H^{m-r}(U,\mathcal H^rK).
\]
Since \(r\le 0\), we have \(m-r\ge m>n\). By AV applied to the constructible sheaf \(\mathcal H^rK\), this group is zero. Therefore \(H^m(R\Gamma(U,K_r))=0\), proving \(P(r)\).

Taking \(r=0\) gives \(K_0=K\), and hence \(H^m(R\Gamma(U,K))=0\) for every integer \(m>n\). This is exactly the required vanishing.

lemma_287.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(X\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension \(d\ge2\) over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(Y\subset X\) be an effective ample divisor defined over \(\mathbb F_q\) and smooth of pure dimension \(d-1\), let \(U=X\setminus Y\) with open immersion \(j:U\hookrightarrow X\) and closed immersion \(i:Y\hookrightarrow X\), let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\) and \(\ell\neq p\) prime. Suppose \(H^n_c(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=0\) for every integer \(n\le d-1\). Then \(i^*:H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) is injective for every integer \(n\) with \(n\le d-1\).
lemma_287.proof:
PROOF. Write \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\). We prove the following slightly more precise assertion: for every integer \(n\in\mathbb Z\) the sequence
\[
H^n_c(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\ \xrightarrow{\ \alpha_{\mathbb Q}\ }\ H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\ \xrightarrow{\ i^*\ }\ H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)
\]\nis exact at the middle term. Taking \(n\le d-1\) and using the hypothesis \(H^n_c(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=0\) then gives \(\ker i^*=\operatorname{im}\alpha_{\mathbb Q}=0\), i.e. injectivity, which is the claim.

Note first which hypotheses are actually used: \(X_k\) is proper over \(k\) (because \(X\) is projective over \(\mathbb F_q\)), \(Y_k\subset X_k\) is a closed subscheme with open complement \(U_k\), and the stated vanishing. Ampleness and smoothness of \(Y\), the inequality \(d\ge2\), and geometric connectedness of \(X\) are not needed for this conclusion; they are simply inherited from the statement.

Throughout, put \(\Lambda_m:=\mathbb Z/\ell^m\mathbb Z\) and let \(j_k:U_k\to X_k\), \(i_k:Y_k\to X_k\) be the base changes of \(j\) and \(i\). Base change preserves open immersions, closed immersions, and the property of being complementary, so \(U_k=X_k\setminus Y_k\) and we write \(j,i\) for \(j_k,i_k\).

STEP 1 (the fundamental short exact sequence). For each \(m\ge1\) there is a short exact sequence of sheaves on \(X_{k,\mathrm{\acute et}}\)
\[
0\longrightarrow j_!\Lambda_m\longrightarrow \Lambda_m\longrightarrow i_*\Lambda_m\longrightarrow 0.\tag{1}
\]
The left map is the canonical map of extension by zero; the right map is the one whose sections over an étale \(X_k\)-scheme \(V\) are the restrictions \(\Gamma(V,\Lambda_m)\to\Gamma(V\times_{X_k}Y_k,\Lambda_m)\). Exactness is checked on stalks at geometric points \(\bar x\to X_k\), using the standard stalk formulas for an open/closed decomposition (Milne, Étale Cohomology, II.1.15--1.17): \((j_!F)_{\bar x}=F_{\bar x}\) if \(x\in U\) and \((j_!F)_{\bar x}=0\) if \(x\in Y\); \((i_*G)_{\bar x}=G_{\bar y}\) if \(x=y\in Y\) and \((i_*G)_{\bar x}=0\) if \(x\in U\). If \(x\in U\) the sequence on stalks reads \(\Lambda_m\xrightarrow{\sim}\Lambda_m\to 0\); if \(x=y\in Y\) it reads \(0\to\Lambda_m\xrightarrow{\sim}\Lambda_m\). Both are exact, so (1) is exact.

STEP 2 (identifying the two outer terms).
(a) For any sheaf \(G\) on \(U_{k,\mathrm{\acute et}}\) one has \(\Gamma(X_k,j_!G)=\Gamma_c(U_k,G)\): a section \(s\in\Gamma(U_k,G)\) comes from a section of \(j_!G\) over \(X_k\) iff \(\operatorname{supp}(s)\) is closed in \(X_k\); since \(X_k\) is proper over \(k\) and \(U_k\hookrightarrow X_k\) is an open immersion of \(k\)-schemes of finite type, a subset of \(U_k\) closed in \(U_k\) is closed in \(X_k\) iff it is proper over \(k\) (if \(S\to\operatorname{Spec}k\) is proper and \(X_k\) separated over \(k\), then \(S\to X_k\) is a closed immersion; conversely closed subsets of a proper \(k\)-scheme are proper over \(k\)). The functor \(j_!\) is exact (stalkwise, by Step 1), so the Grothendieck spectral sequence for the composition \(\Gamma(X_k,-)\circ j_!=\Gamma_c(U_k,-)\) degenerates and yields functorial isomorphisms
\[
H^n(X_k,j_!G)\ \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\ H^n_c(U_k,G)\qquad\text{for all }n\ge0 .
\]
(b) A closed immersion is affine, hence \(i_*\) is exact on étale sheaves, \(R^qi_*=0\) for \(q>0\), and \(i^*i_*\cong\mathrm{id}\). The adjunction therefore gives functorial isomorphisms \(H^n(X_k,i_*G)\cong H^n(Y_k,G)\). Moreover, under this isomorphism the map \(H^n(X_k,\Lambda_m)\to H^n(X_k,i_*\Lambda_m)\) induced by the morphism \(\Lambda_m\to i_*\Lambda_m\) of (1) is exactly the pullback \(i^*:H^n(X_k,\Lambda_m)\to H^n(Y_k,\Lambda_m)\): the map \(\Lambda_m\to i_*\Lambda_m\) in (1) is the adjoint of the canonical identification \(i^{-1}\Lambda_m\cong\Lambda_m\), hence it is the structure morphism of the morphism of ringed topoi \((Y_k,\Lambda_m)\to(X_k,\Lambda_m)\) defined by \(i\), and the induced map on cohomology is, by definition, \(i^*\).

STEP 3 (long exact sequence with finite coefficients). Applying cohomology to (1) and using Step 2 we obtain, for every \(n\in\mathbb Z\), an exact sequence
\[
H^n_c(U_k,\Lambda_m)\xrightarrow{\ \alpha_m\ }H^n(X_k,\Lambda_m)\xrightarrow{\ \beta_m\ }H^n(Y_k,\Lambda_m),\qquad \beta_m=i^*,\qquad \operatorname{im}\alpha_m=\ker\beta_m.\tag{2}
\]
The sequences (2) are compatible with the reduction homomorphisms \(\Lambda_{m+1}\twoheadrightarrow\Lambda_m\): writing \(a_{m+1,m},b_{m+1,m},c_{m+1,m}\) for the induced maps on the three terms, naturality of the long exact sequence gives \(b_{m+1,m}\circ\alpha_{m+1}=\alpha_m\circ a_{m+1,m}\) and \(c_{m+1,m}\circ\beta_{m+1}=\beta_m\circ b_{m+1,m}\).

STEP 4 (finiteness). By the finiteness theorem for étale cohomology with finite coefficients over a separably closed field (SGA 4, Th. de finitude), the groups \(H^n(X_k,\Lambda_m)\) and \(H^n(Y_k,\Lambda_m)\) are finite (both \(k\)-schemes are proper, hence of finite type over \(k\)). The groups \(H^n_c(U_k,\Lambda_m)\) are finite as well; this is again the finitude theorem (\(U_k\) is of finite type over \(k\)), and it also follows without extra input by induction on \(n\) from (2) and the fact that cohomology vanishes in negative degrees: \(H^0_c(U_k,\Lambda_m)\hookrightarrow H^0(X_k,\Lambda_m)\) is finite, and if \(H^n_c(U_k,\Lambda_m)\) is finite then \(H^{n+1}_c(U_k,\Lambda_m)\) sits in an exact sequence
\[
0\to \operatorname{coker}\!\big(H^n(X_k,\Lambda_m)\to H^n(Y_k,\Lambda_m)\big)\to H^{n+1}_c(U_k,\Lambda_m)\to \ker\!\big(H^{n+1}(X_k,\Lambda_m)\to H^{n+1}(Y_k,\Lambda_m)\big)\to 0
\]\nbetween finite groups.

STEP 5 (passage to the \(\ell\)-adic limit at the integral level). Fix \(n\) and write \(A_m=H^n_c(U_k,\Lambda_m)\), \(B_m=H^n(X_k,\Lambda_m)\), \(C_m=H^n(Y_k,\Lambda_m)\), with the transition maps of Step 3, and let \(A=\varprojlim_m A_m\), \(B=\varprojlim_m B_m\), \(C=\varprojlim_m C_m\), \(\alpha=\varprojlim\alpha_m\), \(\beta=\varprojlim\beta_m\). Set \(D_m:=\operatorname{im}\alpha_m=\ker\beta_m\subseteq B_m\).
(i) \((D_m)\) is an inverse subsystem of \((B_m)\): if \(x=\alpha_{m+1}(u)\in D_{m+1}\) then \(b_{m+1,m}(x)=\alpha_m(a_{m+1,m}(u))\in D_m\).
(ii) \(\varprojlim_m D_m=\ker(\beta)\), by left exactness of \(\varprojlim\) applied to \(0\to D_m\to B_m\to C_m\).
(iii) \(\operatorname{im}\alpha=\ker\beta\): the maps \(\alpha_m:A_m\twoheadrightarrow D_m\) are surjective and compatible. Given \(d=(d_m)\in\varprojlim D_m\), the fibres \(E_m:=\alpha_m^{-1}(d_m)\subseteq A_m\) are non-empty finite sets, and by the compatibility in (i) the transition maps send \(E_{m+1}\) into \(E_m\). For an inverse system of non-empty finite sets indexed by \(\mathbb N\) the limit is non-empty (the images of \(E_{m'}\) in \(E_m\), \(m'\ge m\), form a decreasing sequence of non-empty finite sets, hence stabilise to non-empty \(F_m\) with surjective transition maps \(F_{m+1}\twoheadrightarrow F_m\), and one lifts inductively). Choosing an element of \(\varprojlim_m E_m\) gives a lift of \(d\) to \(A\). Together with (ii) this proves exactness of \(A\xrightarrow{\alpha}B\xrightarrow{\beta}C\) at \(B\).

STEP 6 (identification with the usual \(\ell\)-adic cohomology). Each of the systems \((A_m),(B_m),(C_m)\) consists of finite groups, hence satisfies the Mittag-Leffler condition, so \(R^1\varprojlim\) vanishes on them. By the standard definition/comparison of \(\ell\)-adic cohomology (SGA 5, I, 1.6.2; Milne, Étale Cohomology, VI.11.1), for \(Z=X_k,Y_k\) and for \(U_k\) with proper supports, the derived-limit exact sequence
\[
0\to R^1\varprojlim_m H^{n-1}(Z,\Lambda_m)\to H^n(Z,\mathbb Z_\ell)\to \varprojlim_m H^n(Z,\Lambda_m)\to 0
\]\ncollapses, giving canonical \(\mathbb Z_\ell\)-linear isomorphisms \(H^n(Z,\mathbb Z_\ell)\cong\varprojlim_m H^n(Z,\Lambda_m)\) and \(H^n(Z,\mathbb Q_\ell):=H^n(Z,\mathbb Z_\ell)\otimes_{\mathbb Z_\ell}\mathbb Q_\ell\); these are the groups appearing in the statement (and are finite-dimensional \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-vector spaces). All identifications are functorial in the coefficients and in the scheme, hence compatible with \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\). Thus the sequence
\[
H^n_c(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\alpha_{\mathbb Q}}H^n(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\beta_{\mathbb Q}}H^n(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)
\]\nis obtained from \(A\to B\to C\) by applying \(-\otimes_{\mathbb Z_\ell}\mathbb Q_\ell\).

STEP 7 (exactness is preserved by tensoring with \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)). Put \(E:=\operatorname{coker}\alpha\). Exactness of \(A\to B\to C\) at \(B\) says precisely that the map \(E\hookrightarrow C\) induced by \(\beta\) is injective. Since \(\mathbb Q_\ell=\mathbb Z_\ell[\ell^{-1}]\) is the localisation of the domain \(\mathbb Z_\ell\) at \(\{1,\ell,\ell^2,\dots\}\), it is a flat \(\mathbb Z_\ell\)-module, so \(E\otimes_{\mathbb Z_\ell}\mathbb Q_\ell\hookrightarrow C\otimes_{\mathbb Z_\ell}\mathbb Q_\ell\) is again injective. On the other hand, right exactness of \(-\otimes\mathbb Q_\ell\) applied to \(\operatorname{im}\alpha\to B\to E\to0\) shows \(E\otimes\mathbb Q_\ell\cong\operatorname{coker}(\alpha_{\mathbb Q})\) (and \(\operatorname{im}\alpha_{\mathbb Q}\) is the image of \((\operatorname{im}\alpha)\otimes\mathbb Q_\ell\to B\otimes\mathbb Q_\ell\)). The composite \(B\otimes\mathbb Q_\ell\to\operatorname{coker}(\alpha_{\mathbb Q})\to C\otimes\mathbb Q_\ell\) is \(\beta_{\mathbb Q}\). Hence \(\ker\beta_{\mathbb Q}=\operatorname{im}\alpha_{\mathbb Q}\): the sequence of Step 6 is exact at the middle term.

STEP 8 (end of the proof). Let \(n\le d-1\). By hypothesis \(H^n_c(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=0\), so \(\operatorname{im}\alpha_{\mathbb Q}=0\) and therefore \(\ker\beta_{\mathbb Q}=0\) by Step 7. By Step 2(b) and the functoriality used in Step 6, \(\beta_{\mathbb Q}\) is the pullback along the closed immersion \(i:Y\hookrightarrow X\),
\[
\beta_{\mathbb Q}=i^*:H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\longrightarrow H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell).
\]
Thus \(i^*\) is injective for every integer \(n\le d-1\), which is exactly the required conclusion. \(\blacksquare\)

lemma_abeljac_proper_surjective_gen_fini.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(C\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected curve of genus \(g\ge1\) over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(p_0\in C(\mathbb F_q)\) be a rational point, and let \(J=\operatorname{Pic}^0_{C/\mathbb F_q}\) be the Jacobian of \(C\). Let \(a:C\times_{\mathbb F_q}\cdots\times_{\mathbb F_q}C\to J\) (\(g\) factors) be the \(\mathbb F_q\)-morphism obtained by composing the Abel map \((x_1,\dots,x_g)\mapsto[\mathcal O_C(\textstyle\sum_i x_i)]\) with translation of the Picard scheme by \(-[\mathcal O_C(g p_0)]\). Then \(a\) is proper, surjective, and generically finite.
lemma_abeljac_proper_surjective_gen_fini.proof:
Proof. Write \(C^g=\underbrace{C\times_{\mathbb F_q}\cdots\times_{\mathbb F_q}C}_{g\ \text{factors}}\) and \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\); for an \(\mathbb F_q\)-scheme \(Z\) write \(Z_k=Z\times_{\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_q}\operatorname{Spec}k\).

STEP 0. Background theorems invoked (standard results of algebraic geometry, used as black boxes; everything specific to this lemma is proved below).
(P1) (Picard scheme, Grothendieck.) For the smooth projective geometrically connected curve \(C/\mathbb F_q\), the fppf sheafification of \(T\mapsto \operatorname{Pic}(C\times T)/\operatorname{pr}_1^*\operatorname{Pic}(T)\) is represented by a scheme \(\operatorname{Pic}_{C/\mathbb F_q}\) which is SEPARATED and LOCALLY of finite type over \(\mathbb F_q\) (it is not of finite type: it is the disjoint union \(\bigsqcup_{d\in\mathbb Z}\operatorname{Pic}^d_{C/\mathbb F_q}\), where \(\operatorname{Pic}^d\) parametrises line bundles of degree \(d\) on the geometric fibres, and each \(\operatorname{Pic}^d\) is open and closed).
(P2) (Jacobian.) \(\operatorname{Pic}^0_{C/\mathbb F_q}=J\) is an abelian variety of dimension \(g\) (its tangent space at the origin is \(H^1(C,\mathcal O_C)\), of dimension \(g\) by definition of the genus). Hence \(J\) is proper, smooth, geometrically integral and of finite type over \(\mathbb F_q\).
(P3) (Torsor structure.) Each non-empty \(\operatorname{Pic}^d\) is a principal homogeneous space under \(J\); since \(p_0\in C(\mathbb F_q)\), the line bundle \(\mathcal O_C(dp_0)\) is an \(\mathbb F_q\)-point of \(\operatorname{Pic}^d\), and tensoring with it gives an \(\mathbb F_q\)-isomorphism \(\tau_d:\operatorname{Pic}^d\xrightarrow{\sim}J\), \(\mathcal M\mapsto\mathcal M\otimes\mathcal O_C(-dp_0)\), with inverse \(\mathcal N\mapsto\mathcal N\otimes\mathcal O_C(dp_0)\).
(P4) (Geometric points.) For every field extension \(\Omega/\mathbb F_q\), \(\operatorname{Pic}_{C/\mathbb F_q}(\Omega)=\operatorname{Pic}(C_\Omega)\) because \(\operatorname{Pic}(\operatorname{Spec}\Omega)=0\), and the \(\Omega\)-point defined by a line bundle is its class.
(T1) (Riemann–Roch.) For a vector bundle \(E\) on the smooth projective geometrically connected curve \(C_\Omega\) of genus \(g\), \(\chi(C_\Omega,E)=\deg E+\operatorname{rk}(E)(1-g)\).
(T2) (Divisor of a section.) If \(\mathcal L\) is a line bundle on an integral projective curve and \(0\neq s\in H^0\), the vanishing scheme of \(s\) is an effective Cartier divisor \(D\) with \(\mathcal L\simeq\mathcal O(D)\) and \(\deg D=\deg\mathcal L\).
(T3) (Dimension of fibres, dominant case.) A dominant morphism of finite type \(f:X\to Y\) between irreducible varieties over a field admits a dense open \(U\subset Y\) with \(\dim X_y=\dim X-\dim Y\) for all \(y\in U\).
(T4) (Upper semicontinuity of fibre dimension.) If \(f:X\to Y\) is closed and of finite presentation with locally Noetherian fibres, then \(\{y:\dim X_y\ge m\}\) is closed for every \(m\ge0\).
(T5) (Zariski's main theorem, finiteness form.) A proper quasi-finite morphism is finite.

STEP 1. Construction of \(a\) over \(\mathbb F_q\). For \(1\le i\le g\) let \(\Delta_i\subset C^g\times_{\mathbb F_q}C\) be the graph of the \(i\)-th projection. The diagonal \(C\hookrightarrow C\times C\) is a closed immersion of the regular (smooth) scheme \(C\times C\) onto a codimension-1 subscheme, hence an effective Cartier divisor; base change preserves this, so each \(\Delta_i\) is an effective Cartier divisor. Put \(\mathcal L=\mathcal O_{C^g\times C}(\Delta_1+\cdots+\Delta_g)\). By (P1)/(P4) this line bundle on \(C\times_{\mathbb F_q}C^g\) defines a morphism \(\alpha:C^g\to\operatorname{Pic}_{C/\mathbb F_q}\).
The sets \(\alpha^{-1}(\operatorname{Pic}^d)\) are open and closed in \(C^g\) and partition it. \(C\) is smooth and geometrically connected over the perfect field \(\mathbb F_q\), hence geometrically integral (smooth \(\Rightarrow\) geometrically regular \(\Rightarrow\) geometrically reduced; a connected locally Noetherian scheme with integral local rings is irreducible); products of geometrically integral \(\mathbb F_q\)-schemes are geometrically integral, so \(C^g\) is integral, in particular connected. Thus exactly one member of the partition is non-empty. Since \(p_0\in C(\mathbb F_q)\), the point \(s=(p_0,\dots,p_0)\in C^g(\mathbb F_q)\) exists, and \((s\times\mathrm{id})^{-1}(\Delta_i)=\{p_0\}\) as Cartier divisors, so \((s\times\mathrm{id})^*\mathcal L=\mathcal O_C(gp_0)\), of degree \(g\); by (P4) \(\alpha(s)\in\operatorname{Pic}^g(\mathbb F_q)\). Hence the non-empty member is \(\alpha^{-1}(\operatorname{Pic}^g)=C^g\), i.e. \(\alpha\) factors uniquely through the open-and-closed immersion \(\operatorname{Pic}^g_{C/\mathbb F_q}\hookrightarrow\operatorname{Pic}_{C/\mathbb F_q}\). Define \(a:=\tau_g\circ\alpha:C^g\to J\). This is an \(\mathbb F_q\)-morphism (so it is defined over \(\mathbb F_q\) by construction, not merely on geometric points), of finite type since source and target are of finite type over \(\mathbb F_q\). By (P3) and (P4), for every algebraically closed \(\Omega/\mathbb F_q\) and \((x_1,\dots,x_g)\in C(\Omega)^g\), \(a(x_1,\dots,x_g)=[\mathcal O_{C_\Omega}(\sum_i x_i-gp_0)]\in\operatorname{Pic}^0(C_\Omega)=J(\Omega)\): the Abel map followed by translation by \(-[\mathcal O(gp_0)]\), as required.

STEP 2. Properness. \(C\) is projective, hence proper, over \(\mathbb F_q\); finite products of proper morphisms are proper, so \(C^g\to\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_q\) is proper. By (P2), \(J\) is an abelian variety, hence separated over \(\mathbb F_q\). General fact: if \(f:X\to Y\) is an \(S\)-morphism with \(X\) proper over \(S\) and \(Y\) separated over \(S\), then \(f\) is proper — the graph \(\Gamma_f:X\to X\times_S Y\) is the base change of the closed immersion \(Y\hookrightarrow Y\times_S Y\) (diagonal, closed because \(Y/S\) separated), hence a closed immersion, and \(X\times_S Y\to Y\) is proper as a base change of \(X\to S\); a composition of a closed immersion with a proper morphism is proper. With \(X=C^g\), \(Y=J\), \(S=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_q\), \(a\) is proper.

STEP 3. Surjectivity.
3a. Every \(k\)-rational point of \(J_k\) lies in \(\operatorname{Im}(a_k)\). By (P4), \(J(k)=\operatorname{Pic}^0(C_k)\), the degree-\(0\) line bundles on \(C_k\). Let \([L]\in J(k)\) and set \(\mathcal L'=L\otimes\mathcal O_{C_k}(gp_0)\); then \(\deg\mathcal L'=g\). By (T1), \(\chi(C_k,\mathcal L')=\deg\mathcal L'+1-g=1\), so \(h^0(C_k,\mathcal L')=1+h^1(C_k,\mathcal L')\ge1\). Pick \(0\neq s\in H^0(C_k,\mathcal L')\). Since \(C_k\) is integral and \(\mathcal L'\) is invertible, \(s\) is a non-zero-divisor; by (T2) its vanishing scheme is an effective divisor \(D=\sum_x n_x x\) with \(n_x\ge0\), \(\mathcal L'\simeq\mathcal O(D)\), and \(\sum_x n_x=\deg D=\deg\mathcal L'=g\). Closed points of \(C_k\) are \(k\)-rational (their residue fields are finite over the algebraically closed field \(k\)), so listing the support of \(D\) with multiplicities gives \((x_1,\dots,x_g)\in C(k)^g=C^g(k)\) with \(D=\sum_i x_i\). By the description in Step 1, \(a_k(x_1,\dots,x_g)=[\mathcal O(D-gp_0)]=[L]\).
3b. The closed points of \(J_k\) are exactly \(J(k)\): \(J_k\) is of finite type over the field \(k\), and a point of a finite type scheme over a field is closed iff its residue field is algebraic over the ground field; since \(k\) is algebraically closed these are exactly the \(k\)-rational points.
3c. \(a_k\) is surjective. \(a_k=a\times_{\mathbb F_q}\mathrm{id}_k\) is a base change of the proper morphism \(a\), hence proper, hence closed; so \(\operatorname{Im}(a_k)\) is CLOSED in \(J_k\). By 3a and 3b it contains every closed point of \(J_k\). A scheme of finite type over a field is Jacobson, so its closed points are dense; a closed subset containing a dense subset is the whole space. Hence \(a_k\) is surjective.
3d. Descent to \(\mathbb F_q\). The projection \(\pi:J_k\to J\) is surjective: the fibre over \(y\in J\) is \(\operatorname{Spec}(k\otimes_{\mathbb F_q}\kappa(y))\), non-empty because the tensor product of two non-zero algebras over the field \(\mathbb F_q\) is non-zero (equivalently, \(k/\mathbb F_q\) is faithfully flat, being the filtered colimit \(k=\varinjlim_n\mathbb F_{q^{n!}}\) of finite separable, hence finite locally free, hence flat extensions). Given \(y\in J\), choose \(\tilde y\in J_k\) with \(\pi(\tilde y)=y\), choose \(\tilde x\in C^g_k\) with \(a_k(\tilde x)=\tilde y\) (3c), and let \(x\in C^g\) be the image of \(\tilde x\). The square \(C^g_k\to C^g\), \(J_k\xrightarrow{\pi}J\) with vertical maps \(a_k,a\) is a base-change square, hence commutes, so \(a(x)=\pi(a_k(\tilde x))=\pi(\tilde y)=y\). Thus \(a\) is surjective (and therefore dominant).

STEP 4. The general geometric fibre is 0-dimensional. \(C^g_k=(C_k)^g\) is integral: \(C_k\) is geometrically integral (Step 1), and products of geometrically integral schemes over a field are integral. \(J_k\) is integral by (P2). Both are of finite type over \(k\), with \(\dim C^g_k=g\cdot\dim C=g\) (dimension of a product of varieties over a field is the sum of the dimensions) and \(\dim J_k=\dim J=g\) by (P2). The morphism \(a_k\) is dominant (3c) and of finite type, so (T3) gives a dense open \(U\subset J_k\) with \(\dim (a_k)^{-1}(y)=\dim C^g_k-\dim J_k=0\) for all \(y\in U\); in particular \(U\ne\varnothing\).

STEP 5. Lemma (dimension is unchanged by extending the ground field). If \(W\) is of finite type over a field \(F\) and \(F'/F\) is a field extension, then \(\dim(W\times_FF')=\dim W\). Proof. (i) If \(Z\) is a variety over a field and \(Z_0\subset Z\) a non-empty open, then \(\dim Z_0=\dim Z\): reduce to \(Z=\operatorname{Spec}B\) affine with \(B\) a domain and \(Z_0\supset D(f)\), \(f\ne0\); Noether normalisation gives \(B\) finite over \(F[y_1,\dots,y_d]\), \(d=\operatorname{trdeg}_F\operatorname{Frac}B=\dim B\), and \(B_f\) is still of dimension \(d\) since it is a domain of finite type over \(F\) with the same fraction field. (ii) For any finite type scheme \(X\) over a field, \(\dim X=\sup\{\dim V:V\subset X\ \text{affine open}\}\): every irreducible closed \(Z\subset X\) meets some affine open \(V\) in a non-empty open subset, so \(\dim Z=\dim(Z\cap V)\le\dim V\) by (i); the reverse inequality is immediate. Applying (ii) to \(W\) and \(W_{F'}\) (affine opens of \(W\) base-change to affine opens of \(W_{F'}\)) reduces to \(W=\operatorname{Spec}A\), \(A\) a finitely generated \(F\)-algebra. Let \(\mathfrak p_1,\dots,\mathfrak p_r\) be the minimal primes of \(A\); then \(\dim A=\max_i\dim A/\mathfrak p_i\). Flatness of \(F'/F\) gives \((A/\mathfrak p_i)_{F'}=A_{F'}/\mathfrak p_iA_{F'}\), so \(\dim A_{F'}\ge\dim(A/\mathfrak p_i)_{F'}\). For a domain \(B\) of finite type over \(F\), Noether normalisation makes \(B\) finite over \(F[y_1,\dots,y_d]\) with \(d=\operatorname{trdeg}_F\operatorname{Frac}B=\dim B\); base change gives \(B_{F'}\) finite over \(F'[y_1,\dots,y_d]\) (module-finiteness is preserved by base change; the \(y_j\) stay algebraically independent over \(F'\) because \(F[y_1,\dots,y_d]\hookrightarrow B\) remains injective after the flat base change \(F\to F'\)), and an integral extension does not change dimension (lying over + going-up + incomparability), so \(\dim B_{F'}=d=\dim B\). Hence \(\dim A_{F'}\ge\max_i\dim A/\mathfrak p_i=\dim A\). Conversely each minimal prime \(\mathfrak q\) of \(A_{F'}\) contracts to a prime of \(A\) containing the nilradical, hence containing some \(\mathfrak p_i\); then \(A_{F'}/\mathfrak q\) is a domain which is a quotient of \((A/\mathfrak p_i)_{F'}\), so \(\dim A_{F'}/\mathfrak q\le\dim(A/\mathfrak p_i)_{F'}=\dim A/\mathfrak p_i\le\dim A\), and taking the maximum over \(\mathfrak q\) gives \(\dim A_{F'}\le\dim A\). Equality follows. \(\square\)

STEP 6. A non-empty open of \(J\) with 0-dimensional fibres. The morphism \(a\) is proper, hence closed, of finite presentation (finite type between Noetherian schemes), with Noetherian fibres. By (T4), \(Z_m:=\{y\in J:\dim a^{-1}(y)\ge m\}\) is closed in \(J\) for each \(m\ge0\). We show \(Z_1\ne J\). For \(\tilde y\in J_k\) with image \(y\in J\), associativity of fibre products gives a canonical isomorphism \((a_k)^{-1}(\tilde y)=C^g\times_J\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(\tilde y)\cong\big(C^g\times_J\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(y)\big)\times_{\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(y)}\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(\tilde y)=a^{-1}(y)\times_{\kappa(y)}\kappa(\tilde y)\) (the map \(\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(\tilde y)\to J\) factors through \(\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(y)\to J\)). By Step 5, \(\dim(a_k)^{-1}(\tilde y)=\dim a^{-1}(y)\). Therefore \(\{\tilde y\in J_k:\dim(a_k)^{-1}(\tilde y)\ge1\}=\pi^{-1}(Z_1)\). If \(Z_1=J\), then every fibre of \(a_k\) would have dimension \(\ge1\), contradicting Step 4 (points of \(U\) have 0-dimensional fibre). Hence \(Z_1\) is a proper closed subset, and \(V:=J\setminus Z_1\) is a non-empty open subset of \(J\); since \(J\) is integral by (P2), \(V\) is dense, and every fibre \(a^{-1}(y)\), \(y\in V\), is 0-dimensional.

STEP 7. Finiteness over \(V\); generic finiteness. Fix \(y\in V\), put \(F=\kappa(y)\) and \(X=a^{-1}(y)=C^g\times_J\operatorname{Spec}F\). Then \(X\) is of finite type and proper over \(F\) (base change of \(a\)) and \(\dim X=0\). We prove \(X\to\operatorname{Spec}F\) is finite. \(X\) is Noetherian of dimension \(0\), so all its points are closed and it has finitely many points; in particular it is quasi-compact and quasi-separated. Grothendieck vanishing gives \(H^i(X,\mathcal F)=0\) for \(i>\dim X=0\) for every quasi-coherent \(\mathcal F\); Serre's criterion for affineness of qcqs schemes then makes \(X\) affine, \(X=\operatorname{Spec}A\). Since \(X\) is of finite type over \(F\), \(A\) is a finitely generated \(F\)-algebra; it is Noetherian of dimension \(0\), hence Artinian, so \(A\simeq\prod_{j=1}^n A_j\) with \(A_j\) Artin local with maximal ideal \(\mathfrak m_j\). By Zariski's lemma \(A_j/\mathfrak m_j\) is finite over \(F\); with \(\mathfrak m_j^N=0\), induction on \(N\) using that each \(\mathfrak m_j^i/\mathfrak m_j^{i+1}\) is a finite \(A_j/\mathfrak m_j\)-module shows \(A_j\) is finite-dimensional over \(F\). Thus \(A\) is a finite \(F\)-algebra and \(X\to\operatorname{Spec}F\) is finite.
Consequently \(a^{-1}(V)\to V\) is of finite type with finite fibres, i.e. quasi-finite, and it is proper as a base change of \(a\). By (T5) (Zariski's main theorem) it is FINITE. Since \(V\subset J\) is a dense open, this is exactly the assertion that \(a\) is generically finite. (Equivalently, the generic fibre \(C^g\times_J\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(J)\) is the base change of the finite morphism \(a^{-1}(V)\to V\) to the generic point \(\eta\in V\), hence the spectrum of a finite \(\kappa(J)\)-algebra, and localising shows \(\kappa(C^g)\) is a finite extension of \(\kappa(J)\).) Note that no affineness of a generic fibre was needed, and the edge case \(g=1\) (where \(C^g=C\)) is covered by the same argument: Riemann–Roch in Step 3a gives \(h^0(\mathcal L')=1+h^1(\mathcal L')\ge1\) for every \(g\ge1\), and \(\dim C=1=\dim J\).

STEP 8. Conclusion. Step 2 gives properness, Step 3 gives surjectivity, and Step 7 gives generic finiteness of the \(\mathbb F_q\)-morphism \(a:C^g\to J=\operatorname{Pic}^0_{C/\mathbb F_q}\) constructed in Step 1, which is precisely the map of the statement (Abel map \((x_1,\dots,x_g)\mapsto[\mathcal O(\sum x_i)]\) composed with translation by \(-[\mathcal O(gp_0)]\), the translation being an \(\mathbb F_q\)-isomorphism \(\operatorname{Pic}^g\xrightarrow{\sim}J\) precisely because \(p_0\in C(\mathbb F_q)\)). This proves the lemma. \(\blacksquare\)

Remark (not used above, and no semisimplicity is asserted here): since an abelian variety of dimension \(g\) is smooth, projective and geometrically connected of pure dimension \(g\), the morphism \(a\) satisfies exactly the hypotheses required of \(f:C_1\times\cdots\times C_r\to X\) in Spark's lemma_278 with \(r=g\), \(C_1=\cdots=C_g=C\) and \(X=J\).

lemma_292.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(i:V\hookrightarrow X\) be a closed immersion of smooth projective geometrically connected varieties over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, and for \(Z\in\{V,X\}\) write \(F_Z=(\mathrm{id}_{Z_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(c)=c^q\), for the \(q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius automorphism of \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\). Fix an integer \(n\ge0\). If \(i^*:H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(V_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) is injective and \(F_V\) acts semisimply on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(V_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\), then \(F_X\) acts semisimply on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\).
lemma_292.proof:
Write $H_X^n:=H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$, $H_V^n:=H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(V_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$, and $T:=F_V\in\mathrm{GL}(H_V^n)$, $S:=F_X\in\mathrm{GL}(H_X^n)$ as in the statement. We must show $S$ is semisimple.

**Step 0 (finite dimensionality and invertibility).** Both $X$ and $V$ are proper over $\mathbb F_q$ (they are projective). Applying lemma_45_finite_frob to $X$ and to $V$, with $K=\mathbb Q_\ell$ the constant sheaf equipped with its natural arithmetic Frobenius isomorphism $\psi:F_Z^*\mathbb Q_\ell\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell$, gives that $H_X^n$ and $H_V^n$ are finite-dimensional $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector spaces, and that the induced $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear automorphisms are exactly the $q$-power arithmetic Frobenius operators $F_Z=(\mathrm{id}_{Z_k}\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma)^*$, $\sigma(c)=c^q$. By lemma_6a these pullback maps are indeed $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear automorphisms of the (finite-dimensional) cohomology groups. Hence $S\in\mathrm{GL}(H_X^n)$ and $T\in\mathrm{GL}(H_V^n)$ are well-defined invertible operators, so that lemma_5 and lemma_8 (which both require finite dimensionality and invertibility) are applicable.

**Step 1 (functoriality of Frobenius).** The closed immersion $i:V\hookrightarrow X$ is a morphism of schemes of finite type over $\mathbb F_q$. Lemma_214 applied to $f=i$ (so that the lemma's source is $V$ and its target is $X$) yields, for our fixed $n\ge0$,
$$i^*\circ F_X \;=\; F_V\circ i^*,\qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad i^*\circ S \;=\; T\circ i^* \;:\; H_X^n\longrightarrow H_V^n.$$

**Step 2 (the image is a Frobenius-stable subspace).** Put $W:=\mathrm{im}(i^*)\subseteq H_V^n$. By hypothesis $i^*$ is injective, so
$$\alpha:=i^*:\; H_X^n \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } W$$
is a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear isomorphism. Moreover $W$ is $T$-stable: for $w\in W$ write $w=i^*(x)$ with $x\in H_X^n$; then by Step 1, $T(w)=T(i^*x)=i^*(Sx)\in W$. Since $T$ is invertible and $W$ is a finite-dimensional $T$-stable subspace, $T(W)\subseteq W$ forces $T|_W:W\to W$ to be injective, hence bijective (a injective endomap of a finite-dimensional vector space is surjective); thus $T(W)=W$ and $T|_W\in\mathrm{GL}(W)$. By construction, $\alpha$ intertwines $S$ with $T|_W$:
$$\alpha\circ S \;=\; (T|_W)\circ\alpha.$$

**Step 3 (restriction of a semisimple operator to a stable subspace is semisimple).** Hypothesis: $T$ is semisimple on $H_V^n$. We prove $T|_W$ is semisimple. By lemma_5, semisimplicity of $T$ means that $T_{\bar\ell}:=T\otimes\mathrm{id}$ is diagonalisable on $\bar H:=H_V^n\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$. Let $\bar W:=W\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$; since $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$ is free, hence flat, over $\mathbb Q_\ell$, the map $W\hookrightarrow H_V^n$ remains injective after extension of scalars, so we regard $\bar W\subseteq\bar H$. On elementary tensors both $T_{\bar\ell}|_{\bar W}$ and $(T|_W)\otimes\mathrm{id}$ act by $\sum_j w_j\otimes c_j\mapsto\sum_j T(w_j)\otimes c_j$ (which lands in $\bar W$ because $W$ is $T$-stable); hence
$$(*)\qquad T_{\bar\ell}\big|_{\bar W} \;=\; (T|_W)\otimes\mathrm{id}_{\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell}.$$
Let $\Lambda\subset\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$ be the finite set of distinct eigenvalues of $T_{\bar\ell}$, and $\bar H_\lambda:=\ker(T_{\bar\ell}-\lambda)$ the eigenspaces, so $\bar H=\bigoplus_{\lambda\in\Lambda}\bar H_\lambda$. For each $\lambda\in\Lambda$ set
$$P_\lambda(t):=\prod_{\mu\in\Lambda,\ \mu\ne\lambda}\frac{t-\mu}{\lambda-\mu}\;\in\;\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell[t],$$
which satisfies $P_\lambda(\lambda)=1$ and $P_\lambda(\mu)=0$ for $\mu\in\Lambda\setminus\{\lambda\}$. Since $T_{\bar\ell}$ acts on $\bar H_\mu$ as the scalar $\mu$, the operator $P_\lambda(T_{\bar\ell})$ acts as the identity on $\bar H_\lambda$ and as $0$ on each $\bar H_\mu$ with $\mu\ne\lambda$; i.e. $P_\lambda(T_{\bar\ell})$ is the spectral projection $\bar H\twoheadrightarrow\bar H_\lambda$ along $\bigoplus_{\mu\ne\lambda}\bar H_\mu$.

Because $\bar W$ is stable under $T_{\bar\ell}$, it is stable under every polynomial in $T_{\bar\ell}$, in particular under each $P_\lambda(T_{\bar\ell})$. For any $w\in\bar W$ we have $w=\sum_{\lambda\in\Lambda}P_\lambda(T_{\bar\ell})w$ (this is the identity $\sum_\lambda P_\lambda\equiv 1$ on $\bar H$, which holds since both sides agree on each $\bar H_\mu$ and the $\bar H_\mu$ span $\bar H$), and each summand $P_\lambda(T_{\bar\ell})w$ lies in $\bar W$ and in $\bar H_\lambda$. Hence
$$\bar W \;=\; \bigoplus_{\lambda\in\Lambda}\bigl(\bar W\cap\bar H_\lambda\bigr),$$
a decomposition of $\bar W$ into $T_{\bar\ell}$-eigenspaces. Thus $T_{\bar\ell}|_{\bar W}$ is diagonalisable over $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$. By $(*)$ this says $(T|_W)\otimes\mathrm{id}$ is diagonalisable on $\bar W$, and lemma_5 applied to $T|_W\in\mathrm{GL}(W)$ gives that $T|_W$ is semisimple on $W$. (Edge case: if $\Lambda=\varnothing$, i.e. $H_V^n=0$, then $W=0$ and $T|_W=\mathrm{id}_0$, which is semisimple; the argument below is unaffected.)

**Step 4 (transfer along the equivariant isomorphism).** We now have finite-dimensional $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector spaces $H_X^n$ and $W$, invertible operators $S$ and $T|_W$, and a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear isomorphism $\alpha:H_X^n\xrightarrow{\sim}W$ with $\alpha\circ S=(T|_W)\circ\alpha$ (Step 2). Lemma_8 applied to this data yields: $S$ is semisimple if and only if $T|_W$ is semisimple. By Step 3 the latter holds, so $S=F_X$ is semisimple on $H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$.

Concretely, one may read Step 4 as follows: if $\overline{w}_1,\dots,\overline{w}_r$ is a basis of $\bar W$ consisting of $T_{\bar\ell}$-eigenvectors (which exists by Step 3), then $\bar\alpha^{-1}(\overline{w}_1),\dots,\bar\alpha^{-1}(\overline{w}_r)$ with $\bar\alpha:=\alpha\otimes\mathrm{id}$ is a basis of $H_X^n\otimes\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$ consisting of $S\otimes\mathrm{id}$-eigenvectors, since $\bar\alpha$ intertwines $S\otimes\mathrm{id}$ with $T_{\bar\ell}|_{\bar W}$; thus $S$ is diagonalisable over $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$, which by lemma_5 is exactly semisimplicity.

This proves that $F_X$ acts semisimply on $H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$, as required. $\qquad\blacksquare$
