lemma_dual_basis_trace_contraction.statement: Let ℓ be a prime, let U and W be finite-dimensional Q_ℓ-vector spaces, and let ⟨ , ⟩: U × W → Q_ℓ and [ , ]: W × U → Q_ℓ be perfect bilinear pairings. Let (x_i)_{i∈I} be a basis of U, let (u_i)_{i∈I} be the basis of W satisfying ⟨x_i,u_k⟩=δ_{ik}, let (y_j)_{j∈J} be a basis of W, and let (v_j)_{j∈J} be the basis of U satisfying [y_j,v_m]=δ_{jm}. Then for every linear endomorphism T of W, ∑_{i∈I,j∈J} [T u_i,v_j]⟨x_i,y_j⟩ = Tr(T).
lemma_dual_basis_trace_contraction.proof:
Throughout, all vector spaces are over the field $\mathbb Q_\ell$, all sums that appear are finite (the index sets below are finite), and no property relating the two pairings $\langle\,,-\,\rangle$ and $[\,,-]$ is used: they are completely independent perfect pairings, and no symmetry, graded-commutativity or sign convention is invoked.

**Step 0 (the zero-dimensional case).** If $U=W=0$ then $I=J=\varnothing$, the double sum is an empty sum equal to $0$, and the only endomorphism $T$ of $W$ is $0$, whose trace is $0$. The identity holds. Henceforth assume $N:=\dim W\ge 1$.

**Step 1 (the two dimensions agree; the index sets are identified).** The map $\Phi:U\to W^{\vee}:=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(W,\mathbb Q_\ell)$, $\Phi(u)=[\,w\mapsto\langle u,w\rangle]$, is injective because $\langle\,,-\,\rangle$ is perfect on the right, and it is surjective because $\dim U=\dim W^{\vee}$ would otherwise be violated... more precisely, perfectness on the right says exactly that $\Phi$ is an isomorphism: if $\Phi$ were not surjective, there would be a nonzero $w\in W$ with $\langle u,w\rangle=0$ for all $u$, contradicting non-degeneracy on the right. Thus $\dim U=\dim W^{\vee}=\dim W=:N<\infty$. Since $(x_i)_{i\in I}$ is a basis of $U$ and $(y_j)_{j\in J}$ is a basis of $W$, both $I$ and $J$ are finite with $|I|=|J|=N$. Choose any bijection $J\xrightarrow{\sim} I$ and use it to identify $I=J=\{1,\dots,N\}$; all matrices below are $N\times N$, and the claimed identity is manifestly independent of this choice of identification (the left-hand side is a sum indexed by $I\times J$ written in the original labels).

**Step 2 (the matrices $D$ and $E$, and $DE=I_N\Rightarrow ED=I_N$).** Define
$$D_{ij}:=\langle x_i,y_j\rangle\in\mathbb Q_\qquad (1\le i,j\le N).$$
Since $(y_j)$ is a basis of $W$, each $u_k$ has unique coordinates in that basis; write
$$u_k=\sum_{j=1}^{N}E_{jk}\,y_j ,\qquad E_{jk}\in\mathbb Q_\ell .$$
Using bilinearity of $\langle\,,-\,\rangle$ in the second slot and the defining property $\langle x_i,u_k\rangle=\delta_{ik}$,
$$\delta_{ik}=\langle x_i,u_k\rangle=\Big\langle x_i,\sum_j E_{jk}y_j\Big\rangle=\sum_j E_{jk}\langle x_i,y_j\rangle=\sum_j D_{ij}E_{jk}=(DE)_{ik}.$$
Hence $DE=I_N$. View $D$ as the linear operator of $\mathbb Q_\ell^{N}$. For every $v\in\mathbb Q_\ell^{N}$ one has $v=D(Ev)$, so $D$ is surjective; by rank--nullity on the finite-dimensional space $\mathbb Q_\ell^{N}$, $D$ is then injective and hence invertible. Multiplying $DE=I_N$ on the left by $D^{-1}$ gives $E=D^{-1}$, and therefore
$$ED=D^{-1}D=I_N,\qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad \sum_{j}E_{ij}D_{jk}=\delta_{ik}.\tag{2.1}$$
(Equivalently: $(E_{jk})$ is the change-of-basis matrix from the basis $(u_k)$ to the basis $(y_j)$, so it is invertible and $D$ is its inverse.)

**Step 3 (the matrix of $T$).** Since $(y_j)$ is a basis of $W$, there are unique scalars $a_{jk}$ with
$$T y_k=\sum_{j=1}^{N}a_{jk}\,y_j,\qquad A:=(a_{jk})_{j,k}.$$
$A$ is the matrix of $T$ in the basis $(y_j)$. We recall the standard fact that the trace of an endomorphism is the trace of its matrix in any basis: if $(y'_k)=\sum_j P_{jk}y_j$ is another basis ($P$ invertible) and $B'$ is the matrix of $T$ in $(y'_k)$, then $B'=P^{-1}AP$, and by cyclic invariance of the trace (proved below) $\operatorname{Tr}(B')=\operatorname{Tr}(P^{-1}AP)=\operatorname{Tr}(APP^{-1})=\operatorname{Tr}(A)$. Thus $\operatorname{Tr}(T)=\operatorname{Tr}(A)=\sum_j a_{jj}$ is well defined.

*Cyclic invariance (proved for completeness).* For $N\times N$ matrices $M,M'$ over the commutative field $\mathbb Q_\ell$,
$$\operatorname{Tr}(MM')=\sum_i (MM')_{ii}=\sum_i\sum_j M_{ij}M'_{ji}=\sum_j\sum_i M'_{ji}M_{ij}=\sum_j (M'M)_{jj}=\operatorname{Tr}(M'M),$$
where all rearrangements are legitimate because the sums are finite and $\mathbb Q_\ell$ is commutative.

**Step 4 (the contraction $[Tu_i,v_j]=(AE)_{ji}$).** By linearity of $T$ and Step 3,
$$T u_i=T\Big(\sum_j E_{ji}y_j\Big)=\sum_j E_{ji}\,T y_j=\sum_j E_{ji}\sum_m a_{mj}y_m=\sum_m\Big(\sum_j a_{mj}E_{ji}\Big)y_m=\sum_m (AE)_{mi}\,y_m.$$
Now apply the pairing $[\,,-]$, which is linear in its first argument, and use the defining property $[y_m,v_j]=\delta_{mj}$ of the dual basis $(v_j)$:
$$[Tu_i,v_j]=\Big[\sum_m (AE)_{mi}y_m,\,v_j\Big]=\sum_m (AE)_{mi}[y_m,v_j]=\sum_m (AE)_{mi}\delta_{mj}=(AE)_{ji}.\tag{4.1}$$
Note that only the stated duality relation for $(v_j)$ is used; in particular $(v_j)$ is *not* the $\langle\,,-\,\rangle$-dual of $(x_i)$, and no identification between the two dual bases is made.

**Step 5 (evaluation of the double sum).** Using $D_{ij}=\langle x_i,y_j\rangle$ and (4.1),
$$\sum_{i\in I}\sum_{j\in J}[Tu_i,v_j]\,\langle x_i,y_j\rangle=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}(AE)_{ji}D_{ij}=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\Big(\sum_{j=1}^{N}D_{ij}(AE)_{ji}\Big)=\sum_i\big(D\cdot(AE)\big)_{ii}=\operatorname{Tr}\big(DAE\big).$$
Applying cyclic invariance of the trace twice, together with associativity and (2.1),
$$\operatorname{Tr}(DAE)=\operatorname{Tr}\big((AE)D\big)=\operatorname{Tr}\big(A(ED)\big)=\operatorname{Tr}(A\,I_N)=\operatorname{Tr}(A)=\operatorname{Tr}(T),$$
where the last equality is Step 3.

**Conclusion.** Combining Step 5 with the edge case of Step 0 gives, for every linear endomorphism $T$ of $W$ (invertible or not),
$$\sum_{i\in I,\,j\in J}[T u_i,v_j]\,\langle x_i,y_j\rangle=\operatorname{Tr}(T),$$
as claimed. $\blacksquare$

**Remarks on the hypotheses actually used.** (i) Perfectness of $\langle\,,-\,\rangle$ is used only to force $\dim U=\dim W$ (and to guarantee that the dual basis $(u_i)$ exists); perfectness of $[\,,-]$ is used only to guarantee that the dual basis $(v_j)$ exists. (ii) No relation between the two pairings is assumed or needed. (iii) $T$ is an arbitrary endomorphism; invertibility is never used. (iv) The two dual bases belong to different spaces: $(x_i),(v_j)$ are bases of $U$ and $(u_i),(y_j)$ are bases of $W$, and they are paired by different pairings, which is why the matrices $D$ and $E$ are inverse to each other while $A$ is the matrix of $T$ in the $y$-basis.

lemma_295.statement: Let \(K\) be a field of characteristic zero, let \(d\ge1\), let \(V=\bigoplus_{n\in\mathbb Z}V_n\) be a finite-dimensional \(\mathbb Z\)-graded \(K\)-vector space with \(V_n=0\) for \(n<0\) and for \(n>2d\), and let \(L:V\to V\) be a \(K\)-linear endomorphism with \(L(V_n)\subseteq V_{n+2}\) such that \(L^{d-m}:V_m\to V_{2d-m}\) is an isomorphism for every \(0\le m\le d\). For \(0\le m\le d\) set \(P^m=\ker\bigl(L^{d-m+1}:V_m\to V_{2d-m+2}\bigr)\). Then \(\dim_K P^m=\dim_K V_m-\dim_K V_{m-2}\) for every \(0\le m\le d\), where \(V_j=0\) is understood for \(j<0\).
lemma_295.proof:
We prove the statement by a direct dimension count; no input from Frobenius cohomology is needed, and in fact the argument never uses the hypothesis char K = 0 (it is valid over any field).

Notation. Write (HL)_t for the hard-Lefschetz hypothesis at level t: for 0 \le t \le d the map L^{d-t}: V_t \to V_{2d-t} is an isomorphism. By assumption (HL)_t holds for every 0 \le t \le d. All V_n are finite-dimensional over K because V is finite-dimensional, so rank-nullity applies to every linear map between them.

Step 1 (grading of powers of L). We claim L^j(V_n) \subseteq V_{n+2j} for all j \ge 0 and all n \in \mathbb Z. For j = 0 this is V_n \subseteq V_n. If it holds for j, then for x \in V_n, L^j x \in V_{n+2j}, and by the hypothesis L(V_r) \subseteq V_{r+2} applied with r = n+2j we get L^{j+1}x = L(L^j x) \in V_{n+2j+2} = V_{n+2(j+1)}. Induction gives the claim.

Step 2 (P^m is the kernel of a map between graded pieces). Fix m with 0 \le m \le d and set k := d-m+1 \ge 1. By Step 1, L^k(V_m) \subseteq V_{m+2k} = V_{m+2(d-m+1)} = V_{2d-m+2}. Hence L^k restricts to a well-defined K-linear map
\[\varphi := L^k|_{V_m} : V_m \longrightarrow V_{2d-m+2},\]
and by definition P^m = \ker(\varphi).

We now distinguish two cases according as the target V_{2d-m+2} is forced to vanish or not.

Step 3 (the cases m = 0 and m = 1). If m = 0 then 2d-m+2 = 2d+2 > 2d, and if m = 1 then 2d-m+2 = 2d+1 > 2d. In both cases the vanishing hypothesis V_n = 0 for n > 2d gives V_{2d-m+2} = 0. Thus \varphi is the (necessarily zero) map V_m \to 0, its kernel is all of V_m, and P^m = V_m. Since m-2 < 0 in both cases, the convention of the statement gives V_{m-2} = 0, whence
\[\dim_K P^m = \dim_K V_m = \dim_K V_m - 0 = \dim_K V_m - \dim_K V_{m-2}.\]
(This already covers the whole statement when d = 1, since then m \in \{0,1\}.)

Step 4 (the case 2 \le m \le d). Then 0 \le m-2 \le d-2 \le d, so (HL) applies at level t := m-2: the map
\[\Lambda := L^{d-(m-2)} = L^{d-m+2} : V_{m-2} \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } V_{2d-(m-2)} = V_{2d-m+2}\]
is an isomorphism. In particular \dim_K V_{m-2} = \dim_K V_{2d-m+2} (both finite).

Consider the composite
\[ V_{m-2} \xrightarrow{\ L\ } V_m \xrightarrow{\ \varphi\ } V_{2d-m+2}. \]
Since L(V_{m-2}) \subseteq V_m (Step 1 with j=1), this composite is literally the restriction to V_{m-2} of L^k \circ L = L^{k+1}, and k+1 = (d-m+1)+1 = d-m+2 = d-(m-2). Thus the composite equals \Lambda, which is an isomorphism onto V_{2d-m+2}. Two consequences:

(a) Surjectivity of \varphi. For every w \in V_{2d-m+2} there is y \in V_{m-2} with \Lambda y = w; putting x := Ly \in V_m we get \varphi(x) = L^k x = L^{k+1} y = \Lambda y = w. Hence \operatorname{im}\varphi = V_{2d-m+2}.

(b) (Not needed for the count, but it shows consistency.) \Lambda injective forces L|_{V_{m-2}} injective, so \dim_K V_m \ge \dim_K V_{m-2}, as the formula below requires.

Step 5 (rank-nullity). Apply the rank-nullity theorem to \varphi : V_m \to V_{2d-m+2}, using (a) and Step 2:
\[\dim_K V_m = \dim_K\ker\varphi + \dim_K\operatorname{im}\varphi = \dim_K P^m + \dim_K V_{2d-m+2} = \dim_K P^m + \dim_K V_{m-2},\]
where the last equality is the dimension equality from Step 4. Rearranging,
\[\dim_K P^m = \dim_K V_m - \dim_K V_{m-2}.\]

Step 6 (conclusion). Steps 3 and 5 together cover every integer m with 0 \le m \le d (for d \ge 2 the two cases are m \in\{0,1\} and 2 \le m \le d; for d = 1 only Step 3 occurs). In each case we have shown
\[\dim_K P^m = \dim_K V_m - \dim_K V_{m-2}\]
with the convention V_j = 0 for j < 0, which is exactly the claim. \qedsymbol

lemma_dual_complex_pairing.statement: Let \(\ell\) be a prime, let \(N\ge 0\) be an integer, and let \((K^{\bullet},d_K)\) and \((L^{\bullet},d_L)\) be cochain complexes of finite-dimensional \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-vector spaces with \(K^i=L^i=0\) for \(i<0\) and \(i>N\). Suppose that for each \(i\) there is given a perfect bilinear pairing \(\langle-,-\rangle_i:K^i\times L^{N-i}\to\mathbb Q_\ell\) such that \(\langle d_K x,\,y\rangle_{i+1}=(-1)^{i+1}\langle x,\,d_L y\rangle_i\) for all \(x\in K^i\) and \(y\in L^{N-i-1}\). Then for every \(i\) the pairing \(H^i(K^{\bullet})\times H^{N-i}(L^{\bullet})\to\mathbb Q_\ell\) induced by \(\langle-,-\rangle_i\) is a perfect pairing of finite-dimensional \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-vector spaces.
lemma_dual_complex_pairing.proof:
We prove the statement by pure linear algebra; no geometric duality theorem is used, and the argument is self-contained.

NOTATION. For each \(i\in\mathbb Z\) write
\(Z^i_K=\ker(d_K:K^i\to K^{i+1})\), \(B^i_K=\operatorname{im}(d_K:K^{i-1}\to K^i)\), and similarly \(Z^i_L,B^i_L\) for \(L^\bullet\). Since \(d_K^2=0\) and \(d_L^2=0\), \(B^i\subseteq Z^i\) for every \(i\), and \(H^i(K^\bullet)=Z^i_K/B^i_K\), \(H^i(L^\bullet)=Z^i_L/B^i_L\). All these spaces are finite-dimensional, being subquotients of the finite-dimensional terms.

STEP 0 (EXTENDING THE DATA TO ALL INTEGERS). For \(i\notin[0,N]\) we have simultaneously \(K^i=0\) and \(L^{N-i}=0\): if \(i<0\) then \(K^i=0\) by hypothesis and \(L^{N-i}=0\) because \(N-i>N\); if \(i>N\) then \(K^i=0\) because \(i>N\) and \(L^{N-i}=0\) because \(N-i<0\). For \(i\notin[0,N]\) define \(\langle-,-\rangle_i:K^i\times L^{N-i}\to\mathbb Q_\ell\) to be the unique map \(0\times 0\to\mathbb Q_\ell\); it is perfect because both structure maps \(0\to(0)^\vee\) are isomorphisms. We claim that the compatibility identity
\[(*)\qquad \langle d_Kx,\,y\rangle_{i+1}=(-1)^{i+1}\langle x,\,d_Ly\rangle_i\quad\text{for all }x\in K^i,\ y\in L^{N-i-1}\]
holds for EVERY \(i\in\mathbb Z\). For \(0\le i\le N-1\) this is exactly the hypothesis. For \(i<0\) we have \(K^i=0\), so \(x=0\) and both sides of \((*)\) are \(0\). For \(i\ge N\) we have \(N-i-1\le -1<0\), hence \(L^{N-i-1}=0\), so \(y=0\) and both sides of \((*)\) are \(0\). This covers all integers. Differentials outside \([0,N]\) are the zero maps between zero spaces, and \(d_K^2=d_L^2=0\) holds on all of \(K^\bullet,L^\bullet\). Consequently every computation below is valid for every integer \(i\), with no boundary exceptions; the two extreme cases are nevertheless verified directly at the end of Steps 2 and 3.

RECALL (definition). A bilinear pairing \(\langle-,-\rangle:V\times W\to\mathbb Q_\ell\) on finite-dimensional \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-spaces is perfect if the two maps \(V\to W^\vee\), \(v\mapsto\langle v,-\rangle\), and \(W\to V^\vee\), \(w\mapsto\langle -,w\rangle\), are isomorphisms; equivalently (by finite dimensionality) each is injective, i.e. no nonzero vector pairs trivially against everything in the other factor. Perfectness forces \(\dim V=\dim W\).

STEP 1 (ANNIHILATOR CALCULUS). Let \(V,W\) be finite-dimensional \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-spaces with a perfect pairing \(\langle-,-\rangle:V\times W\to\mathbb Q_\ell\). For a subspace \(U\subseteq V\) set \(U^\perp=\{w\in W:\langle v,w\rangle=0\ \forall v\in U\}\); for a subspace \(S\subseteq W\) set \({}^\perp S=\{v\in V:\langle v,s\rangle=0\ \forall s\in S\}\). Then
(a) \(\dim U^\perp=\dim W-\dim U\) and \(\dim{}^\perp S=\dim V-\dim S\);
(b) \({}^\perp(U^\perp)=U\) and \({}^\perp S)^\perp=S\).

Proof. Let \(V^0:=\{\varphi\in V^\vee:\varphi|_U=0\}\) be the annihilator of \(U\) and, for \(S\subseteq V^\vee\), let \({}^0S:=\{v\in V:\varphi(v)=0\ \forall\varphi\in S\}\) be its pre-annihilator. Compute \(\dim V^0\) explicitly: choose a basis \(u_1,\dots,u_r\) of \(U\) and extend it to a basis \(u_1,\dots,u_r,e_1,\dots,e_s\) of \(V\) (possible since we work over a field); with \((u_i^*,e_j^*)\) the dual basis of \(V^\vee\), a functional lies in \(V^0\) iff its coefficients on \(u_1^*,\dots,u_r^*\) vanish, so \(V^0=\bigoplus_j\mathbb Q_\ell e_j^*\) and \(\dim V^0=s=\dim V-\dim U\).
Next, \(U\subseteq U^{00}\) because \(v\in U\) satisfies \(\varphi(v)=0\) for every \(\varphi\in V^0\) by the definition of \(V^0\); and \(\dim U^{00}=\dim V^\vee-\dim V^0=\dim V-(\dim V-\dim U)=\dim U\) by the previous paragraph applied to \(U^0\subseteq V^\vee\) (identifying \(V^{\vee\vee}=V\)). Hence \(U^{00}=U\). Similarly \(S\subseteq({}^0S)^0\) holds by the definition of \({}^0S\), and \(\dim({}^0S)^0=\dim V-\dim{}^0S=\dim V-(\dim V-\dim S)=\dim S\), so \(({}^0S)^0=S\). These are the two double-annihilator identities we use: \(U^{00}=U\) for \(U\subseteq V\), and \(({}^0S)^0=S\) for \(S\subseteq V^\vee\).
Finally, perfectness gives isomorphisms \(\theta_W:W\xrightarrow{\sim}V^\vee\), \(w\mapsto\langle-,w\rangle\), and \(\theta_V:V\xrightarrow{\sim}W^\vee\), \(v\mapsto\langle v,-\rangle\). By definition, \(\theta_W(U^\perp)=V^0\) and \(\theta_V({}^\perp S)={}^0S\) (the latter, viewed inside \(W^\vee\)). Hence \(\dim U^\perp=\dim V^0=\dim V-\dim U=\dim W-\dim U\) (using \(\dim V=\dim W\)) and \(\dim{}^\perp S=\dim{}^0S=\dim W^\vee-\dim S=\dim W-\dim S=\dim V-\dim S\), proving (a). For (b), \(U\subseteq{}^\perp(U^\perp)\) is immediate from the definitions, and \(\dim{}^\perp(U^\perp)=\dim V-\dim U^\perp=\dim V-(\dim W-\dim U)=\dim U\) by (a), so equality holds; likewise \(S\subseteq({}^\perp S)^\perp\) and \(\dim({}^\perp S)^\perp=\dim W-\dim{}^\perp S=\dim W-(\dim V-\dim S)=\dim S\), giving equality. This proves Step 1. (Note the two identities are used in the two different directions needed below: \({}^\perp(A^\perp)=A\) for \(A\subseteq V\) and \(({}^\perp C)^\perp=C\) for \(C\subseteq W\).)

STEP 2 (FIRST ORTHOGONALITY IDENTITY). For every \(i\in\mathbb Z\), \((B^i_K)^\perp=Z^{N-i}_L\) as subspaces of \(L^{N-i}\), the orthogonal being taken in the perfect pairing \(\langle-,-\rangle_i:K^i\times L^{N-i}\to\mathbb Q_\ell\).
Proof. Let \(y\in L^{N-i}\). Then, with all pairings subscripted by their index:
\[
y\in(B^i_K)^\perp\iff\langle b,y\rangle_i=0\ \ \forall b\in B^i_K\quad[\text{definition of }\perp]\]
\[\iff\langle d_Kx,\,y\rangle_i=0\ \ \forall x\in K^{i-1}\quad[B^i_K=\{d_Kx:x\in K^{i-1}\}\subseteq K^i,\ y\in L^{N-i}]\]
\[\iff(-1)^i\langle x,\,d_Ly\rangle_{i-1}=0\ \ \forall x\in K^{i-1}.\]
Indeed, the last equivalence is \((*)\) applied at the index \(i-1\), to \(x\in K^{i-1}\) and to the same \(y\), which lies in \(L^{N-i}=L^{N-(i-1)-1}\): it reads \(\langle d_Kx,y\rangle_{(i-1)+1}=\langle d_Kx,y\rangle_i=(-1)^{(i-1)+1}\langle x,d_Ly\rangle_{i-1}=(-1)^i\langle x,d_Ly\rangle_{i-1}\). Both occurrences of \(\langle d_Kx,y\rangle\) have subscript \(i\) (well-typed: \(d_Kx\in K^i\), \(y\in L^{N-i}\)), and the occurrence of \(\langle x,d_Ly\rangle\) has subscript \(i-1\) (well-typed: \(x\in K^{i-1}\), \(d_Ly\in L^{N-i+1}=L^{N-(i-1)}\)).
Since \((-1)^i\in\mathbb Q_\ell^\times\), the last condition is \(\langle x,d_Ly\rangle_{i-1}=0\) for all \(x\in K^{i-1}\). The pairing \(\langle-,-\rangle_{i-1}:K^{i-1}\times L^{N-(i-1)}\to\mathbb Q_\ell\) is perfect, so \(L^{N-(i-1)}\to (K^{i-1})^\vee\), \(w\mapsto\langle-,w\rangle_{i-1}\), is injective; applying this to \(w=d_Ly\in L^{N-i+1}=L^{N-(i-1)}\) shows the condition is equivalent to \(d_Ly=0\), i.e. to \(y\in\ker(d_L:L^{N-i}\to L^{N-i+1})=Z^{N-i}_L\). This chains the equivalences and proves Step 2.
Boundary check \(i=0\) (also covered by Step 0): \(B^0_K=\operatorname{im}(K^{-1}\to K^0)=0\) since \(K^{-1}=0\), so \((B^0_K)^\perp=L^N\); and \(Z^N_L=\ker(L^N\to L^{N+1})=L^N\) since \(L^{N+1}=0\). Both sides are \(L^N\). No appeal is made to a pairing at index \(-1\) here.

STEP 3 (SECOND ORTHOGONALITY IDENTITY). For every \(i\in\mathbb Z\), \({}^\perp(B^{N-i}_L)=Z^i_K\) as subspaces of \(K^i\), the orthogonal being taken in \(\langle-,-\rangle_i:K^i\times L^{N-i}\to\mathbb Q_\ell\).
Proof. Let \(z\in K^i\). Then
\[
z\in{}^\perp(B^{N-i}_L)\iff\langle z,c\rangle_i=0\ \ \forall c\in B^{N-i}_L\iff\langle z,\,d_Lv\rangle_i=0\ \ \forall v\in L^{N-i-1}\quad[B^{N-i}_L=\operatorname{im}(d_L:L^{N-i-1}\to L^{N-i})]\]
\[\iff\langle d_Kz,\,v\rangle_{i+1}=0\ \ \forall v\in L^{N-i-1},\]
where the last equivalence is \((*)\) at the index \(i\) with \(x=z\in K^i\) and \(y=v\in L^{N-i-1}\): \(\langle d_Kz,v\rangle_{i+1}=(-1)^{i+1}\langle z,d_Lv\rangle_i\). This is well-typed because \(d_Kz\in K^{i+1}\) and \(v\in L^{N-i-1}=L^{N-(i+1)}\), so \(\langle d_Kz,v\rangle_{i+1}\) is a pairing of index \(i+1\). The pairing \(\langle-,-\rangle_{i+1}:K^{i+1}\times L^{N-(i+1)}\to\mathbb Q_\ell\) is perfect, so \(K^{i+1}\to(L^{N-(i+1)})^\vee\), \(u\mapsto\langle u,-\rangle_{i+1}\), is injective; applying it to \(u=d_Kz\) shows the condition is equivalent to \(d_Kz=0\), i.e. \(z\in Z^i_K\). This proves Step 3.
Boundary check \(i=N\): \(B^0_L=\operatorname{im}(L^{-1}\to L^0)=0\) since \(L^{-1}=0\), so \({}^\perp(B^0_L)=K^N\); and \(Z^N_K=\ker(K^N\to K^{N+1})=K^N\) since \(K^{N+1}=0\). Both sides are \(K^N\); no appeal to a pairing at index \(N+1\) is needed (under Step 0 the pairing at \(N+1\) is the perfect pairing \(0\times0\to\mathbb Q_\ell\), and \(K^{N+1}=0\) makes \(d_Kz=0\) automatic).

STEP 4 (THE INDUCED PAIRING IS DEFINED). Consider \(\beta:Z^i_K\times Z^{N-i}_L\to\mathbb Q_\ell\), \(\beta(x,y)=\langle x,y\rangle_i\); it is bilinear because \(\langle-,-\rangle_i\) is. It descends to cohomology: if \(x\in B^i_K\), say \(x=d_Kx_0\) with \(x_0\in K^{i-1}\), and \(y\in Z^{N-i}_L\), then by \((*)\) at index \(i-1\),
\[\langle x,y\rangle_i=\langle d_Kx_0,y\rangle_i=(-1)^i\langle x_0,d_Ly\rangle_{i-1}=0,\]
since \(d_Ly=0\). (Equivalently, Step 2 says \(Z^{N-i}_L=(B^i_K)^\perp\).) Likewise, if \(y\in B^{N-i}_L\), say \(y=d_Lv\) with \(v\in L^{N-i-1}\), and \(x\in Z^i_K\), then by \((*)\) at index \(i\),
\[\langle x,y\rangle_i=\langle x,d_Lv\rangle_i=(-1)^{i+1}\langle d_Kx,v\rangle_{i+1}=0,\]
since \(d_Kx=0\). (Equivalently, Step 3 says \(Z^i_K={}^\perp(B^{N-i}_L)\).) Hence \(\beta\) factors through the quotients and yields a well-defined bilinear map
\[\bar\beta:H^i(K^\bullet)\times H^{N-i}(L^\bullet)\longrightarrow\mathbb Q_\ell,\qquad \bar\beta([x],[y])=\langle x,y\rangle_i,\]
which is independent of the chosen cocycle representatives by the two displayed computations.

STEP 5 (BOTH RADICALS VANISH).
Left radical. Suppose \([x]\in H^i(K^\bullet)\) satisfies \(\langle x,y\rangle_i=0\) for every \(y\in Z^{N-i}_L\); i.e. \(x\in{}^\perp(Z^{N-i}_L)\). By Step 2, \(Z^{N-i}_L=(B^i_K)^\perp\), so Step 1(b) applied with \(V=K^i\), \(W=L^{N-i}\) and \(U=B^i_K\subseteq K^i\) gives \(x\in{}^\perp((B^i_K)^\perp)=B^i_K\). Hence \([x]=0\).
Right radical. Suppose \(y\in Z^{N-i}_L\) satisfies \(\langle x,y\rangle_i=0\) for every \(x\in Z^i_K\); i.e. \(y\in(Z^i_K)^\perp\). By Step 3, \(Z^i_K={}^\perp(B^{N-i}_L)\), so Step 1(b) applied with \(V=K^i\), \(W=L^{N-i}\) and \(S=B^{N-i}_L\subseteq L^{N-i}\) gives \(y\in({}^\perp(B^{N-i}_L))^\perp=B^{N-i}_L\). Hence \([y]=0\) in \(H^{N-i}(L^\bullet)\).

STEP 6 (PERFECTNESS). The spaces \(H^i(K^\bullet)=Z^i_K/B^i_K\) and \(H^{N-i}(L^\bullet)=Z^{N-i}_L/B^{N-i}_L\) are finite-dimensional. The pairing \(\bar\beta\) induces linear maps
\[\alpha:H^i(K^\bullet)\longrightarrow H^{N-i}(L^\bullet)^\vee,\quad [x]\mapsto\bigl([y]\mapsto\langle x,y\rangle_i\bigr),\qquad \gamma:H^{N-i}(L^\bullet)\longrightarrow H^i(K^\bullet)^\vee,\quad [y]\mapsto\bigl([x]\mapsto\langle x,y\rangle_i\bigr).\]
By Step 5 the kernel of \(\alpha\) is the left radical, hence \(\alpha\) is injective and \(\dim H^i(K^\bullet)\le\dim H^{N-i}(L^\bullet)\); by Step 5 the kernel of \(\gamma\) is the right radical, hence \(\gamma\) is injective and \(\dim H^{N-i}(L^\bullet)\le\dim H^i(K^\bullet)\). Both dimensions are finite, so they are equal, and an injective linear map between vector spaces of the same finite dimension is an isomorphism. Thus \(\alpha\) is an isomorphism, which is precisely the assertion that \(\bar\beta\) is a perfect pairing.

CONSISTENCY CHECK (explicit Betti-number count, not needed for the conclusion). By Step 1(a) and Step 3, \(\dim Z^i_K=\dim{}^\perp(B^{N-i}_L)=\dim K^i-\dim B^{N-i}_L\); by Step 1(a) and Step 2, \(\dim Z^{N-i}_L=\dim(B^i_K)^\perp=\dim L^{N-i}-\dim B^i_K\). Therefore
\[\dim H^i(K^\bullet)=\dim K^i-\dim B^{N-i}_L-\dim B^i_K,\qquad \dim H^{N-i}(L^\bullet)=\dim L^{N-i}-\dim B^i_K-\dim B^{N-i}_L,\]
and these agree because \(\langle-,-\rangle_i\) is perfect, whence \(\dim K^i=\dim L^{N-i}\) \u2014 in agreement with Step 6.

STEP 7 (DEGREES OUTSIDE THE RANGE). If \(i<0\) or \(i>N\) then \(K^i=0\), so \(H^i(K^\bullet)=0\), and \(N-i\notin[0,N]\), so \(L^{N-i}=0\) and \(H^{N-i}(L^\bullet)=0\); the pairing \(0\times0\to\mathbb Q_\ell\) is perfect. (This case is in any event already contained in Steps 2\u20136, which were carried out for all \(i\in\mathbb Z\) under the conventions of Step 0.)

CONCLUSION. For every \(i\), the bilinear map \(\bar\beta:H^i(K^\bullet)\times H^{N-i}(L^\bullet)\to\mathbb Q_\ell\) given by \(\bar\beta([x],[y])=\langle x,y\rangle_i\) is a perfect pairing of finite-dimensional \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-vector spaces. This is exactly the claim.

REMARKS ON THE HYPOTHESES. (i) Finite-dimensionality of the terms is used twice: in Step 1 to identify annihilator dimensions and to conclude \(U^{00}=U\), \(({}^0S)^0=S\), and in Step 6 to upgrade two-sided injectivity to an isomorphism. (ii) The sign \((-1)^{i+1}\) in the compatibility is used only through the fact that it is a nonzero scalar, so that \(\langle d_Kx,y\rangle_i=0\iff\langle x,d_Ly\rangle_{i-1}=0\); any fixed sign convention used consistently in both Steps 2 and 3 gives the same conclusion. The sign convention matters only for the identification of the induced pairing as coming from a chain-map-level duality, not for perfectness. (iii) No external duality theorem is invoked; in particular this is not a consequence of any semisimplicity statement.

lemma_298.statement: Let \(k\) be an algebraically closed field, let \(\ell\) be a prime different from the characteristic of \(k\), and let \(U\) be an affine scheme of finite type over \(k\) which is smooth of pure dimension \(d\ge 0\). Suppose that for every integer \(a\) with \(0\le a\le 2d\) the cup-product pairing \(H^a_{c,\mathrm{\acute et}}(U,\mathbb Q_\ell)\times H^{2d-a}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(U,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{2d}_{c,\mathrm{\acute et}}(U,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) is a perfect pairing of finite-dimensional \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-vector spaces. Then \(H^a_{c,\mathrm{\acute et}}(U,\mathbb Q_\ell)=0\) for every integer \(a\) with \(a<d\).
lemma_298.proof:
We write $H^i(U):=H^i_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(U,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ and $H^i_c(U):=H^i_{c,\mathrm{\acute et}}(U,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ throughout, and we abbreviate $\langle-,-\rangle_a$ for the cup-product pairing of the hypothesis, $\langle-,-\rangle_a:H^a_c(U)\times H^{2d-a}(U)\to H^{2d}_c(U)$.

**Step 1: the Krull dimension of $U$ is $d$.** By assumption $U$ is smooth of pure dimension $d$ over the algebraically closed field $k$; in particular $U$ is of finite type over $k$, hence noetherian, and every irreducible component $Z\subseteq U$ has $\dim Z=d$. Since $U$ is of finite type over a field, it is catenary and equidimensional on each component, so every chain of irreducible closed subsets of $U$ is contained in a single irreducible component and therefore has length at most $d$; chains of length exactly $d$ exist inside each component. Hence $\dim U=\sup_{Z\in\operatorname{Irr}(U)}\dim Z=d$, i.e. the Krull dimension of $U$ is $d$.

**Step 2: the constant complex $\mathbb Q_\ell[0]$ is constructible.** The scheme $U$ is quasi-compact and quasi-separated (it is noetherian). For each $n\ge1$ the torsion sheaf $\mathbb Z/\ell^n\mathbb Z$ on $U_{\mathrm{\acute et}}$ is the pullback along the structure morphism $U\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ of the constant sheaf $\mathbb Z/\ell^n\mathbb Z$ on $(\operatorname{Spec}k)_{\mathrm{\acute et}}$; the latter is constructible (it is represented by the finite constant cover $\coprod_{\mathbb Z/\ell^n}\operatorname{Spec}k\to\operatorname{Spec}k$), and constructibility of torsion sheaves is preserved by pullback along morphisms of finite type between noetherian quasi-separated schemes. Thus each $\mathbb Z/\ell^n\mathbb Z$ is constructible on $U_{\mathrm{\acute et}}$, and by the standard definition of the derived category $D^b_c(U_{\mathrm{\acute et}},\mathbb Q_\ell)$ of $\ell$-adic sheaves (objects whose reductions mod $\ell^n$ are uniformly constructible), the complex $\mathbb Q_\ell[0]$ concentrated in degree $0$ is an object of $D^b_c(U_{\mathrm{\acute et}},\mathbb Q_\ell)$. Its cohomology sheaves are $\mathcal H^0(\mathbb Q_\ell[0])=\mathbb Q_\ell$ and $\mathcal H^q(\mathbb Q_\ell[0])=0$ for $q\ne0$; in particular $\mathcal H^q(\mathbb Q_\ell[0])=0$ for all $q>0$.

**Step 3: affine (Artin) vanishing for ordinary cohomology.** We apply the proved lemma \texttt{lemma\_288} (Spark) to the algebraically closed field $k$, the prime $\ell\ne\operatorname{char}k$, the affine $k$-scheme $U$ of finite type, taking $n:=\dim U=d$ (Step 1) and $K:=\mathbb Q_\ell[0]$ (Step 2). Its hypotheses are satisfied, and it yields
$$H^q\bigl(R\Gamma(U_{\mathrm{\acute et}},\mathbb Q_\ell)\bigr)=0\qquad\text{for every integer }q>d.$$
By definition $H^q\bigl(R\Gamma(U_{\mathrm{\acute et}},\mathbb Q_\ell)\bigr)=H^q_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(U,\mathbb Q_\ell)=H^q(U)$. Hence
$$H^q(U)=0\qquad\text{for all }q>d. \tag{$\ast$}$$

**Step 4: vanishing of $H^a_c(U)$ for $a<0$.** The functor $\Gamma_c(U,-)$ of sections with proper support is left exact on the abelian category of $\ell$-adic (equivalently, of torsion) sheaves on $U_{\mathrm{\acute et}}$, and $H^a_c(U,-)$ is by definition its $a$-th right derived functor $R^a\Gamma_c(U,-)$. Computing $R\Gamma_c$ by an injective resolution $0\to\mathbb Q_\ell\to I^0\to I^1\to\cdots$ of the constant sheaf, which is a complex concentrated in degrees $\ge0$, the complex $R\Gamma_c(U,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ is represented by $\Gamma_c(U,I^\bullet)$, again concentrated in degrees $\ge0$. Therefore $H^a_c(U)=0$ for every $a<0$. \tag{$\ast\ast$}

**Step 5: vanishing of $H^a_c(U)$ for $0\le a<d$.** Let $a$ be an integer with $0\le a<d$. Then
$$2d-a\;\ge\;2d-(d-1)=d+1\;>\;d,$$
so by $(\ast)$ we have $H^{2d-a}(U)=0$. Moreover $a\le d-1\le 2d$ (using $d\ge0$), so $0\le a\le 2d$ and the hypothesis of the lemma applies to this $a$: the pairing
$$\langle-,-\rangle_a:H^a_c(U)\times H^{2d-a}(U)\longrightarrow H^{2d}_c(U)$$
is perfect. By definition of perfectness, the induced $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear map
$$\Phi_a:H^a_c(U)\longrightarrow \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\bigl(H^{2d-a}(U),\,H^{2d}_c(U)\bigr),\qquad x\longmapsto\bigl(y\mapsto\langle x,y\rangle_a\bigr)$$
is an isomorphism. Since $H^{2d-a}(U)=0$, the target is $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(0,H^{2d}_c(U))=0$ (there is exactly one linear map from the zero space, namely the zero map). Hence $H^a_c(U)\cong 0$, i.e.
$$H^a_c(U)=0\qquad\text{for all }a\text{ with }0\le a<d.$$

**Step 6: conclusion and edge cases.** Let $a$ be any integer with $a<d$. If $a<0$, the vanishing $H^a_c(U)=0$ is $(\ast\ast)$; if $0\le a<d$, it is Step 5. Thus $H^a_{c,\mathrm{\acute et}}(U,\mathbb Q_\ell)=0$ for every integer $a<d$, which is exactly the claim.

For completeness we record how the degenerate case $d=0$ is covered: then there is no integer $a$ with $0\le a<d$, so the conclusion reduces to the vanishing for $a<0$, which is Step 4 (and indeed a smooth $0$-dimensional $k$-scheme of finite type over an algebraically closed field is a finite disjoint union of copies of $\operatorname{Spec}k$, whose compactly supported cohomology is concentrated in degree $0$). Note also that no use was made of the target space $H^{2d}_c(U)$ beyond the fact that $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(0,-)=0$, so no identification of $H^{2d}_c(U)$ with a Tate twist is needed.

The only external input used is \texttt{lemma\_288} (affine vanishing for cohomology of constructible complexes with cohomology sheaves concentrated in non-positive degrees); all other steps are formal consequences of the definitions of Krull dimension, constructibility, derived functors of $\Gamma_c$, and perfect pairings.

lemma_cup_product_product_of_curves.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(r\ge1\), let \(C_1,\dots,C_r\) be smooth projective geometrically connected curves of genus at least \(1\) over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(X=C_1\times_{\mathbb F_q}\cdots\times_{\mathbb F_q}C_r\), let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), and let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime. For every integer \(n\ge0\), the homomorphism \({\textstyle\bigwedge^n_{\mathbb Q_\ell}}H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) induced by the \(n\)-fold iterated cup product is surjective.
lemma_cup_product_product_of_curves.proof:
Write $H^*(-)$ for $H^*_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(-_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ with $k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q$, and write all tensor products over $\mathbb Q_\ell$. For each $j$ put $g_j:=\mathrm{genus}(C_j)\ge 1$ and $H^i_j:=H^i(C_{j,k})$.

STEP 0 (the map $\mu_n$ is well defined). The cohomology ring $H^*(X_k)$ is graded-commutative: for $a\in H^p$, $b\in H^q$ one has $a\cup b=(-1)^{pq}b\cup a$. Indeed $R\Gamma(X_{k,\mathrm{\acute et}},\mathbb Q_\ell)$ is a commutative algebra object in $D(\mathbb Q_\ell)$: $\mathbb Q_\ell$ is a commutative ring object of the symmetric monoidal category of sheaves of $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector spaces, and $R\Gamma$ is lax symmetric monoidal via $R\Gamma(F)\otimes R\Gamma(G)\to R\Gamma(F\otimes G)$, $(s,t)\mapsto s\otimes t$; concretely one may model $R\Gamma$ by the normalized cochain complex of the cosimplicial commutative $\mathbb Q_\ell$-algebra of sections over the \'etale \v Cech nerve of any surjective \'etale hypercover, whose shuffle product is strictly graded-commutative because $\mathbb Q_\ell\supset\mathbb Q$ (the antisymmetriser $\frac1{p!q!}\sum_{\sigma}\mathrm{sgn}(\sigma)\,\sigma$ is a well defined idempotent). In particular, for $a,b\in H^1$ we have $a\cup b=-\,b\cup a$, and taking $a=b$ gives $2\,a\cup a=0$, hence $a\cup a=0$ since $2\in\mathbb Q_\ell^{\times}$ (true for every prime $\ell$). Thus the $n$-linear map $(H^1(X_k))^n\to H^n(X_k)$, $(x_1,\dots,x_n)\mapsto x_1\cup\cdots\cup x_n$, is alternating (multilinear and vanishing whenever two arguments coincide, by the relation $x_i\cup x_i=0$ applied after swapping, or directly since it is alternating on the nose at the cochain level), and therefore descends to a well-defined $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear homomorphism
$$\mu_n:\textstyle\bigwedge^n_{\mathbb Q_\ell} H^1(X_k)\longrightarrow H^n(X_k),\qquad x_1\wedge\cdots\wedge x_n\longmapsto x_1\cup\cdots\cup x_n .$$
We must prove $\mu_n$ is surjective for every $n\ge0$.

STEP 1 (curve facts). Fix one curve $C=C_j$ of genus $g=g_j\ge1$ and write $H^i:=H^i(C_k)$. We record five facts.

(1a) $H^0=\mathbb Q_\ell\cdot 1$. For each $m\ge1$ the sheaf $\mathbb Z/\ell^m$ is constant on $C_{k,\mathrm{\acute et}}$, so $H^0(C_k,\mathbb Z/\ell^m)$ is the group of locally constant functions $\pi_0(C_k)\to\mathbb Z/\ell^m$. Since $C$ is geometrically connected, $C_k$ is connected, and since $C_k$ is locally noetherian it is locally connected, so these functions are constant: $H^0(C_k,\mathbb Z/\ell^m)=\mathbb Z/\ell^m$, and the transition maps are the natural surjections $\mathbb Z/\ell^{m+1}\twoheadrightarrow\mathbb Z/\ell^m$. Hence $H^0(C_k,\mathbb Z_\ell):=\varprojlim_m H^0(C_k,\mathbb Z/\ell^m)=\mathbb Z_\ell$ and $H^0(C_k,\mathbb Q_\ell):=\mathbb Q_\ell\otimes_{\mathbb Z_\ell}\mathbb Z_\ell=\mathbb Q_\ell\cdot1$.

(1b) $H^i=0$ for $i\ge3$. Choose two distinct closed points $P_1,P_2\in C_k$ (possible since $k$ is algebraically closed and $C_k$ is a curve, so it has infinitely many closed points). Set $U_1=C_k\setminus\{P_1\}$, $U_2=C_k\setminus\{P_2\}$. Each $P_i$ is an effective Cartier divisor of degree $1$ on the proper curve $C_k$, hence its defining line bundle has positive degree and is ample; the complement of the support of an effective ample Cartier divisor is the non-vanishing locus of a section of an ample line bundle, hence affine. Thus $U_1,U_2$ and $U_{12}:=U_1\cap U_2=C_k\setminus\{P_1,P_2\}$ are affine $k$-schemes of finite type of Krull dimension $1$, and $U_1\cup U_2=C_k$. For the constant sheaf $\mathbb Q_\ell$ the short exact sequence of sheaves $0\to\mathbb Q_\ell\to j_{1*}\mathbb Q_\ell\oplus j_{2*}\mathbb Q_\ell\to j_{12*}\mathbb Q_\ell\to0$ (exactness checked on stalks) yields the Mayer--Vietoris long exact sequence
$$\cdots\to H^i\to H^i(U_1)\oplus H^i(U_2)\to H^i(U_{12})\to H^{i+1}\to H^{i+1}(U_1)\oplus H^{i+1}(U_2)\to\cdots .$$
Apply lemma_288 (Spark) to each of the affine $k$-schemes $U_1,U_2,U_{12}$ (algebraically closed ground field $k$, $\ell\ne p=\mathrm{char}k$, Krull dimension $1$) with $K=\mathbb Q_\ell[0]\in D^b_c$, whose cohomology sheaves vanish in degrees $q>0$: it gives $H^q(U_1)=H^q(U_2)=H^q(U_{12})=0$ for all $q>1$. Taking $i=2$ in the displayed sequence gives $0\to H^3\to0$, so $H^3=0$; taking $i\ge3$ gives $0\to H^{i+1}\to0$, so $H^{i}=0$ for all $i\ge3$.

(1c) $\dim_{\mathbb Q_\ell}H^2=1$. Apply lemma_77(a) with $Y=C$ over $\mathbb F_{q^m}$, $m=1$, $d=1$: the cycle-class/Gysin isomorphism gives a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear isomorphism $\operatorname{tr}:H^2(C_k)\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell(-1)$. Since $\mathbb Q_\ell(-1)$ is $1$-dimensional, so is $H^2$.

(1d) $\dim_{\mathbb Q_\ell}H^1=2g\ge2$. The field $k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q$ contains all $\ell^m$-th roots of unity ($\ell\ne p$); fix a compatible system $\zeta=(\zeta_{\ell^m})$, which trivialises $\mathbb Z/\ell^m(1)=\mu_{\ell^m}$ as a constant sheaf. By lemma_kummer_h1 (applied over the algebraically closed field $k$ to the smooth projective geometrically connected variety $C_k$) there are functorial isomorphisms $H^1(C_k,\mu_{\ell^m})\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathrm{Pic}(C_k)[\ell^m]$ compatible with $\zeta\mapsto\zeta^{\ell}$ and with $L\mapsto L^{\otimes\ell}$. Since $C_k$ is a smooth projective geometrically integral curve over $k$, the degree map $\deg:\mathrm{Pic}(C_k)\to\mathbb Z$ is a surjective homomorphism whose kernel is $\mathrm{Pic}^0(C_k)=J(k)$, where $J=\mathrm{Pic}^0_{C/\mathbb F_q}\times_{\mathbb F_q}k$ is the Jacobian, an abelian variety of dimension $g$ over $k$. As $\mathbb Z$ is torsion free, every torsion line bundle has degree $0$, so $\mathrm{Pic}(C_k)[\ell^m]=J(k)[\ell^m]$, and under the above identifications the transition map $L\mapsto L^{\otimes\ell}$ is multiplication by $\ell$ on $J(k)$. Hence
$$H^1(C_k,\mathbb Z_\ell(1)):=\varprojlim_m H^1(C_k,\mathbb Z/\ell^m(1))\;\cong\;\varprojlim_m\bigl(J(k)[\ell^m],\,[\ell]\bigr)=:T_\ell(J).$$
The transition maps are surjective: given $L\in J(k)[\ell^m]$, the isogeny $[\ell]:J\to J$ is surjective on $k$-points (image is a closed subgroup scheme of the smooth connected $J$ of the same dimension, hence all of $J$, over an algebraically closed field), so some $M\in J(k)$ satisfies $M^{\otimes\ell}=L$, and then $M^{\otimes\ell^{m+1}}=L^{\otimes\ell^m}=\mathcal O$, i.e. $M\in J(k)[\ell^{m+1}]$. Thus the system satisfies the Mittag-Leffler condition, no $\varprojlim^1$ term appears, and the standard derived-limit comparison for $0\to\mathbb Z_\ell(1)\to\mathbb Q_\ell(1)\to(\mathbb Q_\ell/\mathbb Z_\ell)(1)\to0$ gives a canonical isomorphism $H^1(C_k,\mathbb Q_\ell(1))\cong\mathbb Q_\ell\otimes_{\mathbb Z_\ell}T_\ell(J)$. By lemma_tate_rank, $T_\ell(J)$ is a free $\mathbb Z_\ell$-module of rank $2\dim J=2g$, so $\dim_{\mathbb Q_\ell}H^1(C_k,\mathbb Q_\ell(1))=2g$. Tensoring with the rank-one free sheaf $\mathbb Q_\ell(-1)$ is an autoequivalence of sheaves of $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector spaces, so $\dim_{\mathbb Q_\ell}H^1(C_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=2g\ge2$.

(1e) The image of $\mu^C_2:\bigwedge^2 H^1\to H^2$ is all of $H^2$. Apply lemma_77(b) with $Y=C$, $m=1$, $d=1$, $n=1$: the pairing $\langle x,y\rangle=\operatorname{tr}(x\cup y)$ on $H^1\times H^1$ with values in $\mathbb Q_\ell(-1)$ is PERFECT. Since $\dim H^1=2g\ge2>0$, pick $0\ne x\in H^1$; left non-degeneracy gives $y\in H^1$ with $\operatorname{tr}(x\cup y)=\langle x,y\rangle\ne0$, hence $x\cup y\ne0$ in $H^2$. Then $\mu^C_2(x\wedge y)=x\cup y$ is a nonzero vector of $H^2$, whose $\mathbb Q_\ell$-span is a nonzero subspace of the $1$-dimensional space $H^2$ by (1c); hence the image is $H^2$. Equivalently: every $u\in H^2$ is a finite sum $u=\sum_s a_s\cup b_s$ with $a_s,b_s\in H^1$.

STEP 2 (multiplicative Künneth for $r$ factors). For $s\ge1$ write $X_s=C_1\times_{\mathbb F_q}\cdots\times_{\mathbb F_q}C_s$ with projections $p_{s,j}:X_s\to C_j$, and for $\varepsilon=(\varepsilon_1,\dots,\varepsilon_s)\in\mathbb N^s$ with $\varepsilon_1+\cdots+\varepsilon_s=n$ define
$$\kappa^{(s)}_{\varepsilon}:H^{\varepsilon_1}_1\otimes\cdots\otimes H^{\varepsilon_s}_s\longrightarrow H^n(X_{s,k}),\qquad x_1\otimes\cdots\otimes x_s\longmapsto p_{s,1}^*x_1\cup\cdots\cup p_{s,s}^*x_s .$$
We claim $\kappa^{(s)}:=\bigoplus_{|\varepsilon|=n}\kappa^{(s)}_{\varepsilon}$ is an isomorphism for all $s,n\ge0$. Induct on $s$. For $s=1$ it is the identity. For $s\ge2$, $X_s=X_{s-1}\times_{\mathbb F_q}C_s$ with projections $\pi_1:X_s\to X_{s-1}$, $\pi_2:X_s\to C_s$, and $p_{s,j}=p_{s-1,j}\circ\pi_1$ ($j\le s-1$), $p_{s,s}=\pi_2$. All $X_s$ are smooth projective over $\mathbb F_q$, so lemma_146 applied to the pair $(X_{s-1},C_s)$ says that $\bigoplus_{a+b=n}H^a(X_{s-1,k})\otimes H^b(C_{s,k})\to H^n(X_{s,k})$, $y\otimes x\mapsto\pi_1^*y\cup\pi_2^*x$, is an isomorphism. Substituting the induction hypothesis for $H^a(X_{s-1,k})$ and using functoriality of pullback, $\pi_1^*(p_{s-1,j}^*x_j)=(p_{s-1,j}\circ\pi_1)^*x_j=p_{s,j}^*x_j$, together with associativity of $\cup$, identifies this composite with $\kappa^{(s)}$. Hence $\kappa^{(s)}$ is an isomorphism; in particular $\kappa:=\kappa^{(r)}$ is an isomorphism for $X=X_r$.

STEP 3 (every class on a curve is built from degree $1$). By (1a), (1b), (1c), (1e): for every $m\ge0$ every $x\in H^m(C_j)$ is a sum of classes of one of the forms $\lambda\cdot1$ ($m=0$, $\lambda\in\mathbb Q_\ell$), $a\in H^1(C_j)$ ($m=1$), or $a\cup b$ with $a,b\in H^1(C_j)$ ($m=2$); for $m\ge3$ there is nothing to prove since $H^m=0$.

STEP 4 (surjectivity of $\mu_n$). Let $\xi\in H^n(X_k)$. Since $\kappa$ is an isomorphism, $\xi=\sum_{|\varepsilon|=n}\kappa_\varepsilon(t_\varepsilon)$ with only finitely many nonzero $t_\varepsilon$, and by $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linearity of $\mu_n$ and of the cup product it suffices to treat $\xi=\kappa_\varepsilon(x_1\otimes\cdots\otimes x_r)=p_1^*x_1\cup\cdots\cup p_r^*x_r$ with $x_j\in H^{\varepsilon_j}(C_{j,k})$ and $\varepsilon_1+\cdots+\varepsilon_r=n$ (here $p_j:=p_{r,j}$).
For each $j$, using Step 3 write $x_j$ as a sum of elementary terms of the three allowed types. By multilinearity of $\cup$ on $H^*(X_k)$, $\xi$ is then a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear combination of products of the shape
$$\lambda\cdot\bigl(y_{1,1}\cup\cdots\cup y_{1,\varepsilon_1}\bigr)\cup\bigl(y_{2,1}\cup\cdots\cup y_{2,\varepsilon_2}\bigr)\cup\cdots\cup\bigl(y_{r,1}\cup\cdots\cup y_{r,\varepsilon_r}\bigr),$$\nwhere $\lambda\in\mathbb Q_\ell$ and each $y_{j,t}\in H^1(X_k)$ is the pullback $p_j^*$ of a class of $H^1(C_{j,k})$ (for $\varepsilon_j=0$ the factor is the empty product $1=p_j^*(1)$; for $\varepsilon_j=1$ it is $p_j^*$ of $x_j$; for $\varepsilon_j=2$ it is $p_j^*a\cup p_j^*b=p_j^*(a\cup b)$ by the fact that pullback is a ring homomorphism). Pullback preserves cohomological degree, so every $y_{j,t}$ lies in $H^1(X_k)$. The total number of degree-$1$ factors in such a product is $\varepsilon_1+\cdots+\varepsilon_r=n$, so each product equals
$$\mu_n\bigl(y_{1,1}\wedge\cdots\wedge y_{1,\varepsilon_1}\wedge y_{2,1}\wedge\cdots\wedge y_{r,\varepsilon_r}\bigr)\in\mathrm{im}(\mu_n),$$\nand so does $\lambda$ times it. Hence $\xi\in\mathrm{im}(\mu_n)$.
(If some $\varepsilon_j\ge3$ then $H^{\varepsilon_j}(C_{j,k})=0$ by (1b), so $x_j=0$ and $\xi=0\in\mathrm{im}(\mu_n)$; the cases $n=0$ and $n=1$ are covered by the same argument, and indeed $\mu_0:\mathbb Q_\ell\to H^0(X_k)$, $1\mapsto1$, is an isomorphism by Step 2 in degree $0$ together with (1a), while $\mu_1=\mathrm{id}$.)

Since $\xi$ was arbitrary, $\mu_n$ is surjective for every $n\ge0$. $\blacksquare$

REMARKS on the hypotheses. The assumption $\mathrm{genus}(C_j)\ge1$ is used exactly in (1e), through $\dim H^1(C_j)=2g_j\ge2$: it makes the perfect pairing of lemma_77(b) nonzero. It cannot be dropped: for $C=\mathbb P^1$ one has $H^1=0$ and $H^2=\mathbb Q_\ell(-1)\ne0$, so $\mu_2$ is not surjective. Only surjectivity is claimed; for $g\ge2$ the map $\mu^C_2$ has a source of dimension $\binom{2g}{2}=g(2g-1)>1=\dim H^2$, so it is not injective.

lemma_299.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(X\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension \(d\ge 2\) over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(Y\subset X\) be an effective ample divisor defined over \(\mathbb F_q\) and smooth of pure dimension \(d-1\), let \(U=X\setminus Y\) with closed immersion \(i:Y\hookrightarrow X\), let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\) and \(\ell\neq p\) prime. Suppose \(H^m_{c,\mathrm{\acute et}}(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=0\) for every integer \(m\) with \(m<d\). Then \(i^*:H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) is an isomorphism for every \(n<d-1\) and is injective for \(n=d-1\).
lemma_299.proof:
Write, for brevity,
  H^n(X) := H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell), \quad H^n(Y) := H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell), \quad H^m_c(U) := H^m_{c,\mathrm{\acute et}}(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell),
so that the hypothesis of the lemma is
  (V)  H^m_c(U) = 0  for every integer m < d.

Step 1: The localisation long exact sequence.  We check that the hypotheses of Spark's lemma_283 are satisfied: q=p^a is a prime power; X is smooth, projective, geometrically connected of pure dimension d\ge 2 over \mathbb F_q; Y\subset X is an effective ample divisor defined over \mathbb F_q and smooth of pure dimension d-1; U=X\setminus Y with open immersion j:U\hookrightarrow X and closed immersion i:Y\hookrightarrow X; k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q; and \ell\neq p is prime. Hence lemma_283 provides a long exact sequence of finite-dimensional \mathbb Q_\ell-vector spaces
  \cdots \to H^n_c(U) \xrightarrow{\alpha_n} H^n(X) \xrightarrow{i^*} H^n(Y) \xrightarrow{\delta_n} H^{n+1}_c(U) \to \cdots \qquad (\ast)
for every n\ge 0, whose middle map is precisely the pullback i^* under consideration. Exactness of (\ast) means, for each n\ge 0,
  \ker(i^*:H^n(X)\to H^n(Y)) = \operatorname{im}(\alpha_n), \qquad
  \operatorname{im}(i^*:H^n(X)\to H^n(Y)) = \ker(\delta_n).

Step 2: Negative degrees.  Étale cohomology and compactly supported étale cohomology are the derived functors of (compactly supported) global sections on the étale topos, hence vanish in strictly negative degrees: H^n(X)=H^n(Y)=H^n_c(U)=0 for n<0. Thus for n<0 the map i^* is the map 0\to 0, which is an isomorphism. Since d\ge 2 implies every n<0 satisfies n<d-1, the required statement holds in this range. It remains to treat n\ge 0.

Step 3: The degrees 0\le n\le d-2 (i.e. n<d-1): injectivity.  Fix n with 0\le n\le d-2. Then n\le d-2<d, so by (V) we have H^n_c(U)=0. Consequently \alpha_n:0\to H^n(X) has image 0, and exactness at H^n(X) in (\ast) gives
  \ker(i^*) = \operatorname{im}(\alpha_n) = 0,
so i^*:H^n(X)\to H^n(Y) is injective.

Step 4: The degrees 0\le n\le d-2: surjectivity.  With the same n, we have n+1\le d-1<d, so (V) gives H^{n+1}_c(U)=0. Hence \delta_n:H^n(Y)\to H^{n+1}_c(U)=0 is the zero map and \ker(\delta_n)=H^n(Y). Exactness at H^n(Y) in (\ast) then yields
  \operatorname{im}(i^*) = \ker(\delta_n) = H^n(Y),
so i^* is surjective. Combining Steps 3 and 4, i^*:H^n(X)\xrightarrow{\sim}H^n(Y) is an isomorphism for every n with 0\le n\le d-2, i.e. for every n<d-1 (together with Step 2).

Step 5: The degree n=d-1: injectivity.  Here d-1<d (indeed d\ge 2\ge 1), so (V) gives H^{d-1}_c(U)=0. Thus \alpha_{d-1}:H^{d-1}_c(U)=0\to H^{d-1}(X) is the zero map, and exactness at H^{d-1}(X) in (\ast) gives
  \ker\!\bigl(i^*:H^{d-1}(X)\to H^{d-1}(Y)\bigr) = \operatorname{im}(\alpha_{d-1}) = 0,
so i^* is injective in degree d-1. (No conclusion about surjectivity is claimed here, and indeed the group H^d_c(U) need not vanish, so exactness gives no surjectivity statement in this degree.)

Step 6: Conclusion.  Steps 2 and 4 (with Step 3) show i^* is an isomorphism for all n<d-1, and Step 5 shows i^* is injective for n=d-1. Note that the two ranges are exhaustive for the degrees asserted in the statement, and that d\ge 2 guarantees d-1\ge 1 so that the range 0\le n\le d-2 is exactly the set of non-negative integers <d-1. This completes the proof.

(Remark on the use of the hypotheses: the vanishing assumption (V) was used exactly three times, for m=n and m=n+1 with n\le d-2 and for m=n with n=d-1; in each case the inequality m<d was verified explicitly above. No other input beyond the long exact sequence of lemma_283 and the formal properties of exact sequences is used.)

lemma_296.statement: Let \(K\) be a field of characteristic zero, let \(d\ge1\), let \(V=\bigoplus_{n\in\mathbb Z}V_n\) be a finite-dimensional \(\mathbb Z\)-graded \(K\)-vector space with \(V_n=0\) for \(n<0\) and for \(n>2d\), and let \(L:V\to V\) be a \(K\)-linear endomorphism with \(L(V_n)\subseteq V_{n+2}\) such that \(L^{d-m}:V_m\to V_{2d-m}\) is an isomorphism for every \(0\le m\le d\). For \(0\le m\le d\) set \(P^m=\ker\bigl(L^{d-m+1}:V_m\to V_{2d-m+2}\bigr)\) and set \(P^m=0\) for \(m<0\) and for \(m>d\). Then for every integer \(n\ge0\) the \(K\)-linear map \(\bigoplus_{r\ge\max(0,\,n-d)}P^{\,n-2r}\to V_n\) given by \((x_r)_r\mapsto\sum_r L^{r}x_r\) is injective.
lemma_296.proof:
Throughout, we use the conventions stated in the lemma: $V_m:=0$ for $m<0$ (this is consistent with the hypothesis $V_n=0$ for $n<0$) and for $n>2d$; $L^a$ denotes the $a$-fold iterate of $L$, so that $L^a(V_m)\subseteq V_{m+2a}$; $P^m:=\ker\bigl(L^{d-m+1}:V_m\to V_{2d-m+2}\bigr)$ for $0\le m\le d$, and $P^m:=0$ for $m<0$ and for $m>d$. (The hypothesis $\operatorname{char}K=0$ is never used below; the argument is valid over any field.)

**Well-definedness of the map.** Fix $n\ge 0$ and put $r_0:=\max(0,n-d)$. For $r\ge r_0$ we have $P^{n-2r}\subseteq V_{n-2r}$: indeed if $0\le n-2r\le d$ then $P^{n-2r}$ is by definition a subspace of $V_{n-2r}$, while if $n-2r<0$ or $n-2r>d$ then $P^{n-2r}=0$. Hence $L^r$ maps $P^{n-2r}$ into $V_{n-2r+2r}=V_n$. Moreover $P^{n-2r}=0$ as soon as $2r>n$, so only the finitely many indices $r_0\le r\le \lfloor n/2\rfloor$ contribute nonzero summands; thus $\sum_r L^r x_r$ is a finite sum and
$$\varphi_n:\bigoplus_{r\ge r_0}P^{\,n-2r}\longrightarrow V_n,\qquad (x_r)_r\longmapsto \textstyle\sum_r L^r x_r$$
is a well-defined $K$-linear map.

**Step 1. ($L$ is injective in the lower half.)** For every $m$ with $0\le m\le d-1$, the map $L:V_m\to V_{m+2}$ is injective.

*Proof.* If $m\le d-2$, the hypothesis at index $m$ says $L^{d-m}:V_m\to V_{2d-m}$ is an isomorphism, with $d-m\ge2$. Writing $L^{d-m}=L^{d-m-1}\circ L$ as maps $V_m\to V_{2d-m}$ (valid since $L^{d-m-1}:V_{m+2}\to V_{m+2+2(d-m-1)}=V_{2d-m}$), we get: $v\in V_m$, $Lv=0\ \Rightarrow\ L^{d-m}v=L^{d-m-1}(Lv)=0\ \Rightarrow\ v=0$, the last step using injectivity of the isomorphism $L^{d-m}$. If $m=d-1$, the hypothesis at index $d-1$ says precisely that $L^{d-(d-1)}=L:V_{d-1}\to V_{2d-(d-1)}=V_{d+1}$ is an isomorphism, hence injective. $\square$

*Iterated form.* If $a\ge0$, $r\ge0$ and $a+2j\le d-1$ for all $0\le j\le r-1$ (equivalently, $a+2(r-1)\le d-1$ when $r\ge1$), then $L^r:V_a\to V_{a+2r}$ is injective, being a composite $V_a\xrightarrow{L}V_{a+2}\xrightarrow{L}\cdots\xrightarrow{L}V_{a+2r}$ of injective maps given by Step 1.

**Step 2. (Primitive decomposition in the lower half.)** For every $m$ with $0\le m\le d$ one has an internal direct-sum decomposition
$$V_m=P^m\oplus L(V_{m-2}).$$

*Proof.* *Case $m\le1$.* Then $V_{m-2}=0$ because $m-2<0$. Also $2d-m+2\ge 2d+1>2d$, so $V_{2d-m+2}=0$ and the map $L^{d-m+1}:V_m\to V_{2d-m+2}$ is the zero map; hence $P^m=V_m$. Thus $V_m=P^m=P^m\oplus 0=P^m\oplus L(V_{m-2})$, and the sum is trivially direct.

*Case $2\le m\le d$.* Then $0\le m-2\le d-2\le d$, so the hypothesis applies at index $m-2$: the map $L^{d-(m-2)}=L^{d-m+2}:V_{m-2}\to V_{2d-(m-2)}=V_{2d-m+2}$ is an isomorphism (note $d-m+2\ge2\ge0$, and $2d-m+2\le 2d$ since $m\ge2$, so this is genuinely one of the stated hypotheses).

*Sum.* Let $x\in V_m$. Both $L^{d-m+1}x$ and (for $y\in V_{m-2}$) $L^{d-m+2}y$ lie in $V_{2d-m+2}$: indeed $L^{d-m+1}x\in V_{m+2(d-m+1)}=V_{2d-m+2}$. By surjectivity of $L^{d-m+2}:V_{m-2}\xrightarrow{\sim}V_{2d-m+2}$ there is $y\in V_{m-2}$ with $L^{d-m+2}y=L^{d-m+1}x$. Then $L^{d-m+1}(x-Ly)=L^{d-m+1}x-L^{d-m+2}y=0$, so $x-Ly\in P^m$, and $x=(x-Ly)+Ly\in P^m+L(V_{m-2})$.

*Intersection.* Let $x\in P^m\cap L(V_{m-2})$, say $x=Ly$ with $y\in V_{m-2}$. Then $0=L^{d-m+1}x=L^{d-m+1}(Ly)=L^{d-m+2}y$. Since $L^{d-m+2}:V_{m-2}\to V_{2d-m+2}$ is an isomorphism, $y=0$, hence $x=0$. So the sum is direct. $\square$

**Step 3. (Lower half: the asserted map is an isomorphism for $0\le n\le d$.)** We prove by induction on $m$ that for $0\le m\le d$ the map
$$\Phi_m:\bigoplus_{r\ge0}P^{\,m-2r}\longrightarrow V_m,\qquad (x_r)_r\mapsto \textstyle\sum_r L^r x_r$$
is an isomorphism (again the sum is finite since $P^{m-2r}=0$ for $2r>m$).

*Base $m=0,1$.* By Step 2 (case $m\le1$), $P^m=V_m$, and for $r\ge1$ one has $m-2r<0$, so $P^{m-2r}=0$. Hence $\bigoplus_{r\ge0}P^{m-2r}=P^m=V_m$ and $\Phi_m=\mathrm{id}_{V_m}$, an isomorphism.

*Inductive step $2\le m\le d$.* Assume $\Phi_{m-2}$ is an isomorphism; equivalently, $V_{m-2}=\bigoplus_{r\ge0} L^r P^{\,m-2-2r}$ (internal direct sum). First we record that
$$L(V_{m-2})=\bigoplus_{r\ge0} L^{r+1}P^{\,m-2-2r}.$$
Indeed, applying $L$ to the decomposition of $V_{m-2}$ gives $L(V_{m-2})=\sum_{r\ge0}L^{r+1}P^{m-2-2r}$; for directness, suppose $\sum_r L^{r+1}x_r=0$ with $x_r\in P^{m-2-2r}$ (finitely many nonzero). Then $L\bigl(\sum_r L^r x_r\bigr)=0$ with $\sum_r L^r x_r\in V_{m-2}$. Since $m-2\le d-2\le d-1$, Step 1 gives injectivity of $L:V_{m-2}\to V_m$, so $\sum_r L^r x_r=0$; the induction hypothesis (directness in $V_{m-2}$) gives $L^r x_r=0$ for each $r$; and $x_r\in V_{m-2-2r}$ with $L^r:V_{m-2-2r}\to V_{m-2}$ injective by the iterated form of Step 1 (its intermediate indices are $m-2-2r+2j\le m-2\le d-2\le d-1$ for $0\le j\le r-1$). Hence $x_r=0$ for all $r$.

Now, by Step 2, $V_m=P^m\oplus L(V_{m-2})=P^{m-0}\oplus\bigl(\bigoplus_{r\ge0}L^{r+1}P^{m-2-2r}\bigr)=\bigoplus_{s\ge0}L^s P^{\,m-2s}$ as an internal direct sum (re-index $s=r+1$ for $s\ge1$). Surjectivity of $\Phi_m$ is immediate: $v=p+\sum_r L^{r+1}y_r$ with $p\in P^m$, $y_r\in P^{m-2-2r}$ is $\Phi_m$ of the tuple with $0$-component $p$ and $s$-component $y_{s-1}$. Injectivity: if $\sum_r L^r x_r=0$ with $x_r\in P^{m-2r}$, then $x_0=-\sum_{r\ge1}L^r x_r$; the right-hand side equals $L\bigl(\sum_{r\ge1}L^{r-1}x_r\bigr)\in L(V_{m-2})$ (each $L^{r-1}x_r\in V_{m-2r+2r-2}=V_{m-2}$), while $x_0\in P^m$; directness of $V_m=P^m\oplus L(V_{m-2})$ forces $x_0=0$ and $\sum_{r\ge1}L^r x_r=0$, and the directness of $L(V_{m-2})=\bigoplus_{r\ge0}L^{r+1}P^{m-2-2r}$ (applied with index $r-1$) forces $x_r=0$ for all $r\ge1$. Thus $\Phi_m$ is an isomorphism, completing the induction.

For $0\le n\le d$ we have $\max(0,n-d)=0$, so the map of the lemma at $n$ is exactly $\Phi_n$, hence an isomorphism; in particular it is injective.

**Step 4. (Upper half: $d<n\le 2d$.)** Put $j:=2d-n$; then $0\le j<d$ (as $n\le2d$ gives $j\ge0$, and $n>d$ gives $j<d$). The hypothesis at index $j$ says that
$$\psi:=L^{d-j}=L^{n-d}:V_j\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }V_{2d-j}=V_n$$
is an isomorphism (using $d-j=d-(2d-n)=n-d$ and $2d-j=n$).

Let $(x_r)_{r\ge n-d}$ be a tuple with $x_r\in P^{\,n-2r}$, finitely many nonzero, and suppose $\sum_{r\ge n-d}L^r x_r=0$ in $V_n$. Re-index by $s:=r-(n-d)\ge0$ and set $u_s:=x_{s+n-d}$. The change of index is a bijection $\{s\in\mathbb Z:s\ge0\}\xrightarrow{\sim}\{r\in\mathbb Z:r\ge n-d\}$, and
$$j-2s=(2d-n)-2\bigl(r-(n-d)\bigr)=2d-n-2r+2n-2d=n-2r,$$
so $u_s\in P^{\,j-2s}$. Each $L^s u_s$ lies in $V_{j-2s+2s}=V_j$, and the relation $\sum_r L^r x_r=0$ becomes
$$0=\sum_{s\ge0}L^{s+n-d}u_s=L^{n-d}\Bigl(\sum_{s\ge0}L^s u_s\Bigr)=\psi\Bigl(\sum_{s\ge0}L^s u_s\Bigr),$$
where $\sum_{s\ge0}L^s u_s\in V_j$. Since $\psi:V_j\to V_n$ is an isomorphism, $\sum_{s\ge0}L^s u_s=0$ in $V_j$. Because $j\le d$, Step 3 applies to $j$: $\Phi_j:\bigoplus_{s\ge0}P^{j-2s}\to V_j$ is an isomorphism, so $L^s u_s=0$ for every $s$. Finally $u_s\in V_{j-2s}$ and $L^s:V_{j-2s}\to V_j$ is injective by the iterated form of Step 1 (its intermediate indices are $j-2s+2t\le j-2\le d-3\le d-1$ for $0\le t\le s-1$, using $j\le d-1$; the case $s=0$ is trivial). Hence $u_s=0$ for all $s$, i.e. $x_r=0$ for all $r$. This proves injectivity of $\varphi_n$ for $d<n\le2d$.

(For orientation: the same computation shows $\varphi_n$ is actually surjective here, since $V_j=\bigoplus_{s\ge0}L^sP^{j-2s}$ and $\psi$ is an isomorphism, so $V_n=\bigoplus_{r\ge n-d}L^rP^{\,n-2r}$; only injectivity is required.)

**Step 5. ($n>2d$.)** Then $V_n=0$. For a summand of the domain to be nonzero we need $0\le n-2r\le d$; but $r\ge n-d$ gives $n-2r\le n-2(n-d)=2d-n<0$, so $P^{\,n-2r}=0$ for every $r\ge n-d$ by the convention $P^m=0$ for $m<0$. The domain is therefore $0$, and $\varphi_n:0\to0$ is injective.

**Conclusion.** Steps 3, 4 and 5 cover all integers $n\ge0$ (namely $0\le n\le d$, $d<n\le2d$, $n>2d$), and in each case the map $\varphi_n:\bigoplus_{r\ge\max(0,\,n-d)}P^{\,n-2r}\to V_n$, $(x_r)_r\mapsto\sum_r L^r x_r$, is injective. This is exactly the statement of the lemma. $\blacksquare$

*Remark on the range restriction.* The restriction $r\ge\max(0,n-d)$ is essential: without it the statement is false (e.g. $d=2$, $V_0=K\cdot1$, $V_2=Ke_1\oplus Ke_2$, $V_4=Kt$, $L(1)=e_1$, $L(ae_1+be_2)=at$, $L=0$ elsewhere, where $P^2=Ke_2\ne0$ and the $r=1$ component $e_2$ of the unrestricted sum at $n=4$ maps to $L(e_2)=0$). Our argument uses the restriction exactly in Step 4, where $r\ge n-d$ is what makes $\psi=L^{n-d}$ factor out of the sum, and in Step 5.

lemma_identity_component_clopen_subgroup.statement: Let \(k\) be a perfect field and let \(H\) be a group scheme of finite type over \(k\). Then the connected component of the identity element of the underlying topological space of \(H\) is open and closed, and the corresponding open-and-closed subscheme \(H^{0}\subseteq H\) is a closed \(k\)-subgroup scheme of \(H\).
lemma_identity_component_clopen_subgroup.proof:
Throughout, |X| denotes the underlying topological space of a scheme X, and e ∈ |H| (equivalently the section e: Spec k → H) denotes the identity of the group scheme H. The proof is organized in eight claims; everything is proved from scheme theory and field theory, no result from the proved corpus is used.

=== Claim 1 (field theory over a perfect field) ===
(a) (Standard) If k is perfect, every finitely generated field extension L/k is separably generated: there are elements t_1,…,t_r ∈ L algebraically independent over k such that L/k(t_1,…,t_r) is finite separable (in characteristic 0 any transcendence basis works; in characteristic p this is the theorem that finitely generated extensions of a perfect field are separable, equivalently admit a separating transcendence basis).
(b) If k is perfect and K, M are finitely generated field extensions of k, then K ⊗_k M is reduced.
Proof of (b). By (a) applied to M, with F := k(t_1,…,t_r) ⊂ M and M/F finite separable, M ≅ F[T]/(f) with f ∈ F[T] monic irreducible and separable, i.e. gcd_{F[T]}(f,f') = 1. Tensoring the exact sequence 0 → F[T] → F[T] → M → 0 (multiplication by f) with K ⊗_k F over F gives
   K ⊗_k M ≅ (K ⊗_k F) ⊗_F M ≅ R[T]/(f),   R := K ⊗_k F = S^{-1}K[t_1,…,t_r],  S = k[t_1,…,t_r]\{0},
where the last identification uses that R is an F-algebra, so f ∈ F[T] ⊂ R[T]. R is a localization of the polynomial ring K[t_1,…,t_r], hence a domain and a UFD, with fraction field C := k'(t_1,…,t_r) where k' := Frac of the polynomial ring; write C = Frac(R).
We show C_0 := R[T]/(f) is reduced. Let h̄ ∈ C_0 with h̄² = 0, and choose a representative h ∈ R[T] with deg h < deg f (division by the monic polynomial f is valid inside R[T]). Then h² = f·q in R[T], hence also in C[T]. In C[T] (a UFD) factor f = g_1⋯g_s into distinct monic irreducibles: they are distinct because gcd_{F[T]}(f,f') = 1 yields a Bézout relation af + bf' = 1 with a,b ∈ F[T] ⊂ C[T], hence gcd_{C[T]}(f,f') = 1, i.e. f is squarefree. Each g_i is prime in C[T]; g_i | h² forces g_i | h; since the g_i are distinct and pairwise coprime, f = ∏ g_i divides h in C[T], say h = f·h_0 with h_0 ∈ C[T]. Comparing degrees, deg h_0 = deg h − deg f < 0, so h_0 = 0 and h = 0. Hence h̄ = 0, and C_0 is reduced. ∎(Claim 1b)

=== Claim 2 (geometric reducedness over a perfect field) ===
Let k be perfect.
(a) Every reduced k-algebra A of finite type is geometrically reduced: A ⊗_k K' is reduced for every field extension K'/k.
Proof. First, filtered colimits of reduced rings are reduced: if R = colim_{i∈I} R_i with I filtered and each R_i reduced, and x ∈ R satisfies x^n = 0, write x as the image of x_i ∈ R_i; then x_i^n maps to 0 in R, hence to 0 in R_j for some j ≥ i (filtered colimits are exact), so the image of x_i in R_j is 0 by reducedness of R_j, whence x = 0 in R.
Now write K' as the filtered colimit of its finitely generated k-subextensions; then A ⊗_k K' = colim(A ⊗_k K'_i), so by the previous paragraph it suffices to treat K'/k finitely generated. Let p_1,…,p_m be the minimal primes of A (finitely many, A noetherian); since A is reduced, A ↪ ∏_i A/p_i, and tensoring over k with the flat k-module K' gives an injection A ⊗_k K' ↪ ∏_i (A/p_i ⊗_k K'). So we may assume A is a domain. Then A ↪ Frac(A) gives, by flatness of K'/k and of Frac(A)/k, injections A ⊗_k K' ↪ Frac(A) ⊗_k K' ↪ Frac(A) ⊗_k Frac(K'), and the right-hand ring is reduced by Claim 1(b). Subrings of reduced rings are reduced. ∎
(b) If A and B are reduced k-algebras of finite type, then A ⊗_k B is reduced.
Proof. As above reduce to B a domain with fraction field M: A ⊗_k B ↪ A ⊗_k M, and A ⊗_k M is reduced by (a) applied to A and the extension M/k. ∎

=== Claim 3 (the reduction of H is a closed subgroup scheme) ===
H_red is a closed k-subgroup scheme of H. Indeed, by Claim 2(b) the product H_red ×_k H_red is reduced. The composite H_red ×_k H_red → H ×_k H → H therefore factors uniquely through H_red, by the universal property of the reduction (Hom(T, X_red) = Hom(T, X) for every reduced scheme T). The same argument applies to the inverse ι: H → H restricted to H_red (source reduced), and to the unit e: Spec k → H (Spec k is reduced). The group axioms on H_red follow from the corresponding axioms on H together with uniqueness in the universal property. ∎

=== Claim 4 (a reduced group scheme of finite type over a perfect field is smooth) ===
Let K be perfect and let R be a reduced group scheme of finite type over K. Then R → Spec K is smooth.
Proof. By Claim 2(a), R is geometrically reduced, so R_{K̄} := R ×_K K̄ (K̄ an algebraic closure of K) is a reduced group scheme of finite type over K̄. Since smoothness is fpqc local on the base and Spec K̄ → Spec K is faithfully flat, it suffices to prove R_{K̄} smooth over K̄. Thus we may (and do) assume K = K̄ algebraically closed.
Let U ⊂ R be the smooth locus of R → Spec K; it is open, because smoothness is open in the source for morphisms locally of finite presentation (R is of finite type over the field K, hence locally of finite presentation).
Step (i): U contains every generic point of R. Indeed, let η be a generic point, represented on an affine open V = Spec B (B a finitely generated K-algebra) by a minimal prime p. Since B is reduced and noetherian, B_p is a field, namely O_{R,η} = κ(η) = Frac(B/p), a finitely generated field extension of K. By Claim 1(a), κ(η)/K is separably generated, hence κ(η) is a smooth K-algebra (K → K(t_1,…,t_r) is smooth, and a finite separable extension is étale, hence smooth; smoothness is preserved by composition). For a morphism locally of finite presentation, smoothness at a point is equivalent to smoothness of the local ring of the point over the base local ring; hence R is smooth at η, i.e. η ∈ U.
Step (ii): U(K) ≠ ∅. Since K is algebraically closed and R is of finite type over K, the closed points of R are K-rational (Zariski's lemma: residue fields of closed points are finite algebraic over K) and are dense in R (R is Jacobson). As U is a nonempty open (Step (i)), U(K) ≠ ∅; choose s ∈ U(K).
Step (iii): R(K) ⊂ U. For x ∈ R(K), left translation t_{xs^{-1}}: R → R by the K-point xs^{-1} ∈ R(K) is a K-automorphism of R with t_{xs^{-1}}(s) = x. A K-automorphism of R preserves the smooth locus (it identifies the local rings at s and at x as K-algebras, and smoothness at a point is invariant under K-isomorphism), so t_{xs^{-1}}(U) = U, whence x ∈ U.
Step (iv): U = R. The complement Z := R \ U is closed and satisfies Z(K) = ∅ by Step (iii). If Z were nonempty, being noetherian it would contain a closed point, which is K-rational since K is algebraically closed and Z is of finite type over K — contradiction. Hence Z = ∅. ∎

=== Claim 5 (components of a smooth scheme over a field) ===
Let S be a scheme smooth over a field K. Then the irreducible components of |S| are open and closed, each point of |S| lies in a unique irreducible component, and the connected components of |S| are open and closed.
Proof. For every s ∈ S the local ring O_{S,s} is regular (smooth over a field), and a regular local ring is a domain (Auslander–Buchsbaum). Irreducible components of |S| through s correspond bijectively to minimal primes of O_{S,s}; since O_{S,s} is a domain it has exactly one minimal prime, so s lies in a unique irreducible component.
Irreducible components are always closed. To see they are open, let Z be an irreducible component and x ∈ Z. Choose a quasi-compact open neighbourhood V of x in S; V is noetherian, so its irreducible components V_1,…,V_m are closed in V and V = ∪V_j. Each V_j, being irreducible, is contained in an irreducible component X_{i(j)} of S, and this is unique: if V_j ⊂ X_i ∩ X_{i'} with i ≠ i', the generic point of V_j (which exists, V_j being noetherian and irreducible) would lie in two distinct irreducible components. Since the unique component through x is Z, we have i(j) = index(Z) for some j, so x ∈ W := ∪_{i(j)=index(Z)} V_j. W is a finite union of closed subsets of V, and its complement in V is the finite union of the remaining V_j, hence also closed; so W is clopen in V. Moreover W ⊂ Z ∩ V. Thus Z is a neighbourhood of each of its points, i.e. Z is open.
Finally, each irreducible component is connected, hence contained in a unique connected component; so every connected component is a union of irreducible components, hence a union of open sets, hence open. Connected components are always closed. ∎

=== Claim 6 (products over an algebraically closed field) ===
Let k be algebraically closed and let X, Y be nonempty connected schemes of finite type over k. Then X ×_k Y is connected.
Proof. Suppose X ×_k Y = Z_1 ⊔ Z_2 with Z_1, Z_2 nonempty clopen. The projection pr: X ×_k Y → Y is the base change of X → Spec k, which is flat (every k-module is flat) and locally of finite presentation; hence pr is flat and locally of finite presentation, therefore an open map. For y ∈ Y(k) the fibre pr^{-1}(y) = X ×_k Spec κ(y) = X ×_k Spec k ≅ X is nonempty and connected, so it lies entirely in Z_1 or entirely in Z_2. Put U_i := pr(Z_i) (open in |Y|) and D := Y(k), which is dense in |Y| (closed points of a finite type scheme over an algebraically closed field are rational and dense). For y ∈ D, y ∈ U_1 ∩ U_2 would mean the fibre over y meets both Z_1 and Z_2, impossible; and U_1 ∩ D and U_2 ∩ D cover D (fibres are nonempty). Hence U_1 ∩ U_2 is an open set disjoint from the dense set D, so U_1 ∩ U_2 = ∅, and |Y| \ (U_1 ∪ U_2) is closed and disjoint from D, so U_1 ∪ U_2 = |Y|. Thus |Y| is a disjoint union of two open sets, and since Y is connected exactly one U_i is empty; the corresponding Z_i is then empty, contradiction. ∎

=== Claim 7 (the algebraically closed case) ===
Let k be algebraically closed and H a group scheme of finite type over k. Let C ⊂ |H| be the connected component of e. Then C is open and closed in |H|, and the corresponding open-and-closed subscheme C ⊂ H is a subgroup scheme.
Proof. By Claim 3, H_red is a closed subgroup scheme, and by Claim 4 it is smooth over k. By Claim 5, the connected components of |H_red| = |H| are open and closed; so C is clopen, and we denote by C also the corresponding open-and-closed subscheme of H.
Multiplication. The scheme C ×_k C is nonempty (it contains e × e) and its factors C are nonempty, connected and of finite type over k (C is an open subscheme of the noetherian k-scheme H, hence quasi-compact and of finite type). By Claim 6, C ×_k C is connected. The multiplication morphism m: H ×_k H → H is continuous, so m(|C ×_k C|) is a connected subset of |H|; it contains e, because m(e,e) = e. Hence m(|C ×_k C|) ⊂ C, C being the maximal connected subset of |H| containing e. Since C → H is an open immersion, a morphism factors through it if and only if the image of its underlying topological space is contained in |C|; thus m restricts to a morphism C ×_k C → C.
Inverse. The image ι(|C|) is connected (continuous image of a connected space) and contains e (ι(e) = e); hence ι(|C|) ⊂ C, and ι restricts to a morphism C → C.
Unit. The section e: Spec k → H has image {e} ⊂ |C|, hence factors through the open subscheme C.
Associativity, unit and inverse axioms on C hold because they hold on H and C → H is a monomorphism. Hence C is an open subgroup scheme; being clopen it is also a closed subscheme. ∎

=== Claim 8 (descent of the clopen subgroup scheme) ===
Let k be perfect, H a group scheme of finite type over k, k̄/k an algebraic closure, p: H_{k̄} := H ×_k k̄ → H the projection, and let C ⊂ H_{k̄} be the open-and-closed subgroup scheme of Claim 7 applied to H_{k̄}. Then:
(a) For every τ ∈ Gal(k̄/k), the automorphism σ_τ := id_H × Spec τ of H_{k̄} satisfies σ_τ(C) = C.
Proof. σ_τ is the base change of the identity homomorphism id_H along Spec τ: Spec k̄ → Spec k, hence is compatible with the group structures: on k̄-points it is the τ-conjugation map H(k̄) → H(k̄), a group isomorphism carrying e to e. Consequently σ_τ is a homeomorphism of |H_{k̄}| preserving e, so it maps the connected component of e onto itself. ∎
(b) There is a unique open-and-closed subscheme H^0 ⊂ H with (H^0)_{k̄} = C.
Proof. Clopen subschemes of a scheme X correspond bijectively to idempotents of Γ(X, O_X): an idempotent ε gives the clopen set D(ε), and a clopen U gives the section which is 1 on U and 0 on the complement (glued along the two open pieces). So C corresponds to an idempotent ε ∈ Γ(H_{k̄}, O). By (a), σ_τ^*(ε) = ε for all τ.
We show ε descends. Cover H by affine opens V_λ = Spec A_λ; then p^{-1}(V_λ) = Spec(A_λ ⊗_k k̄) and ε|_{p^{-1}(V_λ)} is a Gal(k̄/k)-invariant idempotent of A_λ ⊗_k k̄. Such an ε_λ lies in A_λ ⊗_k k' for some finite subextension k'/k; enlarging k' inside k̄ we may take k'/k finite Galois (k̄/k is Galois). The restriction map Gal(k̄/k) → Gal(k'/k) is surjective, so ε_λ is fixed by Gal(k'/k), and by Galois descent for vector spaces (equivalently the normal basis theorem: k' ≅ k[Gal(k'/k)] as a module with Galois action, so (A ⊗_k k')^{Gal(k'/k)} = A for every k-vector space A) we get ε_λ ∈ A_λ. Uniqueness of the preimage (A_λ → A_λ ⊗_k k̄ is faithfully flat, hence injective) guarantees that the ε_λ agree on overlaps and glue to a unique idempotent ε_0 ∈ Γ(H, O_H) restricting to ε. Let H^0 ⊂ H be the corresponding clopen subscheme. Since O_H → p_*O_{H_{k̄}} is faithfully flat, ε_0 and ε define the same subscheme after base change, i.e. (H^0)_{k̄} = C. ∎
(c) H^0 is a k-subgroup scheme of H.
Proof. We use that for an open immersion j: V ↪ X, a morphism f: T → X factors through V if and only if f(|T|) ⊂ |V|, and that this condition can be checked after any surjective flat quasi-compact (in particular faithfully flat) base change of T, because such a map is surjective on underlying topological spaces and j is a monomorphism (so the factorization, when it exists, is unique).
Multiplication: base change along the faithfully flat morphism (H^0 ×_k H^0)_{k̄} = C ×_{k̄} C → H^0 ×_k H^0. After this base change the multiplication is m_{k̄}|_{C × C}, which factors through C by Claim 7. Hence m|_{H^0 ×_k H^0} factors through H^0.
Inverse: base change along the faithfully flat H_{k̄} → H; ι_{k̄}|_C factors through C by Claim 7, hence ι|_{H^0} factors through H^0.
Unit: base change along Spec k̄ → Spec k; the unit section of H_{k̄} factors through C by Claim 7, hence so does e: Spec k → H.
The group axioms hold since H^0 → H is a monomorphism and they hold in H. ∎
(d) |H^0| is the connected component of e in |H|.
Proof. The map |H^0_{k̄}| = |C| → |H^0| is surjective (p is faithfully flat) and |C| is connected, so |H^0| is connected; it contains e by (c). Thus |H^0| ⊂ U, where U is the connected component of e.
For the reverse inclusion, note that |H| = |H_red| and that H_red is smooth over k by Claims 3 and 4; hence by Claim 5 the irreducible components of |H| are open and closed, and each point of |H| lies in a unique one. Since H^0 is open in H, any irreducible component of |H| meeting |H^0| is contained in |H^0| (it would otherwise split into two nonempty clopen pieces); so |H^0| is a union of irreducible components. If U ≠ |H^0|, pick u ∈ U \ |H^0| and let Z be the irreducible component containing u. Then Z ⊂ U (Z is connected and meets U) and Z ∩ |H^0| = ∅ (otherwise Z ⊂ |H^0|, contradicting u ∉ |H^0|). Then U = |H^0| ⊔ (U \ |H^0| expresses U as a disjoint union of two nonempty sets that are open in U (|H^0| is open in |H|; U \ |H^0| is a union of the open sets Z ⊂ U not contained in |H^0|), contradicting the connectedness of U. Hence |H^0| = U. ∎

=== Conclusion ===
By Claim 8(d) the connected component U of e in |H| equals |H^0|, which is open and closed in |H| by Claim 8(b); this proves the first assertion. The open-and-closed subscheme of H on U is precisely H^0, which is a k-subgroup scheme by Claim 8(c) and a closed subscheme because its complement in H is open (H^0 is clopen). Therefore H^0 ⊆ H is a closed k-subgroup scheme, which proves the second assertion. ∎

lemma_302.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(X\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, let \(G\) be a finite group of \(\mathbb F_q\)-automorphisms of \(X\) whose order is prime to \(\ell\), let \(\pi:X\to Z:=X/G\) be the quotient morphism, and suppose \(Z\) is smooth and geometrically connected over \(\mathbb F_q\). Write \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\) and \(F_Z,F_X\) for the \(q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius \((\mathrm{id}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(c)=c^q\), of \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) and \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\). If \(F_X\) is semisimple on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) for every \(n\ge0\), then \(F_Z\) is semisimple on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) for every \(n\ge0\).
lemma_302.proof:
We prove that the $q$-power arithmetic Frobenius $F_Z=(\mathrm{id}_{Z_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*$, $\sigma(c)=c^q$, is semisimple (equivalently, diagonalizable over $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$, cf. the standard equivalence between the two formulations) on $H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ for every $n\ge 0$.

STEP 0. Geometry of $X$ and $Z$. Write $D:=\dim X$. A smooth scheme over a field is regular, hence locally integral; a regular noetherian scheme has open irreducible components (regular local rings are domains), so a connected smooth scheme has exactly one irreducible component, is irreducible, and is therefore integral. Since $X$ is smooth and geometrically connected over $\mathbb F_q$, each $X_{\overline{\mathbb F}_q}$-geometric fibre is connected and smooth, hence integral; thus $X$ is integral of pure dimension $D$ (and non-empty, a variety being non-empty by convention; if $X=\varnothing$ then $Z=\varnothing$ and all cohomology groups below are $0$, so the statement is vacuous). The same argument applied to $Z$ (smooth and geometrically connected over $\mathbb F_q$ by hypothesis) shows $Z$ is integral of pure dimension $\dim Z$. Since $G$ consists of $\mathbb F_q$-automorphisms, the quotient $\pi:X\to Z$ is a morphism over $\mathbb F_q$, and $G$ acts on $\pi$ trivially on the base: $\pi\circ g=\pi$ for all $g\in G$.

STEP 1. The quotient map is finite, surjective, and $\mathcal O_Z=(\pi_*\mathcal O_X)^G$. We use the standard theorem on geometric quotients by finite groups (SGA 1, Exp. V, Prop. 1.8): if a finite group $G$ acts on a scheme $X$ projective over an affine noetherian base $S$, the geometric quotient $\pi:X\to X/G$ exists, $\pi$ is finite, $X/G$ is projective over $S$, and $\mathcal O_{X/G}=(\pi_*\mathcal O_X)^G$. Taking $S=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_q$ (affine noetherian) and $X$ projective over $\mathbb F_q$, we obtain: $Z$ is projective (hence proper) over $\mathbb F_q$, $\pi$ is finite (hence proper), and $\mathcal O_Z=(\pi_*\mathcal O_X)^G$. Together with the hypothesis that $Z$ is smooth and geometrically connected over $\mathbb F_q$, this shows that $X$ and $Z$ both satisfy the standing hypotheses ("smooth projective geometrically connected") of lemmas lemma_242 and lemma_266.

STEP 2. Function fields and degree of $\pi$. Let $\eta\in Z$ be the generic point. Localising the equality $\mathcal O_Z=(\pi_*\mathcal O_X)^G$ at $\eta$ gives
$$\mathbb F_q(Z)=(\pi_*\mathcal O_X)^G_{\eta}.$$ We claim invariants commute with this localisation. Indeed, let $A$ be an $\mathcal O_{Z,\eta}$-algebra with $G$ acting trivially on $\mathcal O_{Z,\eta}$, and let $S=\mathcal O_{Z,\eta}\setminus\{0\}$; if $a/s\in (S^{-1}A)^G$ then for each $g\in G$ there is $t_g\in S$ with $t_g(s\,ga-s\,a)=0$; putting $t=\prod_{g}t_g\in S$ gives $t(ga-a)=0$ for all $g$, hence $ta\in A^G$ and $a/s=(ta)/(ts)\in S^{-1}A^G$. The reverse inclusion is clear. Thus
$$\mathbb F_q(Z)=\bigl((\pi_*\mathcal O_X)_{\eta}\bigr)^G.$$
Now $\pi$ is finite, so for an affine open $\operatorname{Spec}B\subset Z$ we have $\pi^{-1}(\operatorname{Spec}B)=\operatorname{Spec}A$ with $A$ a finite $B$-algebra; $X$ integral and $\pi$ dominant (as we now see, $\mathbb F_q(Z)\subset\mathbb F_q(X)$ is a field extension) imply $A$ is a domain with $\operatorname{Frac}A=\mathbb F_q(X)$, and
$$(\pi_*\mathcal O_X)_{\eta}=A\otimes_B \operatorname{Frac}B=\operatorname{Frac}A=\mathbb F_q(X),$$
because localising the domain $A$, which is finite (hence integral) over the domain $B$, at $B\setminus\{0\}$ gives an artinian domain, i.e. a field, namely $\operatorname{Frac}A$. Hence
$$\mathbb F_q(Z)=\mathbb F_q(X)^G.$$
Since $X$ is integral, an $\mathbb F_q$-automorphism of $X$ is determined by its action on $\mathbb F_q(X)$, so the given inclusion $G\hookrightarrow\operatorname{Aut}_{\mathbb F_q}(X)$ identifies $G$ with a finite group of $\mathbb F_q$-automorphisms of the field $K:=\mathbb F_q(X)$. By Artin's theorem on Galois theory of fields, $K/K^G$ is Galois with group $G$ and $[K:K^G]=|G|$. Therefore $\pi$ is generically finite of degree
$$d:=[\mathbb F_q(X):\mathbb F_q(Z)]=|G|\ge 1,$$
and $\dim Z=\operatorname{trdeg}_{\mathbb F_q}\mathbb F_q(Z)=\operatorname{trdeg}_{\mathbb F_q}\mathbb F_q(X)=\dim X=D$, so $X$ and $Z$ have the same pure dimension $D$. Finally $\pi$ is surjective: $\pi$ is finite, hence closed, so its image is closed; the image contains $\eta$ (the fibre over $\eta$ is $\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_q(X)\ne\varnothing$), hence is dense; a closed dense subset of the irreducible space $Z$ is $Z$.

By hypothesis $\ell\nmid |G|=d$; hence $d\in\mathbb Z_{(\ell)}^{\times}\subset\mathbb Z_\ell^{\times}\subset\mathbb Q_\ell^{\times}$, i.e. $d$ is invertible in $\mathbb Q_\ell$.

STEP 3. Vanishing above twice the dimension. We record the standard fact that if $W$ is a smooth projective variety of pure dimension $D$ over an algebraically closed field $k$ and $\ell\neq\operatorname{char}k$, then $H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(W,\mathbb Q_\ell)=0$ for $n>2D$ (this is the vanishing that is implicitly built into the statements of lemmas such as lemma_295, where $V_n=0$ for $n>2d$ is assumed). Proof. (a) By Noether normalization for projective varieties (Zariski's form: after a Veronese embedding, a general linear projection is finite), there is a finite surjective morphism $p:W\to\mathbb P^D_k$.
