(b) A finite morphism is exact on étale sheaves: for $\bar y\to\mathbb P^D$ a geometric point, $W\times_{\mathbb P^D}\operatorname{Spec}\mathcal O^{\mathrm{sh}}_{\mathbb P^D,\bar y}$ is a finite scheme over a strictly henselian local ring, hence a finite disjoint union of strictly henselian local schemes, whose étale cohomology is that of a geometric point; so $R^qp_*=0$ for $q>0$ and $\mathbb H^n(W,\mathcal F)=H^n(\mathbb P^D,p_*\mathcal F)$ for any (constructible) sheaf, and $p_*\mathcal F$ is constructible. Thus $H^n(W,\mathbb Q_\ell)=H^n(\mathbb P^D,p_*\mathbb Q_\ell)$ with $p_*\mathbb Q_\ell$ constructible. (c) We show inductively on $D$ that $H^n(\mathbb P^D,G)=0$ for $n>2D$ for every constructible $\mathbb Q_\ell$-sheaf $G$ on $\mathbb P^D_k$. For $D=0$, $\mathbb P^0$ is a geometric point and $H^n=0$ for $n>0$. For $D\ge1$, write $\mathbb P^D=U\sqcup H$ with $U\simeq\mathbb A^D$ open, $H\simeq\mathbb P^{D-1}$ closed, $j:U\hookrightarrow\mathbb P^D$, $i:H\hookrightarrow\mathbb P^D$; the short exact sequence $0\to j_!j^*G\to G\to i_*i^*G\to0$ yields the long exact sequence
$$\cdots\to H^n_c(U,j^*G)\to H^n(\mathbb P^D,G)\to H^n(H,i^*G)\to H^{n+1}_c(U,j^*G)\to\cdots.$$
For $n>2D$: $H^n(H,i^*G)=0$ by the induction hypothesis since $n>2D>2D-2=2\dim H$ and $i^*G$ is constructible; and $H^n_c(U,j^*G)=0$ by the standard compact-support bound $\mathrm{cd}_c(U)\le 2\dim U$ for quasi-projective varieties over an algebraically closed field (equivalently, by Artin--Verdier/Poincaré duality for the smooth $D$-fold $U$, which identifies $H^n_c(U,-)$ with the dual of $H^{2D-n}(U,-^{\vee}(D))$, a group that vanishes because $2D-n<0$). Hence $H^n(\mathbb P^D,G)=0$, completing the induction and the proof of the claim. Applying the claim to $W=Z_k$ (smooth projective of pure dimension $D$ over $k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q$) gives
$$H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=0\qquad\text{for all }n>2D. \tag{$\ast$}$$

STEP 4. The middle range $0\le n\le 2D$. Fix such an $n$.

4.1. Existence of the traces. Since $X$ and $Z$ are smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension $D$ over $\mathbb F_q$, lemma_77(a) (with $m=1$) provides the Poincaré duality trace isomorphisms
$$\operatorname{tr}_X:H^{2D}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell(-D),\qquad \operatorname{tr}_Z:H^{2D}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell(-D),$$
normalised by $\operatorname{tr}_Z(\mathrm{cl}(z))=[\kappa(z):\mathbb F_q]$, and lemma_77(b) shows the pairings $\langle x,y\rangle=\operatorname{tr}(x\cup y)$ are perfect. These are exactly the trace maps appearing in the statement of lemma_242.

4.2. Injectivity of $\pi^*$. The morphism $\pi:X\to Z$ is, by Steps 1--2, a proper surjective generically finite morphism of degree $d=|G|\ge1$ between smooth projective geometrically connected varieties of pure dimension $D$ over $\mathbb F_q$. Hence lemma_242 applies and yields the $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear trace map $\pi_*:H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$, characterised by $\operatorname{tr}_Z(\pi_*x\cup y)=\operatorname{tr}_X(x\cup\pi^*y)$, satisfying
$$\pi_*\circ\pi^*=d\cdot\mathrm{id}\quad\text{on }H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell).$$
Since $d\in\mathbb Q_\ell^{\times}$ (Step 2), the operator $d\cdot\mathrm{id}$ is invertible; if $\pi^*u=0$ then $d\,u=\pi_*\pi^*u=0$, hence $u=0$. Thus
$$\pi^*:H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\hookrightarrow H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\ \text{is injective}.$$

4.3. Descent of semisimplicity. We now apply lemma_266 to the proper surjective morphism $f=\pi$ between the smooth projective geometrically connected varieties $X$ and $Z$, with $Y=Z$: it states that if $\pi^*$ is injective on $H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(-,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ and $F_X$ acts semisimply on $H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$, then $F_Z$ acts semisimply on $H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$. Both hypotheses hold: injectivity was proved in 4.2, and the semisimplicity of $F_X$ on $H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ is precisely the hypothesis of the present lemma (which assumes semisimplicity of $F_X$ in every degree $n\ge0$, hence in particular for our $n$). (Conceptually, lemma_266 works because pullback along an $\mathbb F_q$-morphism is Frobenius-equivariant, so $\operatorname{im}\pi^*$ is an $F_X$-stable subspace of $H^n(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$, and $\pi^*$ identifies $H^n(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ $F$-equivariantly with it; a semisimple operator restricts to a semisimple operator on any invariant subspace, since the minimal polynomial of the restriction divides the minimal polynomial of the operator, which is then square-free.) We conclude that $F_Z$ is semisimple on $H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ for every $0\le n\le 2D$.

STEP 5. The range $n>2D$. By $(\ast)$, $H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=0$, and $F_Z$ is the zero operator on the zero space. The zero space admits the empty basis, which is trivially a basis of eigenvectors; equivalently, the zero operator is diagonalisable over $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$. Hence $F_Z$ is semisimple on $H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ for every $n>2D$.

STEP 6. Conclusion. Steps 4 and 5 cover every integer $n\ge0$, so $F_Z$ is semisimple on $H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ for all $n\ge0$, which is the desired conclusion. (By the standard equivalence of the two formulations, this is the same as diagonalisability of $F_Z\otimes\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$; and since geometric Frobenius is the inverse of arithmetic Frobenius, the same statement holds for geometric Frobenius, the inverse of a semisimple operator being semisimple.)

lemma_304.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(C\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected curve of genus \(g\ge1\) over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(J=\operatorname{Pic}^0_{C/\mathbb F_q}\) be its Jacobian, let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, and let \(F_J=(\mathrm{id}_{J_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(c)=c^q\), be the \(q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius automorphism of \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(J_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\). Then \(F_J\) is semisimple, that is diagonalizable over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\), on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(J_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) for every integer \(n\ge0\).
lemma_304.proof:
PROOF OF lemma_304.

Notation. For a prime power $\nu$ and a variety $Z$ over $\mathbb F_{\nu}$ (in particular over $\mathbb F_q$, since $\mathbb F_q\subset\mathbb F_{\nu}$ whenever $\nu$ is a power of $q$), write
$$F_{Z,\nu}:=(\mathrm{id}_{Z_k}\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma_\nu)^*,\qquad \sigma_\nu(c)=c^{\nu},$$\nfor the $\nu$-power arithmetic Frobenius automorphism of $H^n_{\acute et}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$, where $k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q$. Thus $F_J=F_{J,q}$ is the operator of the statement. Fix an integer $n\ge 0$ and put $V:=H^n_{\acute et}(J_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$. We shall prove that $F_{J,q}$ is diagonalizable over $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$; since $n$ was arbitrary this gives the claim.

=== Step 1. A closed point of $C$, and the field over which it becomes rational. ===

$C$ is a smooth geometrically connected curve over $\mathbb F_q$, hence of pure dimension $1$; in particular $C\ne\emptyset$. Being of finite type over a field, $C$ is noetherian, and a non-empty noetherian topological space possesses a closed point; choose one and call it $x$. Its residue field is a finite extension of $\mathbb F_q$: take an affine open neighbourhood $U=\mathrm{Spec}\,A$ of $x$ (with $A$ a finitely generated $\mathbb F_q$-algebra); since $x$ is closed in $C$ it is closed in $U$, so it corresponds to a maximal ideal $\mathfrak m\subset A$, and $\kappa(x)=A/\mathfrak m$ is a field which is a finitely generated $\mathbb F_q$-algebra, hence finite algebraic over $\mathbb F_q$ by Zariski's lemma. Set
$$d:=[\kappa(x):\mathbb F_q]\ \ge 1,\qquad K:=\kappa(x)\simeq\mathbb F_{q^d},\qquad Q:=q^d=p^{ad}.$$
A closed point is by definition an $\mathbb F_q$-morphism $x:\mathrm{Spec}\,K\to C$ over $\mathrm{Spec}\,\mathbb F_q$. By the universal property of the fibre product, for every $\mathbb F_q$-scheme $T$ there is a natural bijection $\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbb F_q}(T,C)=\mathrm{Hom}_{K}(T,C\times_{\mathbb F_q}\mathrm{Spec}\,K)$; applying this to $T=\mathrm{Spec}\,K$ gives a $K$-morphism $\mathrm{Spec}\,K\to C\times_{\mathbb F_q}\mathrm{Spec}\,K$, i.e. a point
$$p_0\in C'(K)=C'(\mathbb F_{q^d}),\qquad C':=C_{\mathbb F_{q^d}}:=C\times_{\mathbb F_q}\mathrm{Spec}\,\mathbb F_{q^d}.$$
Thus no Hasse--Weil input is needed: every curve of finite type over $\mathbb F_q$ acquires a rational point over the residue field of any one of its closed points.

=== Step 2. $C'$ is a smooth projective geometrically connected curve of genus $g\ge1$ over $\mathbb F_{q^d}$. ===

(a) Smoothness: $C\to\mathrm{Spec}\,\mathbb F_q$ is smooth and smoothness is stable under arbitrary base change, so $C'\to\mathrm{Spec}\,\mathbb F_{q^d}$ is smooth.
(b) Projectivity: $C\to\mathrm{Spec}\,\mathbb F_q$ is projective, so there is a closed immersion $C\hookrightarrow\mathbb P^m_{\mathbb F_q}$; base change gives a closed immersion $C'\hookrightarrow\mathbb P^m_{\mathbb F_q}\times_{\mathbb F_q}\mathrm{Spec}\,\mathbb F_{q^d}=\mathbb P^m_{\mathbb F_{q^d}}$, so $C'$ is projective over $\mathbb F_{q^d}$.
(c) Geometric connectedness: $\mathbb F_{q^d}\subset k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q$ and $k$ is algebraic over $\mathbb F_{q^d}$ (it is algebraic over $\mathbb F_q$) and algebraically closed, so $k$ is an algebraic closure of $\mathbb F_{q^d}$. Then
$$C'\times_{\mathbb F_{q^d}}\mathrm{Spec}\,k\;=\;\big(C\times_{\mathbb F_q}\mathrm{Spec}\,\mathbb F_{q^d}\big)\times_{\mathbb F_{q^d}}\mathrm{Spec}\,k\;\cong\;C\times_{\mathbb F_q}\mathrm{Spec}\,k,$$\nwhich is connected because $C$ is geometrically connected over $\mathbb F_q$. Connectedness after base change to one algebraic closure is exactly geometric connectedness.
(d) Genus: the square with vertices $C',C,\mathrm{Spec}\,\mathbb F_{q^d},\mathrm{Spec}\,\mathbb F_q$ is cartesian and $\mathrm{Spec}\,\mathbb F_{q^d}\to\mathrm{Spec}\,\mathbb F_q$ is flat (every field extension is flat), so flat base change for quasi-coherent cohomology of the proper morphism $C\to\mathrm{Spec}\,\mathbb F_q$ gives a canonical isomorphism
$$H^1(C,\mathcal O_C)\otimes_{\mathbb F_q}\mathbb F_{q^d}\;\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\ H^1(C',\mathcal O_{C'}).$$
Hence $\mathrm{genus}(C')=\dim_{\mathbb F_{q^d}}H^1(C',\mathcal O_{C'})=\dim_{\mathbb F_q}H^1(C,\mathcal O_C)=g\ge1$.

=== Step 3. The base change $J_{\mathbb F_{q^d}}$ is the Jacobian of $C'$. ===

We prove (and this is one of the two verifications demanded) the following standard base-change property of the Picard functor.

Sub-claim. Let $E_1/E_0$ be an extension of fields and $D/E_0$ a smooth projective geometrically connected curve. Then the canonical base-change homomorphism of group schemes over $E_1$
$$\varphi:\big(\mathrm{Pic}^0_{D/E_0}\big)_{E_1}\;\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\ \mathrm{Pic}^0_{D_{E_1}/E_1}$$\nis an isomorphism.

Proof of the sub-claim. For an $E_1$-scheme $S$ (regarded also as an $E_0$-scheme via $\mathrm{Spec}\,E_1\to\mathrm{Spec}\,E_0$) there is a canonical isomorphism of $S$-schemes $D_{E_1}\times_{E_1}S\cong D\times_{E_0}S$. Consequently the two presheaves of abelian groups on $(\mathrm{Sch}/E_1)$,
$$S\longmapsto \mathrm{Pic}(D_{E_1}\times_{E_1}S),\qquad S\longmapsto \mathrm{Pic}(D\times_{E_0}S),$$\nare literally identical; the same holds after quotienting by the image of $\mathrm{Pic}(S)$, and after fppf sheafification, which is how the relative Picard functor is defined. By the existence theorem for Picard schemes of smooth projective geometrically connected curves over a field, both $\mathrm{Pic}_{D/E_0}$ and $\mathrm{Pic}_{D_{E_1}/E_1}$ are schemes locally of finite type over their ground fields representing these sheaves. Since $\mathrm{Pic}_{D/E_0}$ is representable, for an $E_1$-scheme $S$ we have $\big(\mathrm{Pic}_{D/E_0}\big)_{E_1}(S)=\mathrm{Hom}_{E_1}(S,\mathrm{Pic}_{D/E_0}\times_{E_0}\mathrm{Spec}\,E_1)=\mathrm{Hom}_{E_0}(S,\mathrm{Pic}_{D/E_0})=\mathrm{Pic}_{D/E_0}(S)$ (universal property of the fibre product). Thus the two functors $\big(\mathrm{Pic}_{D/E_0}\big)_{E_1}$ and $\mathrm{Pic}_{D_{E_1}/E_1}$ on $(\mathrm{Sch}/E_1)$ are canonically isomorphic, and by Yoneda this isomorphism is represented by a unique isomorphism of $E_1$-schemes $\varphi$; because the identification of functors is compatible with tensor product of line bundles, $\varphi$ is a homomorphism of group schemes.

Now compare the degree-zero parts. For any algebraically closed field $\Omega/E_1$ (hence over $E_0$) the geometric fibres agree:
$$D_{E_1}\times_{E_1}\mathrm{Spec}\,\Omega\;=\;D\times_{E_0}\mathrm{Spec}\,\Omega.$$
Since $D$ is geometrically integral over $E_0$ (smooth $\Rightarrow$ geometrically reduced, and geometrically connected $\Rightarrow$ geometrically integral) and likewise $D_{E_1}$ over $E_1$, the degree of a line bundle on the geometric fibre is defined and is locally constant on the base; it yields homomorphisms $\deg_0:\mathrm{Pic}_{D/E_0}\to\underline{\mathbb Z}$ and $\deg_1:\mathrm{Pic}_{D_{E_1}/E_1}\to\underline{\mathbb Z}$ to the constant discrete group scheme $\underline{\mathbb Z}$. On $\Omega$-points both maps send a line bundle to the degree of the *same* line bundle on the *same* scheme $D\times_{E_0}\mathrm{Spec}\,\Omega$; hence $\deg_1\circ\varphi=\deg_0$, so $\varphi$ identifies the open-and-closed subgroup $\deg_0^{-1}(0)$ with $\deg_1^{-1}(0)$ (open and closed because it is the inverse image of the open-and-closed subset $\{0\}\subset\underline{\mathbb Z}$).

Finally, for a smooth projective geometrically connected curve over a field, $\deg^{-1}(0)$ is exactly the identity component of the Picard scheme, i.e. $\mathrm{Pic}^0$, the Jacobian: by lemma_identity_component_clopen_subgroup the identity component of a group scheme of finite type over the perfect field is open and closed, the components of the Picard scheme are precisely the fibres of the degree map, and $\deg^{-1}(0)$ is connected with $\overline{E}$-points the degree-$0$ line bundles (this is the usual construction of the Jacobian as an abelian variety). Therefore $\varphi$ restricts to an isomorphism $\big(\mathrm{Pic}^0_{D/E_0}\big)_{E_1}\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathrm{Pic}^0_{D_{E_1}/E_1}$, as claimed. $\square$ (sub-claim)

Applying the sub-claim with $E_0=\mathbb F_q$, $E_1=\mathbb F_{q^d}$, $D=C$ gives a canonical isomorphism of group schemes over $\mathbb F_{q^d}$
$$J':=\mathrm{Pic}^0_{C'/\mathbb F_{q^d}}\;\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\;J\times_{\mathbb F_q}\mathrm{Spec}\,\mathbb F_{q^d}=:J_{\mathbb F_{q^d}}.$$
In particular $J'$ is an abelian variety of dimension $g$ over $\mathbb F_{q^d}$ (the Jacobian of a genus-$g$ curve); being an abelian variety it is smooth, projective and geometrically connected over $\mathbb F_{q^d}$, and being smooth of relative dimension $g$ over a field it is of pure dimension $g$.

=== Step 4. Application of the Abel--Jacobi lemma and of lemma_278 over $\mathbb F_{q^d}$. ===

Both lemma_abeljac_proper_surjective_gen_finite and lemma_278 are stated for an *arbitrary* prime power in place of $q$; we instantiate them with the prime power $Q=p^{ad}=q^d$. The data required are:
- $C'/\mathbb F_{q^d}$: smooth projective geometrically connected curve of genus $g\ge1$ (Step 2);
- $p_0\in C'(\mathbb F_{q^d})$ (Step 1);
- $J'=\mathrm{Pic}^0_{C'/\mathbb F_{q^d}}$ (Step 3);
- $X:=J'$: smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension $r:=g\ge1$ (Step 3);
- $C_1=\cdots=C_r:=C'$: smooth projective geometrically connected curves over $\mathbb F_{q^d}$ (Step 2).

By lemma_abeljac_proper_surjective_gen_finite (over $\mathbb F_{q^d}$, with $q$ replaced by $q^d$), the morphism obtained from the Abel map $(x_1,\dots,x_g)\mapsto[\mathcal O_{C'}(\sum_i x_i)]$ followed by translation by $-[\mathcal O_{C'}(gp_0)]$,
$$a:\underbrace{C'\times_{\mathbb F_{q^d}}\cdots\times_{\mathbb F_{q^d}}C'}_{g\ \mathrm{factors}}\longrightarrow J',$$\nis proper, surjective and generically finite. Hence all hypotheses of lemma_278 (with $q$ replaced by $q^d$) are satisfied, and it yields: the $q^d$-power arithmetic Frobenius
$$\Psi:=\big(\mathrm{id}_{(J')_k}\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma_{q^d}\big)^*,\qquad \sigma_{q^d}(c)=c^{q^d},$$\nacting on $H^n_{\acute et}\big((J')_k,\mathbb Q_\ell\big)$ with $k=\overline{\mathbb F}_{q^d}$, is semisimple, i.e. diagonalizable over $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$, for every $n\ge0$. We take $k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q$, which is an algebraic closure of $\mathbb F_{q^d}$ as observed in Step 2(c).

=== Step 5. Identification of the cohomology spaces. ===

By associativity of the fibre product,
$$(J')_k\;=\;J_{\mathbb F_{q^d}}\times_{\mathbb F_{q^d}}\mathrm{Spec}\,k\;=\;\big(J\times_{\mathbb F_q}\mathrm{Spec}\,\mathbb F_{q^d}\big)\times_{\mathbb F_{q^d}}\mathrm{Spec}\,k\;\cong\;J\times_{\mathbb F_q}\mathrm{Spec}\,k\;=\;J_k,$$\nand this is an identity of $k$-schemes (both sides are $J\times_{\mathbb F_q}\mathrm{Spec}\,k$), so no cohomological base-change theorem is needed: $H^n_{\acute et}\big((J')_k,\mathbb Q_\ell\big)$ and $V=H^n_{\acute et}(J_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ are the *same* $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector space, and $\Psi$ is a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear operator on $V$. Step 4 therefore says: $\Psi$ is diagonalizable over $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$ on $V$.

=== Step 6. $\Psi=F_{J,q}^{\,d}$. ===

The automorphism $\sigma_{q^d}:c\mapsto c^{q^d}$ of $k$ is the $d$-fold composite $\sigma_q^{\,d}$, and $\sigma_q$ fixes $\mathbb F_q$, so $\mathrm{id}_J\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma_q$ is a well-defined automorphism of $J_k=J\times_{\mathbb F_q}\mathrm{Spec}\,k$. Under the identification $(J')_k\cong J_k$ of Step 5, the automorphism $\mathrm{id}_{(J')_k}\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma_{q^d}$ of $(J')_k$ (a morphism over $\mathbb F_{q^d}$) corresponds exactly to $\mathrm{id}_{J_k}\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma_{q^d}$ (a morphism over $\mathbb F_q$): on the two presentations of the same $k$-scheme the first sends $(j,a,b)$ to $(j,a,\sigma_{q^d}(b))$ and the second sends $(j,b)$ to $(j,\sigma_{q^d}(b))$, and the projection $(j,a,b)\mapsto(j,b)$ intertwines them. Contravariant functoriality of étale pullback, $(g\circ f)^*=f^*\circ g^*$, applied to $\mathrm{id}_J\times\mathrm{Spec}(\tau\circ\rho)=(\mathrm{id}_J\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\tau)\circ(\mathrm{id}_J\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\rho)$, gives
$$\big(\mathrm{id}_{J_k}\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma_{q^d}\big)^*=\big(\mathrm{id}_{J_k}\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma_q^{\,d}\big)^*=\big(\mathrm{id}_{J_k}\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma_q\big)^{*\,d},$$\nby induction on $d$ (the case $d=1$ being trivial and the induction step using $(\sigma^{\,d+1})^*=(\sigma^{\,d})^*\circ\sigma^*$). Hence, as operators on $V$,
$$\Psi=F_{J,q}^{\,d}.$$

=== Step 7. Invertibility and finite dimensionality. ===

$J$ is an abelian variety, hence proper over $\mathbb F_q$. By lemma_45_finite_frob applied to $X=J$ and $K=\mathbb Q_\ell$ equipped with its natural arithmetic Frobenius isomorphism, $V=H^n_{\acute et}(J_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ is finite-dimensional over $\mathbb Q_\ell$. By lemma_6a, $F_{J,q}$ and its inverse $F_{J,\mathrm{geo}}=(\mathrm{id}\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma_q^{-1})^*$ are $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear automorphisms of $V$; in particular $T:=F_{J,q}\in\mathrm{GL}(V)$, and $T^d=\Psi$.

=== Step 8. Linear algebra: diagonalizability of a power forces diagonalizability. ===

Lemma. Let $\ell$ be prime, $V$ a finite-dimensional $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector space, $T\in\mathrm{GL}(V)$ and $m\ge1$. If $T^m$ is diagonalizable over $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$, then so is $T$.

Proof. Extend scalars to $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$ and write $\overline V=V\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$, $\overline T=T\otimes1$. Since $\overline{T^m}$ is diagonalizable and invertible (as $T^m\in\mathrm{GL}(V)$), it has finitely many *distinct, non-zero* eigenvalues $\mu_1,\dots,\mu_s\in\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell^{\times}$, and its minimal polynomial over $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$ is $M(Y)=\prod_{j=1}^{s}(Y-\mu_j)$, a separable polynomial. Consider
$$P(X)=\prod_{j=1}^{s}\big(X^m-\mu_j\big)\in\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell[X].$$
All factors commute, so $P(\overline T)=\prod_j(\overline T^{\,m}-\mu_j\,\mathrm{id})=M(\overline{T^m})=0$. Each $X^m-\mu_j$ has $m$ distinct roots in $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$: its derivative is $mX^{m-1}$, and $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$ has characteristic $0$, so $\gcd(X^m-\mu_j,\,mX^{m-1})=1$ because $0$ is not a root of $X^m-\mu_j$ (as $\mu_j\ne0$). Moreover the root sets of $X^m-\mu_j$ and $X^m-\mu_{j'}$ are disjoint for $j\ne j'$, a root being an $m$-th root of $\mu_j$. Hence $P$ splits over $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$ into $ms$ pairwise distinct linear factors, i.e. $P$ is separable. The minimal polynomial $m_T\in\mathbb Q_\ell[X]\subset\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell[X]$ of $T$ divides $P$ (since $P(T)=0$), so $m_T$ is a product of distinct linear factors over $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$, which is precisely the criterion for $\overline T$ to be diagonalizable. $\square$

Necessity of the hypothesis $T\in\mathrm{GL}(V)$: for the nilpotent $T=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$ one has $T^2=0$, which is diagonalizable, while $T$ is not. This is exactly why lemma_6a was invoked in Step 7.

=== Step 9. Conclusion. ===

Applying the lemma of Step 8 with $T=F_{J,q}\in\mathrm{GL}(V)$ and $m=d\ge1$, and using $T^d=\Psi$ from Step 6 together with the diagonalizability of $\Psi$ over $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$ from Steps 4--5, we conclude that $F_{J,q}=(\mathrm{id}_{J_k}\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma)^*$, $\sigma(c)=c^q$, is diagonalizable over $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$ on $V=H^n_{\acute et}(J_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$. By lemma_5, diagonalizability over $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$ of the base change is equivalent to semisimplicity of the operator on the $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector space, so $F_{J,q}$ is semisimple on $H^n_{\acute et}(J_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$. The argument used nothing about $n$ except $n\ge0$ (for $n>2g$ the group is $0$ and the assertion is trivial), so it holds for every integer $n\ge0$. This is exactly the statement of lemma_304. $\blacksquare$

lemma_307.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(Y\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(\mathcal E\) be a vector bundle of rank \(r+1\ge 1\) on \(Y\) defined over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(\pi:\mathbb P=\operatorname{Proj}(\operatorname{Sym}_{\mathcal O_Y}\mathcal E)\to Y\) be the projective bundle of one-dimensional quotients with tautological line bundle \(\mathcal O(1)\), let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), let \(\ell\ne p\) be prime, and fix a nonzero \(\tau\in\mathbb Q_\ell(1)\); let \(c\in H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(\mathbb P_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) be the unique vector with \(\mathrm{cl}(\mathcal O(1))=c\otimes\tau\) under \(H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(\mathbb P_k,\mathbb Q_\ell(1))\simeq H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(\mathbb P_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\mathbb Q_\ell(1)\). For \(Z\in\{Y,\mathbb P\}\) write \(F_Z=(\mathrm{id}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(u)=u^q\). Then for every \(n\ge 0\) the homomorphism \(\bigoplus_{i=0}^{r}H^{n-2i}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(\mathbb P_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\), \((x_i)_{i=0}^{r}\mapsto\sum_{i=0}^{r}\pi^*x_i\cup c^{\,i}\), is an isomorphism carrying \(\bigoplus_{i=0}^{r}q^{i}F_Y\) to \(F_{\mathbb P}\).
lemma_307.proof:
PROOF OF lemma_307 (proved verbatim, for the truncated sum i = 0,...,r and the source operator \bigoplus_{i=0}^{r} q^{i}F_Y).

NOTATION AND CONVENTIONS. Write H^m(Z_k) := H^m_{\acute et}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) for Z \in \{Y,\mathbb P\}, with the convention H^m(Z_k)=0 for m<0 (étale cohomology vanishes in negative degrees, so the sums below are finite and unambiguous). All maps are \mathbb Q_\ell-linear. For n \ge 0 define
  T_n : \bigoplus_{i=0}^{r} H^{n-2i}(Y_k) \longrightarrow H^n(\mathbb P_k), \qquad T_n\bigl((x_i)_{i=0}^{r}\bigr)=\sum_{i=0}^{r}\pi^*x_i\cup c^{\,i},
with c^0 := 1 \in H^0(\mathbb P_k), and let \Phi := \bigoplus_{i=0}^{r} q^{i}F_Y denote the operator on the source whose restriction to the i-th summand H^{n-2i}(Y_k) is q^{i}F_Y. The goal is: T_n is an isomorphism and F_{\mathbb P}\circ T_n = T_n\circ \Phi.

STEP 1. Geometry of \mathbb P over \mathbb F_q.
The bundle \mathcal E is Zariski-locally free of rank r+1 on Y, so there is a Zariski open cover Y=\bigcup_\alpha U_\alpha with \mathcal E|_{U_\alpha}\simeq \mathcal O_{U_\alpha}^{\oplus(r+1)}; for such U one has a canonical isomorphism \mathbb P(\mathcal E)|_U \simeq U\times_{\mathbb F_q}\mathbb P^r_{\mathbb F_q} under which \mathcal O(1) corresponds to \mathrm{pr}_2^*\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^r}(1) (this is the defining property of \operatorname{Proj}(\operatorname{Sym}\mathcal E) as the bundle of one-dimensional quotients). Hence \pi is Zariski-locally on Y a projection, so \pi is smooth, projective and surjective with every geometric fibre isomorphic to \mathbb P^r. Since Y\to\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_q is smooth and projective and \pi is smooth and projective, the composite \mathbb P\to\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_q is smooth and projective; being smooth over a field, \mathbb P is regular, hence reduced.
Geometric connectedness: base change to k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q gives \pi_k:\mathbb P_k\to Y_k proper, flat, surjective, Zariski-locally a product with \mathbb P^r. Because H^0(\mathbb P^r_K,\mathcal O)=K and H^1(\mathbb P^r_K,\mathcal O)=0 for every field K, cohomology-and-base-change gives \pi_{k*}\mathcal O_{\mathbb P_k}\simeq \mathcal O_{Y_k} (checkable Zariski-locally on Y_k, where \pi_k is a product). Therefore H^0(\mathbb P_k,\mathcal O)=H^0(Y_k,\mathcal O)=k, the last equality because Y is geometrically connected and smooth over k, hence Y_k is reduced and connected, so its only global idempotents are 0 and 1. A reduced scheme of finite type over the algebraically closed field k has H^0 a finite product of copies of k, one per connected component; H^0(\mathbb P_k,\mathcal O)=k forces \mathbb P_k to be connected, i.e. \mathbb P is geometrically connected. Finally \mathbb P_k is smooth over k, hence regular, and in a regular locally noetherian scheme the irreducible components are the connected components (local rings are domains); so \mathbb P_k is irreducible of pure dimension \dim Y + r. Thus \mathbb P is smooth, projective and geometrically connected of pure dimension \dim Y+r over \mathbb F_q.

STEP 2. The class c, and its identification with c_1(\mathcal O(1)).
The \ell-adic cycle class map \mathrm{cl}:\mathrm{CH}^1(\mathbb P)\to H^2(\mathbb P_k,\mathbb Q_\ell(1)) sends a line bundle to its first \ell-adic Chern class; in particular \mathrm{cl}(\mathcal O(1))=c_1(\mathcal O(1)). Since \mathbb Q_\ell(1) is a one-dimensional \mathbb Q_\ell-vector space and \tau\neq 0, the map H^2(\mathbb P_k)\to H^2(\mathbb P_k)\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\mathbb Q_\ell(1)\simeq H^2(\mathbb P_k,\mathbb Q_\ell(1)), v\mapsto v\otimes\tau, is an isomorphism; hence there is a unique c with \mathrm{cl}(\mathcal O(1))=c\otimes\tau, namely the c of the statement.
Non-vanishing when r\ge 1: let \bar y:\operatorname{Spec}k\to Y_k be a geometric point and i:\mathbb P_{\bar y}:=\mathbb P_k\times_{Y_k}\operatorname{Spec}k\to\mathbb P_k the closed immersion of the fibre. By Step 1, \mathbb P_{\bar y}\simeq\mathbb P^r_k and i^*\mathcal O(1)\simeq\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^r}(1). By functoriality of cycle classes (and of Chern classes) under pullback, i^*(\mathrm{cl}(\mathcal O(1)))=\mathrm{cl}(i^*\mathcal O(1))=\mathrm{cl}(\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^r}(1))=h\otimes\tau, where h=c_1(\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^r}(1))\in H^2(\mathbb P^r_k). Uniqueness in the \tau-trivialisation gives i^*c=h. By lemma_201 applied to \mathbb P^r_k with r\ge 1, \mathbb Q_\ell[t]/(t^{r+1})\to\bigoplus_{m\ge0}H^m(\mathbb P^r_k), t^i\mapsto h^i, is a graded isomorphism; since t\neq 0 in \mathbb Q_\ell[t]/(t^{r+1}) for r\ge 1, h\neq 0, hence c\neq 0. (No non-vanishing is needed when r=0.)

STEP 3. F_{\mathbb P}(c)=q\,c (via lemma_78 with j=1).
We produce an \mathbb F_q-rational codimension-1 cycle on \mathbb P whose class is \mathrm{cl}(\mathcal O(1)). Let \eta=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F(\mathbb P) be the generic point. Since \mathcal O(1) is defined over \mathbb F_q, its generic stalk is a one-dimensional \mathbb F_q(\mathbb P)-vector space; choose 0\neq s in it, i.e. a rational section of \mathcal O(1) defined over \mathbb F_q. Then D:=\operatorname{div}(s) is a Cartier divisor on \mathbb P; because s is defined over \mathbb F_q, D is invariant under the action of \mathrm{Gal}(\overline{\mathbb F}_q/\mathbb F_q) on \mathbb P_{\overline{\mathbb F}_q}, hence D is defined over \mathbb F_q. Multiplication by s identifies \mathcal O_{\mathbb P} with \mathcal O(1)(-D), i.e. \mathcal O_{\mathbb P}(D)\simeq\mathcal O(1). Therefore \mathrm{cl}(D)=c_1(\mathcal O(D))=c_1(\mathcal O(1))=\mathrm{cl}(\mathcal O(1))=c\otimes\tau.
Now apply lemma_78 to the smooth projective pure-dimensional \mathbb F_q-variety \mathbb P (Step 1), with j=1 and with its \xi equal to our \tau. It says: for the codimension-1 cycle z=D defined over \mathbb F_q, writing \mathrm{cl}(z)=c_z\otimes\tau with c_z\in H^2(\mathbb P_k) unique, one has F_*c_z=q^{1}c_z, where F_* is exactly (\mathrm{id}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*=F_{\mathbb P}. Uniqueness of the vector representing \mathrm{cl}(D) in the \tau-trivialisation gives c_D=c, hence F_{\mathbb P}(c)=q\,c.

STEP 4. The intertwining identity F_{\mathbb P}\circ T_n=T_n\circ\Phi.
By lemma_220, F_{\mathbb P}=(\mathrm{id}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^* is a graded ring automorphism of H^*(\mathbb P_k): F_{\mathbb P}(u\cup v)=F_{\mathbb P}u\cup F_{\mathbb P}v and F_{\mathbb P}(1)=1. Hence for every i\ge 0, F_{\mathbb P}(c^{\,i})=F_{\mathbb P}(c)^{i}=(qc)^{i}=q^{i}c^{\,i} (for i=0 this reads F_{\mathbb P}(1)=1=q^0\cdot 1, which is correct). By lemma_214 applied to the \mathbb F_q-morphism \pi:\mathbb P\to Y, \pi^*\circ F_Y=F_{\mathbb P}\circ\pi^*. Therefore, for (x_i)\in\bigoplus_{i=0}^{r}H^{n-2i}(Y_k), using \mathbb Q_\ell-linearity of \cup, of \pi^* and of F_Y,
  F_{\mathbb P}\bigl(T_n((x_i))\bigr)=\sum_{i=0}^{r}F_{\mathbb P}(\pi^*x_i)\cup F_{\mathbb P}(c^{\,i})=\sum_{i=0}^{r}\pi^*(F_Yx_i)\cup q^{i}c^{\,i}=\sum_{i=0}^{r}\pi^*(q^{i}F_Yx_i)\cup c^{\,i}=T_n\bigl(\Phi((x_i))\bigr),
where q^i\in\mathbb Q_\ell^\times is a scalar and F_Y is \mathbb Q_\ell-linear, so q^iF_Y=F_Y\circ q^i. This is precisely the assertion that T_n carries \bigoplus_{i=0}^{r}q^{i}F_Y to F_{\mathbb P}.

STEP 5. T_n is an isomorphism (projective bundle formula, lemma_110).
Apply lemma_110 with X:=Y (smooth projective over \mathbb F_q), E:=\mathcal E, and with its rank parameter equal to r+1\ge 1; its index j then runs over 0,\dots,(r+1)-1=0,\dots,r, and its \pi:\mathbb P(\mathcal E)\to X and tautological \mathcal O(1) are exactly ours (same quotients convention, \operatorname{Proj}\operatorname{Sym}\mathcal E). Its conclusion provides \xi\in H^2(\mathbb P_k) corresponding to c_1(\mathcal O(1)), with F\xi=q\xi, and asserts that for every n the map S_n:\bigoplus_{j=0}^{r}H^{n-2j}(Y_k)\to H^n(\mathbb P_k), (x_j)\mapsto\sum_j\pi^*x_j\cup\xi^{j}, is an isomorphism, equivariant for F with q^{j}F_Y on the j-th summand.
Identification of \xi with c: "\xi corresponds to c_1(\mathcal O(1))" means, under the canonical identification H^2(\mathbb P_k,\mathbb Q_\ell(1))=H^2(\mathbb P_k)\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\mathbb Q_\ell(1) and the fixed trivialisation v\mapsto v\otimes\tau, that c_1(\mathcal O(1))=\xi\otimes\tau. By Step 2, c_1(\mathcal O(1))=\mathrm{cl}(\mathcal O(1))=c\otimes\tau; since v\mapsto v\otimes\tau is injective, \xi=c. Hence S_n=T_n, and T_n is an isomorphism.
(Robustness of the normalisation. If one's convention determines \xi only up to a scalar, so that \xi=\lambda c with \lambda\in\mathbb Q_\ell^\times, the conclusion is unchanged: let D:\bigoplus_i H^{n-2i}(Y_k)\to\bigoplus_i H^{n-2i}(Y_k) be the diagonal automorphism D\bigl((y_i)\bigr)=(\lambda^{-i}y_i). Then S_n\circ D\bigl((y_i)\bigr)=\sum_i\pi^*(\lambda^{-i}y_i)\cup(\lambda c)^i=\sum_i\pi^*y_i\cup c^{\,i}=T_n\bigl((y_i)\bigr), so T_n=S_n\circ D is an isomorphism; and D commutes with \Phi because each \lambda^{-i} is a scalar and F_Y is \mathbb Q_\ell-linear. Note the direction: x_i=\lambda^{-i}y_i, not y_i=\lambda^{-i}x_i. In any case Step 4, which uses only F_{\mathbb P}(c)=qc from Step 3 and the two functoriality facts, already establishes the intertwining for T_n itself.)

STEP 6. Edge case r=0 and conclusion.
If r=0 then \mathcal E is a line bundle, \mathbb P=\operatorname{Proj}(\operatorname{Sym}\mathcal E)\simeq Y with \pi=\mathrm{id} and \mathcal O(1)=\mathcal E; the source of T_n is the single group H^n(Y_k), T_n(x)=\pi^*x\cup c^0=x, which is an isomorphism, and \Phi=q^0F_Y=F_Y, so Step 4's identity reads F_{\mathbb P}=F_{\mathbb P}\circ\mathrm{id}. Thus the statement holds also in this case, in agreement with Steps 4-5.

Combining Step 4 (intertwining) and Step 5 (isomorphism), for every n\ge 0 the homomorphism \bigoplus_{i=0}^{r}H^{n-2i}_{\acute et}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^n_{\acute et}(\mathbb P_k,\mathbb Q_\ell), (x_i)\mapsto\sum_{i=0}^{r}\pi^*x_i\cup c^{\,i}, is an isomorphism carrying \bigoplus_{i=0}^{r}q^{i}F_Y to F_{\mathbb P}. This is exactly the statement of lemma_307. \hfill\blacksquare

REMARK on the two corrections built into the statement (consistency checks, not needed for the proof). (i) The truncation at i=r is necessary: with Y=\mathbb P^2_{\mathbb F_q}, \mathcal E=\mathcal O_Y^{\oplus2} (r=1) and n=4, the unrestricted source \bigoplus_{i\ge0}H^{4-2i}(Y_k) has dimension 3 (lemma_201), whereas the projective-bundle formula of lemma_110 gives \dim H^4(\mathbb P_k)=2, so no map from the unrestricted sum can be an isomorphism. (ii) The twist q^{i} is necessary: with Y=\mathbb P^1_{\mathbb F_q}, \mathcal E=\mathcal O_Y^{\oplus2} and n=2, the i=1 summand is H^0(Y_k) on which F_Y is the identity (lemma_265), while F_{\mathbb P}(c)=qc with c\neq 0 (Steps 2-3); equivariance for the untwisted operator applied to (0,1) would force qc=c, i.e. (q-1)c=0, impossible since q>1 and \operatorname{char}\mathbb Q_\ell=0.

lemma_308.statement: Let \(k\) be a field, let \(X\) be a projective scheme over \(k\), let \(\mathcal L\) be an ample line bundle on \(X\), let \(n\ge 1\) be an integer, and let \(s\in H^0(X,\mathcal L^{\otimes n})\) be a global section. Denote by \(X_s\subseteq X\) the open subscheme on which \(s\) generates \(\mathcal L^{\otimes n}\), and let \(S=\bigoplus_{m\ge 0}H^0(X,\mathcal L^{\otimes mn})\) with its natural graded \(k\)-algebra structure, so that \(s\in S_1\). Then \(X_s\) is an affine \(k\)-scheme, and the canonical homomorphism \((S_s)_0\to \Gamma(X_s,\mathcal O_{X_s})\) from the degree-zero part of the localisation of \(S\) at \(s\) is an isomorphism of \(k\)-algebras.
lemma_308.proof:
PROOF OF lemma_308.

NOTATION. Put $\mathcal A:=\mathcal L^{\otimes n}$. A positive tensor power of an ample line bundle is ample, so $\mathcal A$ is an ample line bundle on $X$. Write $S_m:=H^0(X,\mathcal A^{\otimes m})$, so that $S=\bigoplus_{m\ge0}S_m$ with multiplication induced by the canonical isomorphisms $\mathcal A^{\otimes m}\otimes_{\mathcal O_X}\mathcal A^{\otimes m'}\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathcal A^{\otimes(m+m')}$; then $S_0=\Gamma(X,\mathcal O_X)$ and $s\in S_1=\Gamma(X,\mathcal A)$. Put $U:=X_s=\{x\in X: s_x\ \text{generates}\ \mathcal A_x\}$ and let $j:U\hookrightarrow X$ be the open immersion. No result from the list of proved lemmas or references is used; the argument is the standard EGA II 4.5.2/Hartshorne II.5 proof, carried out in full.

PRELIMINARIES.
(P1) $X$ is noetherian. Indeed $X$ is projective over the field $k$, hence is a closed subscheme of some $\mathbf P^r_k$; $\mathbf P^r_k$ is noetherian, hence so is $X$. Consequently every open cover of $X$ has a finite subcover, the affine opens trivialising a given line bundle form a basis, and every subsheaf of a coherent $\mathcal O_X$-module is coherent.
(P2) For every integer $e\ge1$ one has $X_s=X_{s^{\otimes e}}$, where $s^{\otimes e}\in H^0(X,\mathcal A^{\otimes e})$ is the $e$-fold tensor power of $s$. Proof: let $x\in X$ with residue field $k(x)$ and maximal ideal $\mathfrak m_x\subset\mathcal O_{X,x}$. Since $\mathcal A_x$ is a free $\mathcal O_{X,x}$-module of rank $1$, the finitely generated module $\mathcal A_x/s_x\mathcal A_x$ vanishes iff it vanishes modulo $\mathfrak m_x$ (Nakayama's lemma), i.e. iff $s(x):=$ image of $s_x$ in the fibre $\mathcal A(x):=\mathcal A_x\otimes_{\mathcal O_{X,x}}k(x)$ is non-zero. Thus $s_x$ generates $\mathcal A_x$ iff $s(x)\ne0$, and similarly for $s^{\otimes e}$. The canonical map $\mathcal A(x)^{\otimes_{k(x)}e}\to\mathcal A^{\otimes e}(x)$ sends $s(x)^{\otimes e}$ to $s^{\otimes e}(x)$; since $\mathcal A(x)$ is a $1$-dimensional $k(x)$-vector space, writing $s(x)=c\,b$ with $b$ a basis vector gives $s(x)^{\otimes e}=c^{e}b^{\otimes e}$, which is non-zero iff $c\ne0$, i.e. iff $s(x)\ne0$. Hence $s_x$ generates $\mathcal A_x$ iff $s^{\otimes e}_x$ generates $\mathcal A^{\otimes e}_x$. $\square_{(P2)}$
(P3) Let $W=\operatorname{Spec}R$ be an affine open of $X$ on which $\mathcal A$ is trivialised by a frame $e_0$, and write $s|_W=f\,e_0$ with $f\in R$. Then $U\cap W=D(f)$ (by the fibre criterion in (P2), $s$ generates at $\mathfrak p\subset R$ iff $f\notin\mathfrak p$); $\mathcal A^{\otimes m}|_W$ is trivialised by $e_0^{\otimes m}$ with $s^{\otimes m}\leftrightarrow f^{m}$; and $\Gamma(U\cap W,\mathcal O)=\Gamma(D(f),\mathcal O_W)=R_f$, this last identity being the defining property of the structure sheaf of the affine scheme $W$. $\square_{(P3)}$

STEP 1. THE EMPTY CASE $U=\varnothing$.
First note that the empty scheme is affine: $\varnothing\simeq\operatorname{Spec}(0)$ where $0$ is the zero ring, and $\Gamma(\varnothing,\mathcal O)=0$.
If $X=\varnothing$ then $S_m=\Gamma(\varnothing,\mathcal A^{\otimes m})=0$ for all $m$, so $S=0$ is the zero ring, $(S_s)_0=0$, and the canonical map $0\to\Gamma(\varnothing,\mathcal O)=0$ is an isomorphism.
Now suppose $X\ne\varnothing$ and $U=\varnothing$. By (P1) choose a finite affine open cover $X=\bigcup_{i=1}^{t}W_i$, $W_i=\operatorname{Spec}R_i$, trivialising $\mathcal A$, with $s\leftrightarrow f_i\in R_i$ as in (P3). Since $U\cap W_i=D(f_i)=\varnothing$, the element $f_i$ lies in no prime ideal of $R_i$, hence lies in the nilradical $\bigcap_{\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{Spec}R_i}\mathfrak p$, hence $f_i$ is nilpotent: $f_i^{r_i}=0$ for some $r_i\ge1$. Let $r=\max_i r_i$. Under the trivialisation $\mathcal A^{\otimes r}|_{W_i}\simeq\mathcal O_{W_i}$ by $e_0^{\otimes r}$, the section $s^{\otimes r}|_{W_i}$ corresponds to $f_i^{r}=0$; a section of a sheaf restricting to $0$ on an open cover is $0$, so $s^{\otimes r}=0$ in $S_r$. Inverting $s$ makes $s^{\otimes r}$ a unit of $S_s$, and since it is $0$ we get $1=0$ in $S_s$; thus $S_s$ is the zero ring and $(S_s)_0=0$. As $\Gamma(\varnothing,\mathcal O)=0$, the canonical map $(S_s)_0\to\Gamma(U,\mathcal O_U)$ is the unique map $0\to0$, an isomorphism, and $U=\varnothing$ is affine. This settles Step 1; from now on assume $U\ne\varnothing$.

STEP 2. AFFINENESS OF $U$ (very ample model).
(2a) Since $\mathcal L$ is ample and $X$ is of finite type over the noetherian ring $k$, some positive power of $\mathcal L$ is very ample (EGA II 4.5.4, Hartshorne II Thm 7.1): choose $e_1\ge1$ such that $\mathcal M:=\mathcal L^{\otimes e_1}$ is very ample. By definition there is an immersion $i:X\hookrightarrow\mathbf P^N_k$ with $i^*\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^N}(1)\simeq\mathcal M$; since $X$ is proper over $k$ and $\mathbf P^N_k$ is separated over $k$, the morphism $i$ is closed, hence $i$ is a closed immersion.
(2b) Let $\mathcal I:=\ker\bigl(\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^N}\to i_*\mathcal O_X\bigr)$, a coherent sheaf on $\mathbf P^N$. By Serre's vanishing theorem on projective space, there is $m_1\ge1$ with $H^1\bigl(\mathbf P^N,\mathcal I(m)\bigr)=0$ for all $m\ge m_1$.
(2c) Set $e:=e_1m_1$ and $\mathcal B:=\mathcal A^{\otimes e}=\mathcal L^{\otimes ne_1m_1}=\mathcal M^{\otimes(nm_1)}=i^*\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^N}(nm_1)$; note $nm_1\ge m_1$ since $n\ge1$.
(2d) Let $\nu:\mathbf P^N\hookrightarrow\mathbf P^{N'}$ be the closed immersion defined by the complete linear system $|\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^N}(nm_1)|$, so that $\nu^*\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{N'}}(1)\simeq\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^N}(nm_1)$ and $\nu^*:H^0(\mathbf P^{N'},\mathcal O(1))\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }H^0(\mathbf P^N,\mathcal O(nm_1))$ is an isomorphism by construction. The composite $j:=\nu\circ i:X\hookrightarrow\mathbf P^{N'}$ is a closed immersion with $j^*\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{N'}}(1)\simeq\mathcal B$.
(2e) The restriction map $\rho:H^0(\mathbf P^{N'},\mathcal O(1))\to H^0(X,\mathcal B)$ is surjective. Indeed, twisting the exact sequence $0\to\mathcal I\to\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^N}\to i_*\mathcal O_X\to0$ by the locally free sheaf $\mathcal O(nm_1)$ gives $0\to\mathcal I(nm_1)\to\mathcal O(nm_1)\to i_*\mathcal O_X\otimes\mathcal O(nm_1)\to0$, and by the projection formula for the closed immersion $i$ the last term is $i_*\bigl(i^*\mathcal O(nm_1)\bigr)=i_*\mathcal B$. The long exact cohomology sequence gives $H^0(\mathbf P^N,\mathcal O(nm_1))\to H^0(X,\mathcal B)\to H^1(\mathbf P^N,\mathcal I(nm_1))=0$, so the map is surjective; composing with the isomorphism $\nu^*$ gives the surjectivity of $\rho$.
(2f) Put $t:=s^{\otimes e}\in H^0(X,\mathcal B)$. By (P2), $U=X_s=X_t$. Choose $\ell\in H^0(\mathbf P^{N'},\mathcal O(1))$ with $\rho(\ell)=t$; thus $\ell$ is a linear form and $j^*\ell=t$ under the identification $j^*\mathcal O(1)=\mathcal B$. We claim $X_t=j^{-1}(D_+(\ell))$, where $D_+(\ell):=\{y\in\mathbf P^{N'}:\ell_y\ \text{generates}\ \mathcal O(1)_y\}$. For a general morphism $f:Z'\to Z$ and a section $\sigma$ of a line bundle $\mathcal N$ on $Z$, the non-vanishing locus of $f^*\sigma$ equals $f^{-1}$ of the non-vanishing locus of $\sigma$: at $z'\in Z'$, $(f^*\sigma)_{z'}$ generates $(f^*\mathcal N)_{z'}$ iff its image in the fibre $(f^*\mathcal N)(z')=\mathcal N(f(z'))\otimes_{k(f(z'))}k(z')$ is non-zero (fibre criterion as in (P2)), and since $\mathcal N(f(z'))$ is $1$-dimensional over $k(f(z'))$, base change to the field extension $k(z')$ preserves non-vanishing. Applying this to $f=j$ and $\sigma=\ell$ gives $X_{j^*\ell}=j^{-1}(D_+(\ell))$, i.e. $U=j^{-1}(D_+(\ell))$.
(2g) $D_+(\ell)$ is affine: after a linear change of homogeneous coordinates $T_0,\dots,T_{N'}$ we may suppose $\ell=T_0$, and then $D_+(T_0)=\operatorname{Spec}k[T_1/T_0,\dots,T_{N'}/T_0]\simeq\mathbf A^{N'}_k$. A closed subscheme of an affine scheme is affine (a closed subscheme of $\operatorname{Spec}A$ is $\operatorname{Spec}A/\mathfrak a$). Since $j$ is a closed immersion, $U=j^{-1}(D_+(\ell))$ is a closed subscheme of $D_+(\ell)\simeq\mathbf A^{N'}_k$, hence $U$ is an affine $k$-scheme. (Had $U$ been empty, it would again be affine by Step 1.)

STEP 3. CONSTRUCTION OF THE CANONICAL HOMOomORPHISM.
For each $m\ge0$ define $\psi_m:S_m=\Gamma(X,\mathcal A^{\otimes m})\to\Gamma(U,\mathcal O_U)$ as follows. On $U$ the section $s$ generates the line bundle $\mathcal A$, hence is nowhere vanishing and therefore a global frame of $\mathcal A|_U$; consequently $s^{\otimes m}$ is a global frame of $\mathcal A^{\otimes m}|_U$. Given $a\in\Gamma(X,\mathcal A^{\otimes m})$, its restriction $a|_U$ is uniquely of the form $h\cdot s^{\otimes m}$ with $h\in\Gamma(U,\mathcal O_U)$; set $\psi_m(a):=h$, written $a/s^m$. In the situation of (P3) this is the map $R\to R_f$, $u\mapsto u/f^m$.
Compatibility: for $m,r\ge0$ and $a\in S_m$, $\psi_{m+r}(s^{\otimes r}\cdot a)=\psi_m(a)$, because on $U$ one has $(s^{\otimes r}a)/s^{m+r}=a/s^m$.
Well-definedness of the induced map: elements of $(S_s)_0$ are fractions $a/s^m$ with $a\in S_m$, and $a/s^m=a'/s^{m'}$ in $(S_s)_0$ iff $s^{N+m'}a=s^{N+m}a'$ in $S_{m+m'+N}$ for some $N\ge0$. Applying $\psi_{m+m'+N}$ and using the compatibility repeatedly gives $\psi_{m+N}(s^Na)=\psi_m(a)$ and $\psi_{m'+N}(s^Na')=\psi_{m'}(a')$, hence $\psi_m(a)=\psi_{m'}(a')$. Thus there is a unique well-defined map $\varphi:(S_s)_0\to\Gamma(U,\mathcal O_U)$ with $\varphi(a/s^m)=a/s^m|_U$. It is a $k$-algebra homomorphism: $\varphi((a/s^m)(a'/s^{m'}))=(aa')/s^{m+m'}=(a/s^m)(a'/s^{m'})=\varphi(a/s^m)\varphi(a'/s^{m'})$ and $\varphi(1/1)=1$. This is the canonical homomorphism (it is the map obtained by restricting sections to $X_s$ and dividing by the trivialisation there).

STEP 4. INJECTIVITY OF $\varphi$.
Let $\xi\in(S_s)_0$ with $\varphi(\xi)=0$; write $\xi=a/s^m$ with $a\in S_m$. Then $a/s^m=0$ in $\Gamma(U,\mathcal O_U)$, i.e. $a|_U=0$ in $\Gamma(U,\mathcal A^{\otimes m}|_U)$ (multiplication by the frame $s^{\otimes m}$ is an isomorphism $\mathcal O_U\simeq\mathcal A^{\otimes m}|_U$). By (P1) choose a finite affine open cover $X=\bigcup_{\alpha=1}^{t}W_\alpha$, $W_\alpha=\operatorname{Spec}R_\alpha$, trivialising $\mathcal A$, with $s\leftrightarrow f_\alpha$ and $a|_{W_\alpha}\leftrightarrow b_\alpha\in R_\alpha$. Then $a|_{U\cap W_\alpha}=0$ means $b_\alpha/1=0$ in $\Gamma(D(f_\alpha),\mathcal O)=(R_\alpha)_{f_\alpha}$, and by the elementary property of localisations there is $r_\alpha\ge0$ with $f_\alpha^{r_\alpha}b_\alpha=0$. Let $r=\max_\alpha r_\alpha$ (finite, because the cover is finite). Then $s^{\otimes r}a\in S_{m+r}$ restricts to $f_\alpha^{r}b_\alpha=0$ on each $W_\alpha$, hence $s^{\otimes r}a=0$ in $S_{m+r}$. Therefore $\xi=a/s^m=(s^{\otimes r}a)/s^{m+r}=0$ in $(S_s)_0$. So $\varphi$ is injective.

STEP 5. SURJECTIVITY OF $\varphi$.
5.1 (The maps $\alpha_m$ and their images.) For an open $W\subset X$, (P3) shows that $s$ trivialises $\mathcal A$ over $W\cap U$, so the rule $a\mapsto a/s^m$ defines a map $\mathcal A^{\otimes m}(W)\to\Gamma(W\cap U,\mathcal O)=(j_*\mathcal O_U)(W)$; these are compatible with restriction and $\mathcal O_X(W)$-linear, hence give a morphism of $\mathcal O_X$-modules $\alpha_m:\mathcal A^{\otimes m}\to j_*\mathcal O_U$. Locally over $W=\operatorname{Spec}R$ as in (P3), $\alpha_m$ is $R\to R_f$, $u\mapsto u/f^m$. Let $F_m:=\operatorname{im}(\alpha_m)\subset j_*\mathcal O_U$ (image sheaf) and $K_m:=\ker(\alpha_m)$.
5.2 (The $F_m$ are increasing and their colimit is $j_*\mathcal O_U$.) For every open $W$ and $a\in\mathcal A^{\otimes m}(W)$ one has $\alpha_m(a)=\alpha_{m+1}(s^{\otimes}a)$ where $s^{\otimes}a$ is the image of $a$ under multiplication by $s$, $\mathcal A^{\otimes m}\to\mathcal A^{\otimes(m+1)}$; locally this is $u/f^m=fu/f^{m+1}$. Hence $F_m(W)\subset F_{m+1}(W)$ for all $W$: the $F_m$ form an increasing sequence of subsheaves of the single sheaf $j_*\mathcal O_U$. To see $\varinjlim_m F_m=j_*\mathcal O_U$ it suffices to check on stalks. Fix $x\in X$ and an affine neighbourhood $W=\operatorname{Spec}R$ of $x$ trivialising $\mathcal A$ with $s\leftrightarrow f$. A germ of $(j_*\mathcal O_U)_x$ is represented by $y\in\Gamma(W\cap U,\mathcal O)=R_f$, say $y=b/f^m$ with $b\in R$; then $y=\alpha_m(b\,e_0^{\otimes m})$ on $W$, so $y\in F_m(W)\subset(F_m)_x$. Thus $\bigcup_m(F_m)_x=(j_*\mathcal O_U)_x$.
5.3 (The kernels.) We claim $K_m=\{a\in\mathcal A^{\otimes m}: s^{\otimes N}a=0\ \text{locally for}\ N\gg0\}$ and that multiplication gives an isomorphism $\mu_m:K_0\otimes_{\mathcal O_X}\mathcal A^{\otimes m}\xrightarrow{\sim}K_m$. First, for $a\in\mathcal A^{\otimes m}(W)$: $\alpha_m(a)=0$ iff $a|_{W\cap U}=0$ iff for every $x\in W$ there is a neighbourhood $V$ and $N$ with $s^{\otimes N}a|_V=0$: the forward implication is the local computation $u/1=0$ in $R_f\Rightarrow f^Nu=0$ over an affine trivialising $V=\operatorname{Spec}R$; the converse holds because $s^{\otimes N}$ is a frame over $V\cap U$. Next, multiplication $K_0\times\mathcal A^{\otimes m}\to\mathcal A^{\otimes m}$, $(c,a)\mapsto ca$, is $\mathcal O_X$-bilinear and lands in $K_m$ since $(ca)|_U=c|_\,U\,a|_U=0$. On stalks at $x$, trivialise $\mathcal A$ near $x$ with $s\leftrightarrow f\in\mathcal O_{X,x}$ and put $T:=\{c\in\mathcal O_{X,x}:f^Nc=0\ \text{for some}\ N\}$. Then $(K_0)_x=T$ and $(K_m)_x=T\cdot e_0^{\otimes m}$; using the frame $e_0^{\otimes m}$ to identify $(\mathcal A^{\otimes m})_x\simeq\mathcal O_{X,x}$, the map $(K_0)_x\otimes_{\mathcal O_{X,x}}(\mathcal A^{\otimes m})_x\to(K_m)_x$ becomes $T\to T$, $c\mapsto c$, an isomorphism. Hence $\mu_m$ is an isomorphism of sheaves.
5.4 (Coherence and Serre vanishing.) $X$ is noetherian (P1), so $\mathcal O_X$ is coherent and every subsheaf of a coherent sheaf is coherent; $K_0=\ker(\alpha_0:\mathcal O_X\to j_*\mathcal O_U)$ is a subsheaf of $\mathcal O_X$, hence coherent. Since $\mathcal A$ is invertible, $\mathcal A^{\otimes m}$ is locally free of rank $1$, hence coherent; by 5.3, $K_m\simeq K_0\otimes_{\mathcal O_X}\mathcal A^{\otimes m}$ is coherent for every $m$. Serre's vanishing theorem applied to the ample line bundle $\mathcal A$ on the noetherian scheme $X$ and the coherent sheaf $K_0$ yields an integer $m_0\ge0$ with $H^1\bigl(X,K_0\otimes\mathcal A^{\otimes m}\bigr)=0$ for all $m\ge m_0$, i.e. $H^1(X,K_m)=0$ for $m\ge m_0$. The long exact cohomology sequence of $0\to K_m\to\mathcal A^{\otimes m}\to F_m\to0$ then shows that $\Gamma(X,\mathcal A^{\otimes m})=S_m\to\Gamma(X,F_m)$ is surjective for all $m\ge m_0$.
5.5 (Lifting a given section.) Let $g\in\Gamma(U,\mathcal O_U)=\Gamma(X,j_*\mathcal O_U)$. For each $x\in X$ choose an affine open neighbourhood $W_x=\operatorname{Spec}R_x$ of $x$ trivialising $\mathcal A$ with $s\leftrightarrow f_x$ (possible by (P1) and (P3)). Then $g|_{W_x}\in\Gamma(W_x\cap U,\mathcal O)=(R_x)_{f_x}$, so $g|_{W_x}=b_x/f_x^{m_x}$ for some $b_x\in R_x$, $m_x\ge0$; with $a_x:=b_x\,e_x^{\otimes m_x}\in\mathcal A^{\otimes m_x}(W_x)$ we get $\alpha_{m_x}(a_x)=g|_{W_x}$, so $g|_{W_x}\in F_{m_x}(W_x)$ and $g_x\in(F_{m_x})_x$. For each $m$ the set $\Omega_m:=\{x\in X:g_x\in(F_m)_x\}$ is open (by definition of the stalk condition, it is the union of the opens $V$ with $g|_V\in F_m(V)$), $\Omega_m\subset\Omega_{m+1}$ because $F_m\subset F_{m+1}$, and $X=\bigcup_{m\ge0}\Omega_m$. As $X$ is quasi-compact and the $\Omega_m$ are increasing, $X=\Omega_r$ for some $r\ge0$. Since $F_r\hookrightarrow j_*\mathcal O_U$ is a subsheaf, the condition $g_x\in(F_r)_x$ for all $x$ means exactly that $g$ lies in the image of $\Gamma(X,F_r)\hookrightarrow\Gamma(X,j_*\mathcal O_U)$; fix $g_r\in\Gamma(X,F_r)$ mapping to $g$.
5.6 (Conclusion of surjectivity.) Take $m\ge\max(r,m_0)$. Via the inclusion of subsheaves $F_r\subset F_m\subset j_*\mathcal O_U$, the section $g_r$ defines $g_m\in\Gamma(X,F_m)$ whose image in $\Gamma(X,j_*\mathcal O_U)$ is still $g$. By 5.4 there exists $a\in S_m=\Gamma(X,\mathcal A^{\otimes m})$ mapping to $g_m$ under $\Gamma(X,\mathcal A^{\otimes m})\twoheadrightarrow\Gamma(X,F_m)$. Then, by the definition of $\varphi$ and of $\alpha_m$, $\varphi(a/s^m)=\alpha_m(a)=g_m=g$ in $\Gamma(X,j_*\mathcal O_U)=\Gamma(U,\mathcal O_U)$. Hence $\varphi$ is surjective.

CONCLUSION. Steps 4 and 5 show $\varphi:(S_s)_0\to\Gamma(X_s,\mathcal O_{X_s})$ is a $k$-algebra isomorphism, and Step 2 (together with Step 1 for $U=\varnothing$) shows $X_s$ is an affine $k$-scheme. This completes the proof. (Equivalently, $X_s\simeq\operatorname{Spec}(S_s)_0$ as $k$-schemes.)

lemma_306.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(X\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension \(d\ge 2\) over \(\mathbb F_q\), and let \(\mathcal L\) be an ample line bundle on \(X\) defined over \(\mathbb F_q\). Then there exist integers \(m\ge 1\) and \(n\ge 1\) and a section \(s\in H^0(X_{\mathbb F_{q^m}},\mathcal L^{\otimes n})\) whose zero scheme \(Y=V(s)\) is an effective ample Cartier divisor on \(X_{\mathbb F_{q^m}}\) that is smooth and geometrically connected of pure dimension \(d-1\) over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\).
lemma_306.proof:
Proof. Let k=F_q. We prove the statement in several steps.

Step 1. Geometric integrality. For every field extension E/k, X_E is smooth over E, hence regular. Since X is geometrically connected, X_E is connected. A connected locally noetherian scheme whose local rings are domains is irreducible: local rings being domains imply that two irreducible components cannot meet, and connectedness forces a single component. Hence X_E is integral. In particular H^0(X_E,O_{X_E})=E for every E/k. Indeed, properness over E makes H^0 a finite E-algebra, smoothness makes it reduced, connectedness makes it a field L, and geometric connectedness forces L=E.

Step 2. Choice of a very ample power with vanishing H^1. Since L is ample, L^n is very ample for n≫1. By Serre vanishing, H^{d-1}(X,ω_X⊗L^n)=0 for n≫1. By Serre duality for the smooth projective d-fold X, H^1(X,L^{-n}) is dual to H^{d-1}(X,ω_X⊗L^n). Choose n≥1 so large that A=L^n is very ample and H^1(X,A^{-1})=0. Put V=H^0(X,A) and N=dim V-1. Very ampleness gives a closed immersion X⊂P^N_k.

Step 3. The Bertini good locus. Let P be the projective space whose κ-points are lines in V⊗κ; thus [s]∈P(κ) is a nonzero section of A_κ up to scalar. Let J^1(A) be the first jet bundle of A. Since X is smooth of dimension d, J^1(A) is locally free of rank d+1. Very ampleness implies that the evaluation map V⊗O_X→J^1(A) is surjective. To see this, identify A with O_X(1) under X⊂P^N. Sections of A are restrictions of linear forms on P^N. At x∈X, the embedded tangent space T_xX has dimension d, and vanishing of a linear form at x together with vanishing of its differential along T_xX imposes d+1 independent linear conditions on the N+1-dimensional vector space of linear forms. Hence the map from linear forms to the (d+1)-dimensional space of 1-jets is surjective.

Let K be the kernel of V⊗O_X→J^1(A). It is locally free of rank N-d. Let I=P_X(K)⊂X×P. A point (x,[s]) lies in I exactly when the 1-jet of s at x is zero. Let q:I→P be the projection and B=q(I). The morphism q is proper, because I is closed in X×P and X is proper over k; hence B is closed. Set W=P\B.

If [s]∈W(κ) for some field κ, then Y_s=V(s)⊂X_κ is smooth. Smoothness is checked after base change to an algebraic closure Ω/κ. If Y_s were singular at a point x over Ω, then after trivializing A near x the section is a function f with f(x)=0 and df_x=0. The 1-jet j^1_x(s) is zero exactly when f(x)=0 and df_x=0, so (x,[s]) would lie in I_Ω, contradicting [s]∈W(Ω). Thus Y_s is smooth.

We show W is nonempty. Base change to an algebraically closed field Ω. If N=d then K has rank 0 and I_Ω is empty. If N>d, I_Ω→X_Ω is a projective bundle with fiber P^{N-d-1}. Thus dim I_Ω≤N-1. Since B_Ω is the image of I_Ω, dim B_Ω≤N-1, so B_Ω is a proper closed subset of P_Ω and W_Ω is nonempty. Therefore W is nonempty over k.

Step 4. Choose a finite-field point. The scheme W is a nonempty open subscheme of finite type over the finite field k. Choose a closed point w∈W. Its residue field κ=κ(w) is a finite extension of k, hence κ=F_{q^m} for some m≥1. Let [s]∈P(κ) be the corresponding point and choose a nonzero representative s∈V⊗κ. By cohomology base change for projective schemes over fields, V⊗κ≅H^0(X_κ,A_κ); regard s as a section of A on X_κ. Define Y=V(s)⊂X_κ.

Step 5. Cartier, ample, nonempty, pure dimension. The scheme X_κ is integral by Step 1, and s is nonzero. Hence Y is an effective Cartier divisor: locally it is cut out by a non-zero-divisor. The associated line bundle is O_{X_κ}(Y)≅A_κ, so Y is ample because A is ample and ampleness is stable under base change. The divisor Y is nonempty. If s had no zero, it would trivialize A_κ; but a trivial line bundle cannot be very ample on the positive-dimensional integral projective scheme X_κ, since its global sections would give a closed immersion into P^0. Since w∈W, Y is smooth over κ. A nonempty smooth scheme over a field has pure dimension equal to its relative dimension; here the local equation is a non-zero-divisor in a regular d-dimensional local ring, so Y has pure dimension d-1.

Step 6. Geometric connectedness. We prove that for every field extension E/κ, H^0(Y_E,O_{Y_E})=E. Since Y is an effective Cartier divisor defined by s, on X_E there is an exact sequence
0→A_E^{-1}→O_{X_E}→O_{Y_E}→0.
First, H^0(X_E,A_E^{-1})=0. If t were a nonzero section of A_E^{-1}, then st∈H^0(X_E,O_{X_E})=E is nonzero; say st=c∈E^*. Then t/c is a global inverse of s, so s would be nowhere vanishing, impossible as in Step 5.
Second, H^1(X_E,A_E^{-1})=0. This follows from H^1(X,A^{-1})=0 by cohomology base change for coherent sheaves on projective schemes over fields: after embedding X in projective space, the derived global sections of a coherent sheaf are represented by a bounded complex of finite-dimensional k-vector spaces, and tensoring with E computes the cohomology over E.
Taking cohomology of the exact sequence gives
0→H^0(X_E,A_E^{-1})→H^0(X_E,O_{X_E})→H^0(Y_E,O_{Y_E})→H^1(X_E,A_E^{-1}).
The first and last terms are zero, and the middle left term is E. Hence H^0(Y_E,O_{Y_E})=E.
A scheme over a field is connected iff its global function ring has no nontrivial idempotents. Since E is a field, Y_E is connected. This holds for every field extension E/κ, so Y is geometrically connected over κ.

Step 7. Conclusion. The integers m,n and the section s∈H^0(X_{F_{q^m}},L^{⊗n}) constructed above have zero scheme Y satisfying all required properties: Y is an effective Cartier divisor, it is ample, it is smooth and geometrically connected, and it has pure dimension d-1 over F_{q^m}. This proves the lemma.

lemma_311.statement: Let \(\ell\) be a prime, let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-vector space, and let \(T\in\mathrm{GL}(V)\) be an automorphism whose base change to \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\) is diagonalizable. Then for every integer \(n\ge 0\) the automorphism \({\textstyle\bigwedge^n}T\) of the \(n\)-th exterior power \({\textstyle\bigwedge^n_{\mathbb Q_\ell}}V\) is semisimple, that is, its base change to \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\) is diagonalizable.
lemma_311.proof:
Write \(K:=\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\), \(d:=\dim_{\mathbb Q_\ell}V\), \(W:=V\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}K\) and \(T_K:=T\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\mathrm{id}_K\in\mathrm{GL}_K(W)\). By hypothesis \(T_K\) is diagonalizable over \(K\). We must show that \(({\textstyle\bigwedge^n_{\mathbb Q_\ell}}T)\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\mathrm{id}_K\) is diagonalizable over \(K\) for every \(n\ge0\).

Step 1 (the induced map on an exterior power, and its functoriality). Let \(F\) be any field, \(E\) any \(F\)-vector space and \(S:E\to E\) any \(F\)-linear endomorphism. The map \(E^n\to {\bigwedge}^n_FE\), \((v_1,\dots,v_n)\mapsto Sv_1\wedge\cdots\wedge Sv_n\) is \(n\)-linear (because \(S\) is linear) and alternating (because the wedge in \({\bigwedge}^n_FE\) is alternating). By the universal property of \({\bigwedge}^n_FE\) there is a unique \(F\)-linear map \({\bigwedge}^nS:{\bigwedge}^n_FE\to{\bigwedge}^n_FE\) with
\[ {\textstyle\bigwedge}^nS(v_1\wedge\cdots\wedge v_n)=Sv_1\wedge\cdots\wedge Sv_n \tag{1}\]
for all \(v_1,\dots,v_n\in E\). Functoriality: \({\bigwedge}^n\mathrm{id}_E=\mathrm{id}\) and \({\bigwedge}^n(S\circ S')=({\bigwedge}^nS)\circ({\bigwedge}^nS')\), since both sides of each identity are \(F\)-linear maps on \({\bigwedge}^n_FE\) that agree on the spanning set of decomposable wedges \(v_1\wedge\cdots\wedge v_n\) by two applications of (1). Taking \(S=T\), \(S'=T^{-1}\) (and vice versa) gives \(({\bigwedge}^nT)\circ({\bigwedge}^nT^{-1})=\mathrm{id}={\bigwedge}^n(T^{-1})\circ({\bigwedge}^nT)\); hence \({\bigwedge}^nT\in\mathrm{GL}({\bigwedge}^n_{\mathbb Q_\ell}V)\), so the operator in the statement is indeed an automorphism.

Step 2 (exterior powers commute with the extension of scalars \(\mathbb Q_\ell\subset K\)). Fix a \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-basis \(e=(e_1,\dots,e_d)\) of \(V\); then \((e_i\otimes 1)_{1\le i\le d}\) is a \(K\)-basis of \(W\). For an increasing multi-index \(I=\{i_1<\cdots<i_n\}\subseteq\{1,\dots,d\}\) write \(e_I:=e_{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge e_{i_n}\in{\bigwedge}^n_{\mathbb Q_\ell}V\) and \(\varepsilon_I:=(e_{i_1}\otimes1)\wedge\cdots\wedge(e_{i_n}\otimes1)\in{\bigwedge}^n_KW\). By the basis theorem for exterior powers proved in Step 4 below, \(\{e_I\}_I\) is a \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-basis of \({\bigwedge}^n_{\mathbb Q_\ell}V\) and \(\{\varepsilon_I\}_I\) is a \(K\)-basis of \({\bigwedge}^n_KW\); hence \(\{e_I\otimes1\}_I\) is a \(K\)-basis of \(({\bigwedge}^n_{\mathbb Q_\ell}V)\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}K\). Define
\[ \theta_n:\Bigl({\textstyle\bigwedge^n_{\mathbb Q_\ell}}V\Bigr)\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}K\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }{\textstyle\bigwedge^n_K}W,\qquad \theta_n(e_I\otimes1):=\varepsilon_I \]
by \(K\)-linear extension; \(\theta_n\) is a \(K\)-linear isomorphism (a bijection of bases).

We record the explicit form of \(\theta_n\): for all \(v_1,\dots,v_n\in V\) and \(c\in K\),
\[ \theta_n\bigl((v_1\wedge\cdots\wedge v_n)\otimes c\bigr)=c\,(v_1\otimes1)\wedge\cdots\wedge(v_n\otimes1). \tag{2}\]
Indeed, fix \(c\) and compare the two maps \(V^n\to{\bigwedge}^n_KW\) given by the left- and right-hand sides. Both are \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-multilinear (left: because \((v_1,\dots,v_n)\mapsto v_1\wedge\cdots\wedge v_n\) is multilinear and \(\theta_n\) is \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear; right: because \(v\mapsto v\otimes1\) is \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear and the wedge in \({\bigwedge}^n_KW\) is \(K\)-multilinear). Their difference is therefore \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-multilinear, and it vanishes on every \(n\)-tuple of basis vectors by the very definition of \(\theta_n\); expanding each \(v_j\) in the basis \(e\) shows the difference vanishes identically. This proves (2).

Intertwining property. For each increasing \(I=\{i_1<\cdots<i_n\}\), writing \(Te_j=\sum_{a=1}^{d}t_{aj}e_a\) with \(t_{aj}\in\mathbb Q_\ell\), we compute
\[ \theta_n\bigl((({\textstyle\bigwedge^n}T)\otimes\mathrm{id})(e_I\otimes1)\bigr)=\theta_n\bigl((Te_{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge Te_{i_n})\otimes1\bigr)=\Bigl(\sum_a t_{a i_1}(e_a\otimes1)\Bigr)\wedge\cdots\wedge\Bigl(\sum_a t_{a i_n}(e_a\otimes1)\Bigr),\]
where the last equality uses (2). On the other hand, using (1) for the operator \(T_K\) and the fact that \(T_K(e_j\otimes1)=Te_j\otimes1=\sum_a t_{aj}(e_a\otimes1)\),
\[ {\textstyle\bigwedge^n}(T_K)(\varepsilon_I)=T_K(e_{i_1}\otimes1)\wedge\cdots\wedge T_K(e_{i_n}\otimes1)=\Bigl(\sum_a t_{a i_1}(e_a\otimes1)\Bigr)\wedge\cdots\wedge\Bigl(\sum_a t_{a i_n}(e_a\otimes1)\Bigr).\]
Thus \(\theta_n\circ(({\bigwedge}^nT)\otimes\mathrm{id}_K)={\bigwedge}^n(T_K)\circ\theta_n\) on the \(K\)-basis \(\{e_I\otimes1\}_I\), hence everywhere.

Reduction. Conjugate operators are simultaneously diagonalizable: if \(A,B\) are \(K\)-linear endomorphisms of \(K\)-vector spaces with \(\theta A=B\theta\) for an isomorphism \(\theta\), then \(Ax=\mu x\) implies \(B\theta(x)=\mu\theta(x)\), and the image under \(\theta\) of an eigenbasis of \(A\) is an eigenbasis of \(B\). By the intertwining relation just proved, \(({\bigwedge}^nT)\otimes\mathrm{id}_K\) is conjugate over \(K\) to \({\bigwedge}^n(T_K)\). It therefore suffices to prove:

(\(*\)) For every \(n\ge0\), \({\bigwedge}^n_K(T_K)\) is diagonalizable on \({\bigwedge}^n_KW\).

Step 3 (eigenbasis of \(T_K\)). Since \(T_K\) is diagonalizable by hypothesis, there is a \(K\)-basis \(\mathcal B=\{b_1,\dots,b_d\}\) of \(W\) and scalars \(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_d\in K\) with \(T_Kb_j=\lambda_j b_j\) for all \(j\). (Invertibility of \(T_K\) forces each \(\lambda_j\ne0\), which we shall not need.)

Step 4 (basis theorem for exterior powers; proof for completeness). Let \(E\) be an \(F\)-vector space with basis \((b_1,\dots,b_d)\) and let \(n\ge0\).
(a) \(n=0\): \({\bigwedge}^0_FE=F\), with basis the empty wedge \(1\).
(b) \(n>d\): \({\bigwedge}^n_FE=0\). First, a wedge with two equal entries vanishes: swapping those two entries by the alternating property gives \(x=-x\), and \(\mathrm{char}\,F=0\) so \(2\in F^\times\) and \(x=0\). Every \(n\)-tuple \((v_1,\dots,v_n)\) is linearly dependent since \(\dim_FE=d<n\); say \(v_n=\sum_{j<n}c_jv_j\). Then \(v_1\wedge\cdots\wedge v_n=\sum_{j<n}c_j\,v_1\wedge\cdots\wedge v_j\wedge\cdots\wedge v_n=0\) by the previous sentence. Decomposable wedges span \({\bigwedge}^n_FE\), so it is \(0\).
(c) \(1\le n\le d\): the wedges \(b_I\), \(I=\{i_1<\cdots<i_n\}\), form an \(F\)-basis of \({\bigwedge}^n_FE\). Spanning: every decomposable wedge \(v_1\wedge\cdots\wedge v_n\) expands, by multilinearity, as an \(F\)-linear combination of wedges \(b_{j_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge b_{j_n}\); those with a repeated index vanish by (b), and any remaining one is \(\pm b_I\) for the increasing rearrangement \(I\) (swapping two entries changes the sign).
Linear independence: for each increasing \(I=\{i_1<\cdots<i_n\}\) define \(\varphi_I:E^n\to F\) on basis tuples by \(\varphi_I(b_{j_1},\dots,b_{j_n}):=\det(\delta_{i_p j_q})_{1\le p,q\le n}\) and extend \(F\)-multilinearly. Swapping two arguments of \(\varphi_I\) transposes two rows of that matrix, hence negates the determinant; so \(\varphi_I\) is alternating. By the universal property of \({\bigwedge}^n_FE\), \(\varphi_I\) factors uniquely through a linear \(\widetilde\varphi_I:{\bigwedge}^n_FE\to F\) with \(\widetilde\varphi_I(b_{j_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge b_{j_n})=\varphi_I(b_{j_1},\dots,b_{j_n})\). For increasing \(I'\), \(\widetilde\varphi_I(b_{I'})=\det(\delta_{i_p i'_q})=\delta_{I,I'}\). Given a relation \(\sum_I a_I b_I=0\), applying \(\widetilde\varphi_{I_0}\) yields \(a_{I_0}=0\) for each \(I_0\). Hence the \(b_I\) are independent, and with spanning they form a basis.

Step 5 (proof of \((*\))). Apply Step 4 to \(E=W\) with the eigenbasis \(\mathcal B\) of Step 3.
- If \(n=0\), \({\bigwedge}^0_KW=K\) and \({\bigwedge}^0(T_K)=\mathrm{id}_K\) (Step 1), which is diagonalizable (the element \(1\in K\) is an eigenvector with eigenvalue \(1\)).
- If \(n>d\), \({\bigwedge}^n_KW=0\) by Step 4(b), and the (unique) endomorphism of the zero space is diagonalizable: the empty family is a \(K\)-basis of the zero space, and the condition \"every basis vector is an eigenvector\" is vacuous.
- If \(1\le n\le d\), Step 4(c) says \(\{b_I: I=\{i_1<\cdots<i_n\}\}\) is a \(K\)-basis of \({\bigwedge}^n_KW\). For each such \(I\), by (1) and then the eigenvector relations \(T_Kb_{i_p}=\lambda_{i_p}b_{i_p}\), and finally the \(K\)-multilinearity of the wedge in \({\bigwedge}^n_KW\),
\[ {\textstyle\bigwedge^n}(T_K)\,(b_{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge b_{i_n})=T_Kb_{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge T_Kb_{i_n}=(\lambda_{i_1}b_{i_1})\wedge\cdots\wedge(\lambda_{i_n}b_{i_n})=\Bigl(\prod_{p=1}^{n}\lambda_{i_p}\Bigr)b_{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge b_{i_n}.\]
Thus every element of this basis is an eigenvector of \({\bigwedge}^n(T_K)\) (with eigenvalue \(\prod_p\lambda_{i_p}\in K\)), i.e. \({\bigwedge}^n(T_K)\) is diagonalizable over \(K\). This completes the proof of \((*\)).

Step 6 (descent to \(\mathbb Q_\ell\) and conclusion). By Step 2, \(({\textstyle\bigwedge^n_{\mathbb Q_\ell}}T)\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\mathrm{id}_K\) is \(K\)-linearly conjugate to \({\bigwedge}^n_K(T_K)\), which is diagonalizable by Step 5; conjugation preserves diagonalizability (Step 2, \"Reduction\"). Hence the base change of \({\bigwedge}^n_{\mathbb Q_\ell}T\) to \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\) is diagonalizable, which is the required conclusion.

Finally, applying the common lemma eoinm/lemma_5 to the finite-dimensional \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-vector space \({\bigwedge}^n_{\mathbb Q_\ell}V\) and the operator \({\bigwedge}^nT\in\mathrm{GL}({\bigwedge}^n_{\mathbb Q_\ell}V)\) (Step 1), semisimplicity of \({\bigwedge}^nT\) on \({\bigwedge}^n_{\mathbb Q_\ell}V\) is equivalent to diagonalizability of its base change to \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\); what we proved is thus exactly the assertion that \({\bigwedge}^nT\) is semisimple. This holds for every \(n\ge0\), which proves the lemma.

lemma_bertini_finite_extension.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(X\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension \(d\ge 2\) over \(\mathbb F_q\), and let \(\mathcal L\) be an ample line bundle on \(X\) defined over \(\mathbb F_q\). Then there exist integers \(m\ge 1\) and \(r\ge 1\) and a global section \(s\in H^0\!\left(X_{\mathbb F_{q^r}},\mathcal L^{\otimes m}\right)\), where \(X_{\mathbb F_{q^r}}:=X\times_{\mathbb F_q}\mathbb F_{q^r}\), whose zero scheme \(Y=V(s)\) is an effective Cartier divisor on \(X_{\mathbb F_{q^r}}\), smooth over \(\mathbb F_{q^r}\) and of pure dimension \(d-1\).
lemma_bertini_finite_extension.proof:
Proof. Let k=overline(F_q).

Step 1. Very ample embedding. Since L is ample on the projective F_q-scheme X, there is an integer m_0≥1 such that A=L^{⊗m_0} is very ample. Put W=H^0(X,A), dim W=N+1, and choose an F_q-basis g_0,...,g_N of W. The complete linear system |A| gives a closed immersion i:X→P^N_{F_q} with i^*O(1)≅A and i^*T_j=g_j. Since X has dimension d, N≥d.

For every field extension F'/F_q we need two standard base-change facts. First, X_{F'} is integral: X is smooth and geometrically connected over a field, hence geometrically integral. Second, H^0(X_{F'},A_{F'})≅W⊗_{F_q}F' (flat base change for H^0, or Cech cohomology on a finite affine cover).

Step 2. Universal hyperplane section. Let S=P^N_{F_q}=Proj F_q[C_0,...,C_N] be the dual projective space of hyperplanes in P^N, and let M=pr_1^*A⊗pr_2^*O_S(1) on X×S. Define σ=Σ g_j⊗C_j ∈H^0(X×S,M). Let Z_0=V(σ)⊂X×S, p_0:Z_0→S, q_0:Z_0→X.

The scheme X×S is integral, because X is geometrically integral and S is integral. The section σ is nonzero: if η is the generic point of S, then the restriction of σ to X_η corresponds under the base-change isomorphism to Σ g_j⊗C_j(η) in W⊗κ(η); the values C_j(η) are not all zero and the g_j are a basis, so this element is nonzero. Since X×S is integral, a nonzero section of a line bundle has nonzero germ at every point (otherwise it would vanish on a nonempty open set, hence on a dense open set, and therefore be zero). Thus the local equation of σ is a nonzero element of a domain at every point, and Z_0 is an effective Cartier divisor in X×S.

For a point u∈S with residue field κ, the fibre Z_{0,u} is the zero scheme in X_κ of the fibre section σ_u. Under H^0(X_κ,A_κ)≅W⊗κ, σ_u corresponds to a linear combination Σ c_j g_j with coefficients c_j not all zero, hence σ_u is nonzero.

We record a fibre lemma. Let F'/F_q be any field extension and let τ be a nonzero section of A_{F'} on X_{F'}. Then V(τ) is nonempty and pure of dimension d-1. Indeed, τ corresponds to a linear form ℓ on P^N_{F'} which does not vanish identically on X_{F'}, so H=V(ℓ) does not contain X_{F'}. Then V(τ)=X_{F'}∩H. Since X_{F'} is integral of dimension d, every proper closed subset has components of dimension at most d-1. The projective dimension theorem gives every component of X_{F'}∩H dimension at least d+N-1-N=d-1. Hence every component has dimension exactly d-1; in particular the intersection is nonempty because d≥1.

Step 3. The differential and the bad locus. On Z_0 define d_Xσ as follows. Locally trivialize M and write σ=f; set d_Xσ=df along X. If the trivialization is changed by a unit, f is multiplied by that unit, and on V(σ) the differential is multiplied by the same unit; hence the vanishing locus is well defined. Equivalently, d_Xσ is a section of q_0^*(A⊗Ω^1_{X/F_q})⊗p_0^*O_S(1). Let Σ_0=V(d_Xσ)⊂Z_0.

Base change to k gives Ω^1_{X_k/k}≅Ω^1_{X/F_q}⊗O_{X_k}, so (Σ_0)_k=Σ, where I:=Z_0(X_k) and Σ⊂I is the zero scheme of the differential along X_k of σ_k.

Step 4. Local smoothness criterion. Let F be a perfect field, Y a smooth d-fold over F, L a line bundle on Y, and τ a nonzero section. Put Z=V(τ). For z∈Z, choose a local trivialization τ=f near z. Then R=O_{Y,z} is a regular local ring, f is a nonzero element of its maximal ideal, and Z is smooth at z iff R/(f) is regular. Since R is regular and f is a nonzero divisor, R/(f) is regular iff f is not in m_z^2, which is equivalent to df(z)≠0. (If f is not in m_z^2, it can be completed to a regular system of parameters; if f∈m_z^2, the embedding dimension of R/(f) is too large for its dimension.)

Step 5. Dimension of the bad locus over k. Work over k. For x∈X_k, the fibre I_x of I→X_k is the projective space of hyperplanes in P^N_k containing x, hence P^{N-1}_{κ(x)}. By the local criterion, (x,H)∈Σ_x iff H contains the embedded tangent space T_xX_k.

Choose a basis element g_0 with g_0(x)≠0 and set u_j=g_j/g_0 for j≥1 on a neighbourhood of x. Since i is a closed immersion, the differentials du_1,...,du_N span Ω_{X_k/k,x}; their rank is d. In homogeneous coordinates (c_1:...:c_N) on I_x, the condition (x,H)∈Σ_x is the linear system Σ c_j du_j(x)=0. This system has rank d. Therefore Σ_x is a linear subspace of P^{N-1}_{κ(x)} of dimension at most N-d-1 (if N=d, it is empty). The morphism q:Σ→X_k is of finite type. By the standard dimension inequality for finite-type morphisms, dim Σ≤dim X_k+sup_x dim Σ_x≤d+(N-d-1)=N-1.

Step 6. Good hyperplanes over k. The projection p:I→S_k is proper, because I is closed in X_k×S_k and X_k is proper. Hence p(Σ) is closed in S_k. Since dim p(Σ)≤dimΣ≤N-1<dim S_k=N, p(Σ) is not all of S_k. Let U=S_k\p(Σ). Then U is a nonempty open subset, and for H∈U the fibre X_k∩H is smooth over k by the local criterion.

Step 7. Descent to F_q. The morphism p_0:Z_0→S is proper, so B:=p_0(Σ_0) is closed in S. Put V_0=S\B. We claim (V_0)_k=U. For s'∈S_k lying over s∈S, the fibre (Σ_0)_{s'} is (Σ_0)_s×_{κ(s)}κ(s'), which is empty iff (Σ_0)_s is empty. Hence s'∈p(Σ) iff s∈B. Thus (V_0)_k=S_k\p(Σ)=U. Since U is nonempty and base change to a field extension preserves nonemptiness, V_0 is nonempty. It is a nonempty open subscheme of finite type over F_q.

Step 8. Choose the finite extension. Let t∈V_0 be a closed point. Since V_0 is of finite type over the finite field F_q, its residue field is a finite extension κ(t)=F_{q^r} for some r≥1. The point t corresponds to a hyperplane H_t⊂P^N_{F_{q^r}}; choose coefficients c_0,...,c_N∈F_{q^r}, not all zero. Under H^0(X_{F_{q^r}},A_{F_{q^r}})≅W⊗F_{q^r}, the fibre section σ_t is s=Σ c_j g_j. Because the g_j form a basis and not all c_j vanish, s≠0. Its zero scheme is Y=V(s)=Z_{0,t}=X_{F_{q^r}}∩H_t.

Step 9. Verification. The scheme X_{F_{q^r}} is integral. As argued above, a nonzero section of a line bundle on an integral scheme has nonzero germ at every point; hence the local equation of s is a nonzero element of the domain O_{X_{F_{q^r}},x} at every x, so it is a non-zero-divisor. Therefore Y is an effective Cartier divisor.

Since t∈V_0, no point z∈Z_{0,t} lies in Σ_0; equivalently d_Xσ(z)≠0 for every z∈Y. Applying the local smoothness criterion over the perfect field F_{q^r} to the section s, Y is smooth at every point, hence smooth over F_{q^r}. By the fibre lemma in Step 2, Y is nonempty and pure of dimension d-1.

Taking m=m_0 gives a section s∈H^0(X_{F_{q^r}},L^{⊗m}) with all required properties.

lemma_313.statement: Let \(\ell\) be a prime, let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-vector space, let \(T\in\mathrm{GL}(V)\), and let \(c\in\mathbb Q_\ell^{\times}\). Suppose there exist a finite subset \(S\subseteq V\) spanning \(V\) over \(\mathbb Q_\ell\) and a bijection \(\pi:S\to S\) such that \(T(s)=c\,\pi(s)\) for every \(s\in S\). Then \(T\) is semisimple, that is, its base change to \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\) is diagonalizable.
lemma_313.proof:
We prove that the base change $\overline{T}:=T\otimes \mathrm{id}$ of $T$ to $W:=V\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$ is diagonalizable. Throughout, $\mathbb Q_\ell$ has characteristic $0$, so $m\cdot 1\neq 0\in\mathbb Q_\ell$ for every integer $m\ge 1$.

**Step 1 (the permutation has finite order).** $S$ is a finite set; write $N=|S|$. The group $\mathrm{Sym}(S)$ of bijections $S\to S$ is finite of order $N!$, so the bijection $\pi$ has finite order: there is a least integer $m\ge 1$ (the order of $\pi$ in $\mathrm{Sym}(S)$) with $\pi^{m}=\mathrm{id}_{S}$. (If $S=\varnothing$ we take $m=1$; then $S$ spans only the zero space, so $V=0$, $W=0$, and $\overline T$ is the identity of the zero $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$-space, which is diagonalizable with respect to the empty basis. In the sequel we argue in the general case; the case $V=0$ is already settled.)

**Step 2 (iteration of the hypothesis).** We claim that for every integer $k\ge 1$ and every $s\in S$,
$$T^{k}(s)=c^{k}\,\pi^{k}(s).\qquad (\ast)$$
For $k=1$ this is exactly the hypothesis $T(s)=c\,\pi(s)$. Assume $(\ast)$ holds for some $k\ge 1$. Since $\pi$ maps $S$ into $S$, the element $\pi^{k}(s)$ lies in $S$, so the hypothesis applies to it: $T(\pi^{k}(s))=c\,\pi^{k+1}(s)$. Using $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linearity of $T$ and $c^{k}\in\mathbb Q_\ell$,
$$T^{k+1}(s)=T\bigl(T^{k}(s)\bigr)=T\bigl(c^{k}\pi^{k}(s)\bigr)=c^{k}\,T(\pi^{k}(s))=c^{k}\cdot c\,\pi^{k+1}(s)=c^{k+1}\pi^{k+1}(s),$$
which is $(\ast)$ for $k+1$. By induction, $(\ast)$ holds for all $k\ge 1$.

**Step 3 ($T$ is annihilated by $X^{m}-c^{m}$).** Taking $k=m$ in $(\ast)$ and using $\pi^{m}=\mathrm{id}_{S}$ gives $T^{m}(s)=c^{m}s$ for every $s\in S$. The two endomorphisms $T^{m}$ and $c^{m}\mathrm{id}_{V}$ of $V$ are $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear and agree on the subset $S$; since $S$ spans $V$, they agree on all of $V$. Hence
$$f(T)=0,\qquad f(X):=X^{m}-c^{m}\in\mathbb Q_\ell[X].$$
(In particular $T^{m}=c^{m}\mathrm{id}_V$ with $c^{m}\neq 0$, which is consistent with, and in fact implies, the given invertibility of $T$.)

**Step 4 ($f$ is square-free over $\mathbb Q_\ell$).** Formally differentiating in $\mathbb Q_\ell[X]$ gives $f'(X)=mX^{m-1}$. We show $\gcd(f,f')=1$ in $\mathbb Q_\ell[X]$. If a $d\in\mathbb Q_\ell[X]$ of positive degree divided both $f$ and $f'$, then, since $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$ is algebraically closed, $d$ would have a root $\alpha\in\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$; then $f(\alpha)=f'(\alpha)=0$. But $f'(\alpha)=m\alpha^{m-1}=0$ forces $\alpha=0$ (as $m\neq 0$ in $\mathbb Q_\ell$), whereas $f(0)=-c^{m}\neq 0$ because $c\in\mathbb Q_\ell^{\times}$. This contradiction shows $\gcd(f,f')=1$, i.e. $f$ is square-free in $\mathbb Q_\ell[X]$; equivalently $f$ has $m$ distinct roots in $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$.

**Step 5 (the minimal polynomial of $T$ is square-free).** Let $\mu_T\in\mathbb Q_\ell[X]$ be the minimal polynomial of $T$. Since $f(T)=0$ and $\mu_T$ generates the ideal of polynomials annihilating $T$, we have $\mu_T\mid f$ in $\mathbb Q_\ell[X]$. Write $\mu_T=\prod_{i=1}^{r}p_i$ into monic irreducibles in $\mathbb Q_\ell[X]$. If some $p_i$ occurred with multiplicity $\ge 2$ in $\mu_T$, then $p_i^{2}\mid f$, contradicting the square-freeness of $f$ from Step 4. Hence
$$\mu_T=\prod_{i=1}^{r}p_i\quad\text{with the }p_i\text{ pairwise distinct monic irreducibles.}\qquad(\dagger)$$

**Step 6 ($\mu_T$ splits over $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$ into distinct linear factors).** Each $p_i$ has characteristic $0$, hence is separable: $\gcd(p_i,p_i')=1$ because $\deg p_i\ge 1$ and $p_i'\neq 0$ with $\deg p_i'<\deg p_i$, so $p_i\nmid p_i'$. Therefore in $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell[X]$,
$$p_i=\prod_{\lambda\in\Lambda_i}(X-\lambda)\quad\text{with the }\lambda\in\Lambda_i\text{ pairwise distinct},$$
and the sets $\Lambda_i$ are pairwise disjoint: a common root $\lambda\in\Lambda_i\cap\Lambda_j$ would give a common divisor $\gcd_{\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell[X]}(X-\lambda)$ of $p_i$ and $p_j$, contradicting their distinctness and irreducibility in $\mathbb Q_\ell[X]$. Combining with $(\dagger)$,
$$\mu_T=\prod_{\lambda\in\Lambda}(X-\lambda)\ \ \text{in }\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell[X],\qquad \Lambda=\bigsqcup_{i=1}^{r}\Lambda_i,\ \ |\Lambda|=\deg\mu_T,$$
a product of pairwise distinct linear factors.
