**Step 7 ($\overline T$ is diagonalizable).** Since $\mu_T(T)=0$ in $\mathrm{End}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V)$, applying $-\otimes\mathrm{id}$ gives $\mu_T(\overline T)=0$ in $\mathrm{End}_{\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell}(W)$. Write $\mu_T=\prod_{j=1}^{t}(X-\lambda_j)$ in $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell[X]$ with the $\lambda_j$ pairwise distinct (so $t=\deg\mu_T$), and put $q_j(X):=\prod_{i\neq j}(X-\lambda_i)$. The ideals $((X-\lambda_j))\subset\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell[X]$ are pairwise comaximal (each $X-\lambda_j$ is irreducible and they are non-associate), so by the Chinese remainder theorem there exist $a_1,\dots,a_t\in\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell[X]$ with
$$\sum_{j=1}^{t}a_j q_j\equiv 1 \pmod{\mu_T}.$$
Define $e_j:=a_j(\overline T)\,q_j(\overline T)\in\mathrm{End}_{\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell}(W)$. Evaluating the congruence at $\overline T$ (valid since $\mu_T(\overline T)=0$) gives $\sum_{j}e_j=\mathrm{id}_W$. For $j\neq k$, the product $q_jq_k$ is divisible by $\mu_T$, hence $e_je_k=0$. Moreover $(X-\lambda_j)a_jq_j$ is divisible by $\mu_T$, so $(\overline T-\lambda_j\mathrm{id})e_j=0$. Consequently $W=\bigoplus_{j=1}^{t}\mathrm{im}(e_j)$ (each $w\in W$ writes uniquely as $w=\sum_j e_jw$, and $\sum_j w_j=0$ with $w_j\in\mathrm{im}(e_j)$ forces $w_j=e_j\sum_k w_k=0$), and $\overline T$ acts on $\mathrm{im}(e_j)$ as the scalar $\lambda_j$. Choosing a basis of each $\mathrm{im}(e_j)$ and concatenating gives a basis of $W$ consisting of eigenvectors of $\overline T$; that is, $\overline T$ is diagonalizable over $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$.

This is precisely the assertion that $T$ is semisimple, which completes the proof. (Note that the argument used only that $S$ spans $V$, that $\pi$ is a self-bijection of $S$, and that $c\neq 0$; the a priori invertibility of $T$ is in fact a consequence, via $T^{m}=c^{m}\mathrm{id}_V$.)

lemma_compact_top_trace.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(X\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension \(d\ge1\) over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(Y\subset X\) be an effective ample divisor defined over \(\mathbb F_q\) and smooth of pure dimension \(d-1\), let \(j:U=X\setminus Y\hookrightarrow X\) be the open immersion, \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), \(\ell\neq p\) prime, and suppose \(H^m_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=0\) for every \(m>2(d-1)\). Let \(\operatorname{tr}_X:H^{2d}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)\) be the Poincaré duality trace normalised by \(\operatorname{tr}_X(\mathrm{cl}(x))=[\kappa(x):\mathbb F_q]\), let \(j_!:H^{2d}_c(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{2d}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) be the extension-by-zero homomorphism of the localisation long exact sequence of the pair \((X,Y)\), and let \(F=(\mathrm{id}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(c)=c^q\), be the \(q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius of \(H^{2d}_c(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\), with \(F\) acting on \(\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)\) as multiplication by \(q^d\). Then \(\operatorname{tr}_X\circ j_!\) is a \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear isomorphism and \((\operatorname{tr}_X\circ j_!)(Fx)=q^d\,(\operatorname{tr}_X\circ j_!)(x)\) for all \(x\).
lemma_compact_top_trace.proof:
We keep the notation of the statement: \(q=p^a\), \(X\) smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension \(d\ge 1\) over \(\mathbb F_q\), \(Y\subset X\) an \(\mathbb F_q\)-rational effective ample divisor smooth of pure dimension \(d-1\), \(i:Y\hookrightarrow X\) the closed immersion, \(j:U=X\setminus Y\hookrightarrow X\) the open immersion, \(k=\overline{\mathbb F_q}\), \(\ell\neq p\), and we write
\[(\ast)\qquad H^m_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=0\quad\text{for every }m>2(d-1)\]
for the stated hypothesis. All cohomology groups below are étale cohomology with \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-coefficients on the base change to \(k\), and \(F\) always denotes the \(q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius \((\mathrm{id}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(c)=c^q\), of the term in question.

**Step 1 (the localisation sequence).** We check the hypotheses of Spark:lemma_283: \(X\) is smooth, projective, geometrically connected of pure dimension \(d\ge 1\) over \(\mathbb F_q\); \(Y\subset X\) is an effective ample divisor defined over \(\mathbb F_q\) and smooth of pure dimension \(d-1\); \(U=X\setminus Y\) with open immersion \(j\) and closed immersion \(i\); \(k=\overline{\mathbb F_q}\); \(\ell\neq p\). All are satisfied by hypothesis. Hence that lemma yields a long exact sequence of **finite-dimensional** \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-vector spaces
\[\cdots\to H^n_c(U_k)\xrightarrow{\;j_!\;}H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k)\xrightarrow{\;i^*\;}H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k)\to H^{n+1}_c(U_k)\to\cdots \tag{1}\]
whose middle map is the pullback \(i^*\), and in which **every** map commutes with the \(q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius automorphisms of the four terms. (The first map of each four-term block is exactly the extension-by-zero homomorphism \(j_!\) of the localisation sequence of the pair \((X,Y)\), which is the map denoted \(j_!\) in the present statement.)

**Step 2 (finite-dimensionality of the top compactly supported group).** Taking \(n=2d\) in (1), the group \(H^{2d}_c(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) occurs as a term of the sequence (1), and (1) is a sequence of finite-dimensional \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-vector spaces by Spark:lemma_283. Hence \(\dim_{\mathbb Q_\ell}H^{2d}_c(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)<\infty\). No finiteness input beyond Spark:lemma_283 is used here.

**Step 3 (the two divisor groups that must vanish).** Since \(d\ge 1\) we have \(2d-1-2(d-1)=1>0\) and \(2d-2(d-1)=2>0\); that is,
\[2d-1>2(d-1)\quad\text{and}\quad 2d>2(d-1).\]
(In particular this holds for \(d=1\), where \(2(d-1)=0\) and the two relevant degrees are \(1\) and \(2\), and \(Y\) is a smooth, hence finite \'etale, \(0\)-dimensional scheme.) Applying \((\ast)\) with \(m=2d-1\) and with \(m=2d\) gives
\[H^{2d-1}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=0,\qquad H^{2d}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=0. \tag{2}\]

**Step 4 (\(j_!\) is an isomorphism).** The segment of (1) with \(n=2d-1\) followed by \(n=2d\) reads
\[H^{2d-1}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k)\longrightarrow H^{2d}_c(U_k)\xrightarrow{\;j_!\;}H^{2d}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k)\xrightarrow{\;i^*\;}H^{2d}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k).\]
Exactness of (1) at \(H^{2d}_c(U_k)\) says \(\ker(j_!)=\operatorname{im}\bigl(H^{2d-1}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k)\to H^{2d}_c(U_k)\bigr)\), which is \(0\) by (2); so \(j_!\) is injective. Exactness at \(H^{2d}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k)\) says \(\operatorname{im}(j_!)=\ker(i^*)\); by (2) the target of \(i^*\) is the zero space, so \(\ker(i^*)=H^{2d}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k)\) and \(j_!\) is surjective. Thus
\[j_!:H^{2d}_c(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\;\sim\;}H^{2d}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\tag{3}\]
is a \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear isomorphism.

**Step 5 (the trace on \(X\)).** Apply eoinm:lemma_77 to the variety \(X\) over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\) with \(m=1\) (so \(\mathbb F_{q^m}=\mathbb F_q\)), which satisfies that lemma's hypotheses: \(X\) is smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension \(d\) over \(\mathbb F_q\), \(k=\overline{\mathbb F_q}\), \(\ell\neq p\). Its part (a) provides a canonical \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear isomorphism
\[\operatorname{tr}_X:H^{2d}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\;\sim\;}\mathbb Q_\ell(-d),\qquad \operatorname{tr}_X(\mathrm{cl}(x))=[\kappa(x):\mathbb F_q]\ \ \text{for every closed point }x\in X,\]
which is arithmetic-Frobenius-equivariant, where \(F\) acts on \(\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)\) as multiplication by \(q^{md}=q^d\). This is exactly the normalised trace appearing in the present statement (the normalisation \([\kappa(x):\mathbb F_{q^m}]=[\kappa(x):\mathbb F_q]\) at \(m=1\)).

**Step 6 (the compactly supported trace is an isomorphism).** Define
\[\operatorname{tr}_c:=\operatorname{tr}_X\circ j_!:H^{2d}_c(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\longrightarrow \mathbb Q_\ell(-d).\]
Both factors are \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear isomorphisms (Step 4 and Step 5), hence so is their composition. This proves the first assertion.

**Step 7 (Frobenius compatibility).** By eoinm:lemma_6a, for the schemes \(X\) and \(Y\) of finite type over \(\mathbb F_q\) the maps \(F_{\mathrm{ar}}=(\mathrm{id}\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma)^*\) are \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear automorphisms of each \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(-_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\), with inverse the geometric Frobenius \((\mathrm{id}\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma^{-1})^*\); and Spark:lemma_283 asserts that the compactly supported terms in (1) likewise carry \(q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius **automorphisms**, and that every map of (1) commutes with them. Writing \(F_c\) and \(F_X\) for the Frobenius automorphisms of \(H^{2d}_c(U_k)\) and \(H^{2d}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k)\), the commutation of \(j_!\) with Frobenius is
\[j_!\circ F_c=F_X\circ j_!.\tag{4}\]
Now let \(x\in H^{2d}_c(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\). Using first the definition of \(\operatorname{tr}_c\), then (4), then the Frobenius-equivariance of \(\operatorname{tr}_X\) from eoinm:lemma_77(a) (where \(F\) on \(\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)\) is multiplication by \(q^d\)), we obtain
\[(\operatorname{tr}_X\circ j_!)(F_c x)=\operatorname{tr}_X\bigl(j_!(F_c x)\bigr)=\operatorname{tr}_X\bigl(F_X\, j_!(x)\bigr)=q^d\,\operatorname{tr}_X\bigl(j_!(x)\bigr)=q^d\,(\operatorname{tr}_X\circ j_!)(x).\]
Since the \(F\) of the statement is precisely \(F_c\), this is the required identity \((\operatorname{tr}_X\circ j_!)(Fx)=q^d(\operatorname{tr}_X\circ j_!)(x)\) for all \(x\).

**Conclusion.** Steps 6 and 7 give that \(\operatorname{tr}_X\circ j_!:H^{2d}_c(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)\) is a \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear isomorphism satisfying \((\operatorname{tr}_X\circ j_!)(Fx)=q^d(\operatorname{tr}_X\circ j_!)(x)\) for all \(x\), and Step 2 records that \(H^{2d}_c(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) is finite-dimensional. Note that the scalar \(q^d\) arises solely from the Frobenius action on the Tate twist \(\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)\) (eoinm:lemma_77(a)); the map \(j_!\) itself commutes with Frobenius without any scalar (Spark:lemma_283). This completes the proof. \(\blacksquare\)

lemma_316.statement: Let \(K\) be a field of characteristic zero, let \(d\ge1\), let \(V=\bigoplus_{n\in\mathbb Z}V_n\) be a finite-dimensional \(\mathbb Z\)-graded \(K\)-vector space with \(V_n=0\) for \(n<0\) and for \(n>2d\), and let \(L:V\to V\) be a \(K\)-linear endomorphism with \(L(V_n)\subseteq V_{n+2}\) such that \(L^{d-m}:V_m\to V_{2d-m}\) is an isomorphism for every \(0\le m\le d\). For \(0\le m\le d\) set \(P^m=\ker\bigl(L^{d-m+1}:V_m\to V_{2d-m+2}\bigr)\) and set \(P^m=0\) for \(m<0\) and for \(m>d\). Then for every integer \(n\ge0\) the \(K\)-linear map \(\bigoplus_{r\ge\max(0,\,n-d)}P^{\,n-2r}\to V_n\) given by \((x_r)_r\mapsto\sum_r L^{r}x_r\) is an isomorphism.
lemma_316.proof:
We keep the notation of the statement: $K$ has characteristic $0$, $d\ge 1$, $V=\bigoplus_{n\in\mathbb Z}V_n$ is a finite-dimensional $\mathbb Z$-graded $K$-vector space with $V_n=0$ for $n<0$ and for $n>2d$, $L:V\to V$ satisfies $L(V_j)\subseteq V_{j+2}$ for all $j$, and $L^{d-m}:V_m\xrightarrow{\sim}V_{2d-m}$ is an isomorphism for every $0\le m\le d$. For $0\le m\le d$ we write $P^m=\ker(L^{d-m+1}:V_m\to V_{2d-m+2})$, and we set $P^m=0$ for $m<0$ and for $m>d$. (Note that $L^{d-m+1}$ does map $V_m$ into $V_{2d-m+2}$, by the grading condition applied $d-m+1$ times, so $P^m$ is well defined.)

Fix an integer $n\ge 0$ and put
\[
R:=\max(0,\,n-d),\qquad R':=\Bigl\lfloor \frac n2\Bigr\rfloor .
\]
For an integer $r$ write $m_r:=n-2r$, and consider
\[
\Phi:\;S_n:=\bigoplus_{r\ge R}P^{\,m_r}\longrightarrow V_n,\qquad (x_r)_{r\ge R}\longmapsto \sum_{r\ge R}L^{r}x_r .
\]
We must show $\Phi$ is an isomorphism. The proof has three steps: (1) $S_n$ is a finite direct sum and $\Phi$ is well defined and $K$-linear; (2) $\Phi$ is injective, by lemma_296; (3) $\dim_K S_n=\dim_K V_n$, by the dimension formula of lemma_295 and a telescoping sum. Injectivity plus equality of finite dimensions then gives bijectivity (rank-nullity: $\dim_K S_n=\dim_K\operatorname{im}\Phi+\dim_K\ker\Phi=\dim_K\operatorname{im}\Phi$, so $\operatorname{im}\Phi$ has dimension $\dim_KV_n$, hence equals $V_n$).

STEP 1 (well-definedness and finiteness). First, only finitely many summands of $S_n$ are nonzero. Indeed, if $r>R'=\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ then $r>n/2$, hence $m_r=n-2r<0$, and by convention $P^{m_r}=0$. Therefore
\[
S_n=\bigoplus_{r=R}^{R'}P^{\,m_r},
\]
the sum being $0$ if $R>R'$. Each $P^{m_r}$ is a $K$-subspace of the finite-dimensional space $V_{m_r}$, so $S_n$ is finite dimensional, and an element of $S_n$ has only finitely many nonzero components, so the expression $\sum_{r\ge R}L^rx_r$ is a finite sum.

Next, $\Phi$ lands in $V_n$: if $x\in P^{m_r}\subseteq V_{m_r}=V_{n-2r}$, then iterating $L(V_j)\subseteq V_{j+2}$ gives $L^{r}(V_{n-2r})\subseteq V_{n-2r+2r}=V_n$. Hence $L^rx_r\in V_n$ for every $r$, so $\Phi((x_r))\in V_n$. Additivity and $K$-homogeneity of $\Phi$ follow immediately from those of each $x\mapsto L^rx$; thus $\Phi$ is a $K$-linear homomorphism.

STEP 2 (injectivity). The data $(K,d,V,L,(P^m))$ satisfy verbatim the hypotheses of Spark's lemma_296 (same grading vanishing ranges, same condition $L(V_j)\subseteq V_{j+2}$, same hard-Lefschetz isomorphism hypothesis for $0\le m\le d$, same definition of $P^m$ including the conventions $P^m=0$ for $m<0$ and $m>d$), and its conclusion is exactly that the map $\bigoplus_{r\ge\max(0,n-d)}P^{\,n-2r}\to V_n$, $(x_r)_r\mapsto\sum_rL^rx_r$, is injective. By lemma_296, $\Phi$ is injective.

STEP 3 (dimension count). We compute $\dim_KS_n$ and compare with $\dim_KV_n$.

3a. Range check for lemma_295. Let $R\le r\le R'$. Then $m_r\ge 0$ because $r\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor$. Moreover $m_r\le d$: if $n\le d$ then $m_r=n-2r\le n\le d$; if $n>d$ then $R=n-d\le r$, so $m_r=n-2r\le n-2(n-d)=2d-n<d$. Hence $0\le m_r\le d$, and lemma_295 applies to $m=m_r$, giving
\[
\dim_KP^{m_r}=\dim_KV_{m_r}-\dim_KV_{m_r-2}=\dim_KV_{n-2r}-\dim_KV_{n-2r-2},
\]
where, as in lemma_295, $V_j=0$ is understood for $j<0$.

3b. Telescoping. If $R\le R'$, summing over $r=R,\dots,R'$ and using that the second term of the summand indexed by $r$ equals the first term of the summand indexed by $r+1$ (both are $\dim_KV_{n-2r-2}$), all intermediate terms cancel:
\[
\dim_KS_n=\sum_{r=R}^{R'}\bigl(\dim_KV_{n-2r}-\dim_KV_{n-2r-2}\bigr)=\dim_KV_{n-2R}-\dim_KV_{n-2R'-2}.
\]
(If $R>R'$ the sum is empty and $S_n=0$; this case is handled separately in 3d.)

3c. The two boundary cases with $R\le R'$.

Case (i): $0\le n\le d$. Then $R=0$, so $n-2R=n$. Also $n-2R'=n-2\lfloor n/2\rfloor=\varepsilon\in\{0,1\}$, hence $n-2R'-2=\varepsilon-2\in\{-2,-1\}<0$, so $V_{n-2R'-2}=0$ by the standing vanishing $V_j=0$ for $j<0$. Thus
\[
\dim_KS_n=\dim_KV_n .
\]
(Here $R=0\le R'$ since $n\ge0$.)

Case (ii): $d<n\le 2d$. Then $R=n-d$, so $n-2R=2d-n$, and as in 3a we have $0\le 2d-n<d$. Again $n-2R'-2=\varepsilon-2<0$ with $\varepsilon=n-2\lfloor n/2\rfloor\in\{0,1\}$, so the second boundary term vanishes and
\[
\dim_KS_n=\dim_KV_{2d-n}.
\n(Here $R\le R'$ holds because $n-d\le n/2$ is equivalent to $n\le 2d$.) Since $d<n\le 2d$ we have $0\le 2d-n\le d$, so the hypothesis on $L$ applied to $m:=2d-n$ says that
\[
L^{\,d-(2d-n)}=L^{\,n-d}:V_{2d-n}\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }V_{2d-(2d-n)}=V_n
\]
is an isomorphism. Consequently $\dim_KV_{2d-n}=\dim_KV_n$, and therefore $\dim_KS_n=\dim_KV_n$ in this case as well.

3d. The remaining case $n>2d$. Then $R=n-d$ (as $n>d$) and $R>n/2\ge R'$, so the index range $R\le r\le R'$ is empty; equivalently, for every $r\ge R$ one has $m_r=n-2r\le n-2(n-d)=2d-n<0$, hence $P^{m_r}=0$. Thus $S_n=0$. On the other hand $V_n=0$ because $n>2d$. So $\Phi:0\to0$ is an isomorphism.

CONCLUSION. In every case $n\ge0$ the $K$-vector spaces $S_n$ and $V_n$ are finite dimensional of the same dimension, and by Step 2 the $K$-linear map $\Phi:S_n\to V_n$ is injective. By rank-nullity $\Phi$ is therefore surjective, hence an isomorphism. Explicitly, $\bigoplus_{r\ge\max(0,n-d)}P^{\,n-2r}\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }V_n$, $(x_r)_r\mapsto\sum_rL^rx_r$, is a $K$-linear isomorphism, which is the required statement. $\qquad\blacksquare$

lemma_318.statement: Let \(k\) be a field, let \(X\) be a projective scheme over \(k\), let \(\mathcal L\) be an ample line bundle on \(X\), let \(n\ge1\) be an integer, and let \(s\in H^0(X,\mathcal L^{\otimes n})\) be a global section. Let \(V(s)\subseteq X\) be the closed subscheme defined as the support of the cokernel of the \(\mathcal O_X\)-module homomorphism \(\mathcal O_X\to\mathcal L^{\otimes n}\) determined by \(s\). Then \(V(s)\) is exactly the complement in \(X\) of the open locus \(X_s\) on which \(s\) generates \(\mathcal L^{\otimes n}\), and the open subscheme \(X\setminus V(s)\) is affine.
lemma_318.proof:
We keep the notation of the statement: $k$ a field, $X$ a projective $k$-scheme, $\mathcal L$ an ample line bundle on $X$, $n\ge 1$, $s\in H^0(X,\mathcal L^{\otimes n})$. Write $\mathcal M:=\mathcal L^{\otimes n}$; this is an invertible (locally free of rank $1$) $\mathcal O_X$-module. Let
$$\varphi:\mathcal O_X\longrightarrow \mathcal M$$
be the $\mathcal O_X$-linear homomorphism corresponding to $s$ under the canonical bijection $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal O_X}(\mathcal O_X,\mathcal M)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\Gamma(X,\mathcal M)$, $u\mapsto u(1)$; thus $\varphi(1)=s$. Put $\mathcal C:=\operatorname{coker}(\varphi)$ and $Z:=\operatorname{Supp}(\mathcal C)$, endowed with its reduced induced closed subscheme structure; this is the closed subscheme $V(s)$ of the statement. (Any other closed subscheme structure on $Z$ gives the same underlying set and hence the same open complement, so the choice of structure is irrelevant for what follows.)

**Step 0: $X$ is noetherian and $\mathcal C$ is coherent.** Since $X$ is projective over $k$, $X$ is a closed subscheme of $\mathbf P^r_k$ for some $r$, hence of finite type over the noetherian ring $k$; therefore $X$ is a noetherian scheme. The sheaf $\mathcal M$ is locally free of rank $1$, hence coherent. The cokernel of a morphism of coherent sheaves on a noetherian scheme is coherent, so $\mathcal C$ is a coherent $\mathcal O_X$-module (it is a quotient of the coherent sheaf $\mathcal M$).

**Step 1: the support of a coherent sheaf is closed.** Let $\mathcal F$ be a coherent sheaf on a scheme $Y$. To see $\operatorname{Supp}(\mathcal F)$ is closed it suffices to check on an affine open $U=\operatorname{Spec}A$, where $\mathcal F|_U=\widetilde M$ for a finitely generated $A$-module $M$. We claim $\operatorname{Supp}(\widetilde M)=V(\operatorname{Ann}_A M)$. Indeed, for $\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{Spec}A$, choosing generators $m_1,\dots,m_t$ of $M$,
$$M_{\mathfrak p}=0\iff \forall i,\ m_i/1=0\iff \forall i\ \exists t_i\notin\mathfrak p:\ t_im_i=0\iff \exists t:=\textstyle\prod_i t_i\notin\mathfrak p:\ tM=0\iff \operatorname{Ann}_A M\not\subseteq\mathfrak p.$$
Hence $\{\mathfrak p: M_{\mathfrak p}\ne 0\}=\{\mathfrak p:\operatorname{Ann}_A M\subseteq\mathfrak p\}=V(\operatorname{Ann}_A M)$, which is closed. (The equivalence $tM=0\Rightarrow$ all $m_i/1=0$ is immediate; the converse uses that $t=\prod t_i\notin\mathfrak p$ since $\mathfrak p$ is prime.) Applying this to $\mathcal C$ shows $Z=\operatorname{Supp}(\mathcal C)$ is a closed subset of $|X|$, so the reduced closed subscheme $V(s)$ is well defined.

**Step 2: stalkwise computation of $\mathcal C$.** Fix $x\in X$ and let $R:=\mathcal O_{X,x}$ with maximal ideal $\mathfrak m_x$, and $M_x:=\mathcal M_x$, a free $R$-module of rank $1$. Choose an open neighbourhood $U$ of $x$ and a trivialisation $\psi:\mathcal M|_U\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\mathcal O_U$. Then $\psi_x\circ\varphi_x:R\to R$ is $R$-linear, hence multiplication by the element
$$a:=\psi(s)(x)\in\Gamma(U,\mathcal M)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\mathcal M_x\xrightarrow{\psi_x}R=\mathcal O_{X,x}.$$
Consequently $\mathcal C_x\cong R/aR$; in particular, with $e$ any basis of $M_x$, $\mathcal C_x=0\iff aR=R\iff a\in R^{\times}$.

**Step 3: identification of the generation locus.** By definition, $s$ generates $\mathcal M$ at $x$ iff the image of $s_x$ in the fibre $\mathcal M_x/\mathfrak m_x\mathcal M_x\cong\kappa(x)$ is a generator, i.e. is nonzero (the fibre is $1$-dimensional over $\kappa(x)$). Under $\psi$ this image is the class of $a$ in $R/\mathfrak m_x$. Thus
$$s\text{ generates }\mathcal M\text{ at }x\iff a\notin\mathfrak m_x\iff a\in R^{\times}\iff \mathcal C_x=0.$$
(The middle equivalence is the elementary fact that an element of a local ring is a unit iff it lies outside the maximal ideal; the first equivalence is Nakayama's lemma applied to the finitely generated $R$-module $\mathcal M_x$: $\varphi_x$ is surjective iff $\varphi_x$ is surjective modulo $\mathfrak m_x$, i.e. iff $a$ generates $R/\mathfrak m_x$.) Hence for every $x$,
$$x\in X_s\iff \mathcal C_x=0\iff x\notin Z .$$
This proves two things at once: (i) $X_s$ is open in $|X|$ (it is the complement of the closed set $Z$), and (ii) as subsets of $|X|$ we have $|X\setminus V(s)|=|X|-Z=X_s$. For completeness we also give the direct local description, which exhibits $X_s$ as a principal open: with $f:=\psi(s)\in\mathcal O(U)$, one has $X_s\cap U=\{\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{Spec}\mathcal O(U): f_{\mathfrak p}\in\mathcal O(U)_{\mathfrak p}^{\times}\}=D(f)$. Indeed $f_{\mathfrak p}$ is a unit iff $f\notin\mathfrak p$: if $f\notin\mathfrak p$ this is clear; if $f/1$ were a unit, there would be $g\in\mathcal O(U)$ and $t,u\notin\mathfrak p$ with $u(fg-t)=0$, so $ut=ufg\in\mathfrak p$, contradicting primality of $\mathfrak p$. Thus $X_s$ is open and its underlying set is $X\setminus Z$.

**Step 4: equality of open subschemes.** Both $X\setminus V(s)$ and $X_s$ are open subschemes of $X$: the former is the open subscheme of $X$ with underlying set $|X|-|V(s)|=|X|-Z$, the latter is the open subscheme with underlying set $X_s$. By Step 3 these two underlying subsets of $|X|$ coincide, and an open subscheme of $X$ is uniquely determined by its underlying open subset (with the sheaf of rings inherited from $\mathcal O_X$). Hence $X\setminus V(s)=X_s$ as $k$-schemes (indeed as open subschemes of $X$).

**Step 5: affineness.** We apply the proved lemma (Spark, lemma_308) to $X$, $\mathcal L$, $n$ and $s$: with $S=\bigoplus_{m\ge0}H^0(X,\mathcal L^{\otimes mn})$ and $s\in S_1$, that lemma asserts that $X_s$ is an affine $k$-scheme (and that $(S_s)_0\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\Gamma(X_s,\mathcal O_{X_s})$). By Step 4, $X\setminus V(s)=X_s$ as $k$-schemes, so $X\setminus V(s)$ is affine.

**Edge cases.** If $s=0$, then $\varphi=0$, $\mathcal C\cong\mathcal M$, $\mathcal C_x\ne0$ for every $x$ (a free rank-$1$ module over a nonzero local ring is nonzero; note $X=\varnothing$ is trivial here), so $Z=|X|$, $X_s=\varnothing$, and $X\setminus V(s)=\varnothing=\operatorname{Spec}(0)$ is affine, in agreement with Step 5. If $s$ generates $\mathcal M$ everywhere, then $\mathcal C=0$, $Z=\varnothing$, $V(s)=\varnothing$ and $X\setminus V(s)=X$, which is affine by Step 5 (and directly, since $X$ is then the trivialisation locus of an invertible sheaf generated by $s$, i.e. $X\cong\operatorname{Spec}\Gamma(X,\mathcal O_X)$). Both are covered by the argument above, which used no non-degeneracy assumption on $s$.

Combining Steps 1–5, $V(s)=\operatorname{Supp}(\operatorname{coker}(\mathcal O_X\to\mathcal L^{\otimes n}))$ is a closed subscheme whose underlying set is exactly $|X|-X_s$, and the open subscheme $X\setminus V(s)$ equals $X_s$ and is affine. This completes the proof.

lemma_319.statement: Let \(\ell\) be a prime, let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-vector space, let \(T\in\mathrm{GL}(V)\), and let \(m\ge1\) be an integer. Then the base change of \(T\) to \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\) is diagonalizable if and only if the base change of \(T^{m}\) to \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\) is diagonalizable.
lemma_319.proof:
We prove both implications by pure linear algebra over the algebraically closed field \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\). No input from the other lemmas is needed.

**Step 0 (Notation; base change commutes with taking powers).** Write \(K:=\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\), \(W:=V\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}K\) (a finite-dimensional \(K\)-vector space with \(\dim_K W=\dim_{\mathbb Q_\ell}V=:n\)), and let \(\overline T:=T\otimes \mathrm{id}_K\in\mathrm{GL}(W)\); this is the base change of \(T\) to \(K\). For every integer \(k\ge 1\) one has
\[
\overline T^{\,k}=T^{k}\otimes \mathrm{id}_K .
\]
Indeed, the identity is clear for \(k=1\), and if it holds for \(k\) then, using \((A\otimes\mathrm{id})\circ(B\otimes\mathrm{id})=(AB)\otimes\mathrm{id}\) (which follows at once from \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-bilinearity of \(\otimes\) applied to \((A\otimes\mathrm{id})((B\otimes\mathrm{id})(v\otimes c))=(A\otimes\mathrm{id})(Bv\otimes c)=ABv\otimes c\)),
\[
\overline T^{\,k+1}=(T^{k}\otimes\mathrm{id})\circ(T\otimes\mathrm{id})=T^{k+1}\otimes\mathrm{id}.
\]
Taking \(k=m\) says precisely that the base change of \(T^{m}\) to \(K\) is \(\overline T^{\,m}\). Thus the two assertions to be compared are:
\[
(\mathrm{A})\ \overline T \text{ is diagonalizable over } K,\qquad (\mathrm{B})\ \overline T^{\,m} \text{ is diagonalizable over } K .
\]
Note that \(\overline T\in\mathrm{GL}(W)\) (since \(T\in\mathrm{GL}(V)\), with inverse \(T^{-1}\otimes\mathrm{id}\)), hence \(\overline T^{\,m}\in\mathrm{GL}(W)\) as well; in particular \(0\) is not an eigenvalue of either operator.

**Step 1 (Diagonalizability criterion).** Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional vector space over a field \(k\) and \(A\in\mathrm{End}_k(E)\). If the minimal polynomial \(\mu_A\in k[x]\) of \(A\) factors in \(k[x]\) as \(\mu_A=\prod_{i=1}^{s}(x-\lambda_i)\) with the \(\lambda_i\in k\) pairwise distinct, then \(A\) is diagonalizable. Proof: the ideals \((x-\lambda_i)\subseteq k[x]\) are pairwise comaximal, for \(\lambda_i\ne\lambda_j\) gives \((\lambda_j-\lambda_i)=(x-\lambda_i)-(x-\lambda_j)\in (x-\lambda_i)+(x-\lambda_j)\), which is the unit ideal. By the Chinese remainder theorem the natural homomorphism
\[
k[x]/(\mu_A)\ \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\ \prod_{i=1}^{s} k[x]/(x-\lambda_i)\ \cong\ k^{s}
\]
is an isomorphism of \(k\)-algebras. Choose polynomials \(e_1,\dots,e_s\in k[x]\) lifting the standard idempotents \((0,\dots,1,\dots,0)\) of \(k^{s}\). Evaluating the \(k[x]\)-module structure of \(E\) (well defined because \(\mu_A(A)=0\)) gives endomorphisms \(e_i(A)\) with:
(i) \(\sum_i e_i(A)=\mathrm{id}_E\), since \(\sum_i e_i\equiv 1\pmod{\mu_A}\);
(ii) \(e_i(A)e_j(A)=0\) for \(i\ne j\), since \(e_ie_j\equiv 0\pmod{\mu_A}\);
(iii) \((A-\lambda_i\,\mathrm{id})\,e_i(A)=0\), since \((x-\lambda_i)e_i\equiv 0\pmod{\mu_A}\).
From (i), \(E=\sum_i e_i(A)E\); the sum is direct, for if \(\sum_i e_i(A)w_i=0\) then applying \(e_j(A)\) and using (ii) yields \(e_j(A)w_j=0\). By (iii), \(A\) acts on the summand \(e_i(A)E\) as the scalar \(\lambda_i\). Concatenating bases of the summands gives a basis of \(E\) consisting of eigenvectors of \(A\), i.e. \(A\) is diagonalizable. \(\triangle\)

**Step 2 (Proof of (A) \(\Rightarrow\) (B)).** Assume \(\overline T\) is diagonalizable, and let \(w_1,\dots,w_n\) be a \(K\)-basis of \(W\) with \(\overline T w_i=\lambda_i w_i\), \(\lambda_i\in K\). By Step 0, \(\overline T^{\,m}w_i=\lambda_i^{\,m} w_i\) for every \(i\). Hence the same basis diagonalises \(\overline T^{\,m}\), so (B) holds. (The \(\lambda_i\) are in fact nonzero, as \(\overline T\) is invertible, but this is not needed here.)

**Step 3 (Proof of (B) \(\Rightarrow\) (A)).** Assume \(\overline T^{\,m}\) is diagonalizable.

*Edge case \(n=0\).* If \(n=0\) then \(W=0\) and both \(\overline T\) and \(\overline T^{\,m}\) are the identity on the zero space, trivially diagonalizable (empty basis); there is nothing to prove. Henceforth suppose \(n\ge 1\).

*3a. An annihilating polynomial for \(\overline T^{\,m}\) with simple roots.* Since \(\overline T^{\,m}\) is diagonalizable, \(W\) has a basis of eigenvectors of \(\overline T^{\,m}\); let \(\mu_1,\dots,\mu_n\in K\) be the corresponding eigenvalues and let \(A:=\{\mu_1,\dots,\mu_n\}=\{\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_s\}\subseteq K\) be the (finite, non-empty) set of **distinct** eigenvalues; it is non-empty because \(n\ge1\) and \(K\) is algebraically closed (so every endomorphism of a non-zero space has an eigenvalue). Set
\[
P(x):=\prod_{\alpha\in A}(x-\alpha)\in K[x].
\]
Then \(P(\overline T^{\,m})=0\): for a basis eigenvector \(w\) with \(\overline T^{\,m}w=\mu w\) one has \(\mu\in A\), hence \(P(\overline T^{\,m})w=P(\mu)w=0\), and the basis spans \(W\).
Moreover every \(\alpha\in A\) is nonzero: if \(\alpha=\mu_i\) then \(\overline T^{\,m}w_i=0\) with \(w_i\ne0\), contradicting the invertibility of \(\overline T^{\,m}\) noted in Step 0.

*3b. Splitting of \(x^{m}-\alpha\).* Fix \(\alpha\in A\) and put \(Z_\alpha:=\{\zeta\in K:\zeta^{m}=\alpha\}\). The polynomial \(f(x)=x^{m}-\alpha\in K[x]\) has \(m\) distinct roots in \(K\) and factors as \(f(x)=\prod_{\zeta\in Z_\alpha}(x-\zeta)\). Indeed: \(K\) is algebraically closed, so \(f=c\prod_{\zeta\in Z_\alpha}(x-\zeta)^{e_\zeta}\) with \(c=1\) (\(f\) is monic) and \(e_\zeta\ge1\). The formal derivative is \(f'(x)=m x^{m-1}\), which is not the zero polynomial because \(\operatorname{char}K=0\) and \(m\ge1\). A repeated root \(\zeta\) (i.e. \(e_\zeta\ge2\)) would be a common root of \(f\) and \(f'\); but the only root of \(f'\) is \(0\), and \(f(0)=-\alpha\ne0\). Hence all \(e_\zeta=1\), giving \(f(x)=\prod_{\zeta\in Z_\alpha}(x-\zeta)\) with the \(\zeta\) pairwise distinct (and \(|Z_\alpha|=m\)). 

*3c. The sets \(Z_\alpha\) are pairwise disjoint.* If \(\zeta\in Z_\alpha\cap Z_\beta\), then \(\alpha=\zeta^{m}=\beta\); so distinct \(\alpha\)'s give disjoint sets.

*3d. An annihilating polynomial for \(\overline T\) with simple roots.* Define
\[
Q(x):=\prod_{\alpha\in A}\ \prod_{\zeta\in Z_\alpha}(x-\zeta)\ \in K[x].
\]
By 3b and 3c, \(Q\) is a product of pairwise distinct linear factors (each \(Z_\alpha\) contributes distinct roots, and different \(\alpha\)'s contribute disjoint roots); that is, \(Q\) is separable and splits completely over \(K\).

Evaluate the \(K\)-algebra homomorphism \(K[x]\to\mathrm{End}_K(W)\), \(g\mapsto g(\overline T)\), on the identity of 3b: since \(x^{m}-\alpha=\prod_{\zeta\in Z_\alpha}(x-\zeta)\) in \(K[x]\),
\[
\overline T^{\,m}-\alpha\,\mathrm{id}=\prod_{\zeta\in Z_\alpha}\bigl(\overline T-\zeta\,\mathrm{id}\bigr).
\]
Therefore, using that all the factors are polynomials in the single operator \(\overline T\) and hence commute,
\[
Q(\overline T)=\prod_{\alpha\in A}\ \prod_{\zeta\in Z_\alpha}\bigl(\overline T-\zeta\,\mathrm{id}\bigr)=\prod_{\alpha\in A}\bigl(\overline T^{\,m}-\alpha\,\mathrm{id}\bigr)=P(\overline T^{\,m})=0,
\]
the last equality being 3a.

*3e. Conclusion.* Let \(\mu_{\overline T}\in K[x]\) be the minimal polynomial of \(\overline T\). The ideal \(I:=\{g\in K[x]:g(\overline T)=0\}\) is the principal ideal \((\mu_{\overline T})\) (standard: division with remainder by the monic polynomial \(\mu_{\over T}\) shows any element of \(I\) is a multiple of \(\mu_{\overline T}\), the remainder having degree \(<\deg\mu_{\overline T}\) and hence being zero by minimality). Since \(Q\in I\), we have \(\mu_{\overline T}\mid Q\) in \(K[x]\). As \(Q\) is a product of pairwise distinct linear factors and \(K[x]\) is a unique factorisation domain, every monic divisor of \(Q\) is likewise a product of pairwise distinct linear factors. Thus \(\mu_{\overline T}=\prod_{i=1}^{t}(x-\zeta_i)\) with the \(\zeta_i\in K\) pairwise distinct, and the criterion of Step 1 applied to \(E=W\), \(A=\overline T\), \(k=K\) shows that \(\overline T\) is diagonalizable, i.e. (A) holds.

**Step 4 (Summary of the hypotheses used).** In the direction (B) \(\Rightarrow\) (A) we used: \(m\ge1\) and \(\operatorname{char}\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell=0\), to ensure \(x^{m}-\alpha\) is separable (Step 3b); \(T\in\mathrm{GL}(V)\), to ensure the eigenvalues \(\alpha\) of \(\overline T^{\,m}\) are nonzero (Step 3a), which is exactly where separability of \(x^{m}-\alpha\) is needed — without invertibility the statement would fail (e.g. a nontrivial unipotent-free nilpotent: \(T=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}\) has \(T^{2}=0\) diagonalizable while \(T\) is not); and \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\) algebraically closed, to split \(x^{m}-\alpha\) and to guarantee eigenvalues. The case \(m=1\) is the tautological case \(Q=P\), and the case \(\dim V=0\) was handled in Step 3.

Combining Steps 2 and 3, \(\overline T\) is diagonalizable over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\) if and only if \(\overline T^{\,m}\) is, which is exactly the required equivalence.

lemma_ker_d_perfect_localization.statement: Let \(k\) be a perfect field of characteristic \(p>0\), let \(n\ge 1\), let \(0\neq s\in k[t_1,\dots,t_n]\), and let \(R=k[t_1,\dots,t_n][1/s]\) with universal \(k\)-derivation \(\mathrm d_{R/k}:R\to\Omega^1_{R/k}\). Then \(\ker(\mathrm d_{R/k})=\{u^{p}:u\in R\}\).
lemma_ker_d_perfect_localization.proof:
Write \(A=k[t_1,\dots,t_n]\), \(S=\{1,s,s^2,\dots\}\subseteq A\), \(R=S^{-1}A\), and \(\mathrm d=\mathrm d_{R/k}:R\to\Omega^1_{R/k}\). Throughout, \(p=\mathrm{char}(k)>0\). No external result is used; this is elementary commutative algebra.

=== Step 0. Elementary facts about \(A\) and \(R\) ===

0.1 (Domain and UFD.) Since \(k\) is a field, \(A\) is an integral domain, and by Gauss's lemma \(A\) is a unique factorisation domain. Every nonzero element of \(A\) has a factorisation into irreducibles, unique up to units and ordering; write \(v_\pi(\cdot)\) for the exponent of an irreducible \(\pi\).

0.2 (Injectivity of \(A\to R\).) If \(a\in A\) maps to \(0\) in \(S^{-1}A\), then \(s^m a=0\) in \(A\) for some \(m\ge0\); as \(s\neq0\) and \(A\) is a domain, \(a=0\). Thus we identify \(A\) with a subring of \(R\); \(R\) is then a domain, \(1\neq0\) in \(R\), and \(s\in R^\times\). Moreover, an element of \(A\) that vanishes in \(R\) already vanishes in \(A\).

0.3 (Perfectness.) Since \(k\) is perfect of characteristic \(p\), the Frobenius \(x\mapsto x^p\) is a bijection of \(k\); equivalently \(k=k^p\): every \(c\in k\) has a (unique) \(p\)-th root \(c^{1/p}\in k\).

0.4 (Which elements of \(A\) become units of \(R\).) For \(0\neq\sigma\in A\), \(\sigma/1\in R^\times\) if and only if \(\sigma\mid s^{l}\) in \(A\) for some \(l\ge0\).
Proof (\(\Leftarrow\)): if \(s^{l}=\sigma\tau\) with \(\tau\in A\), then \((\sigma/1)(\tau/s^{l})=\sigma\tau/s^{l}=s^{l}/s^{l}\), and \(s^{l}/s^{l}=1/1\) in \(S^{-1}A\) because \(s^{0}(s^{l}\cdot 1-1\cdot s^{l})=0\). Hence \(\sigma/1\) is invertible.
Proof (\(\Rightarrow\)): if \((a/s^{m})(\sigma/1)=1/1\) in \(R\), then \(s^{L}(a\sigma-s^{m})=0\) in \(A\) for some \(L\ge0\); by 0.2 (\(A\) a domain, \(s\neq0\)) this gives \(a\sigma=s^{m}\), so \(\sigma\mid s^{m}\). \(\square\)

=== Step 1. Extension of derivations from \(A\) to \(R\) ===

Lemma 1. Let \(M\) be an \(R\)-module (viewed as \(A\)-module via 0.2) and let \(\delta:A\to M\) be a \(k\)-derivation. Then there is a unique \(k\)-derivation \(\tilde\delta:R\to M\) with \(\tilde\delta|_A=\delta\), namely
\(\qquad\tilde\delta(a/s^{m})=s^{-m}\delta(a)-m\,a\,s^{-m-1}\delta(s)\qquad(a\in A,\ m\ge0).\)

Proof. Since \(s\) acts invertibly on \(M\), \(x=y\) in \(M\) iff \(s^{N}x=s^{N}y\) for any fixed \(N\ge0\).

Well-definedness. Suppose \(a/s^{m}=a'/s^{m'}\) in \(R\). By definition of \(S^{-1}A\), \(s^{L}(as^{m'}-a's^{m})=0\) in \(A\) for some \(L\); by 0.2, \(as^{m'}=a's^{m}\). Applying the derivation \(\delta\) and using the Leibniz rule on \(A\),
\(\qquad\delta(a)s^{m'}+m' a s^{m'-1}\delta(s)=\delta(a')s^{m}+m a' s^{m-1}\delta(s).\tag{*}\)
We must prove \(s^{-m}\delta(a)-ma s^{-m-1}\delta(s)=s^{-m'}\delta(a')-m'a's^{-m'-1}\delta(s)\). Multiplying by the unit \(s^{m+m'}\), this is equivalent to
\(\qquad s^{m'}\delta(a)-m a s^{m'-1}\delta(s)=s^{m}\delta(a')-m'a's^{m-1}\delta(s).\)
The difference LHS\(-\)RHS equals \([\delta(a)s^{m'}-\delta(a')s^{m}]+[-ma s^{m'-1}+m'a's^{m-1}]\delta(s)\), and by \((*)\) the bracket equals \(-m'a s^{m'-1}\delta(s)+ma's^{m-1}\delta(s)\). Hence the difference is \((m+m')[a's^{m-1}-a s^{m'-1}]\delta(s)\). Multiplying by \(s\) gives \((m+m')[a's^{m}-as^{m'}]s^{-1}\delta(s)=0\) by the relation \(as^{m'}=a's^{m}\); since multiplication by \(s\) is a bijection of \(M\), the difference is \(0\).

Additivity. Take \(u=a/s^{m}\), \(v=b/s^{l}\) and use the common denominator \(s^{m+l}\): \(u+v=(as^{l}+bs^{m})/s^{m+l}\). Then
\(\qquad\tilde\delta(u+v)=s^{-m-l}\big[\delta(a)s^{l}+l\,a\,s^{l-1}\delta(s)+\delta(b)s^{m}+m\,b\,s^{m-1}\delta(s)\big]-(m+l)(as^{l}+bs^{m})s^{-m-l-1}\delta(s).\)
The coefficient of \(a\,\delta(s)\) is \(l\,s^{l-1-m-l}-(m+l)s^{l-m-l-1}=(l-(m+l))s^{-m-1}=-m s^{-m-1}\); the coefficient of \(b\,\delta(s)\) is \(m s^{m-1-m-l}-(m+l)s^{m-m-l-1}=-l s^{-l-1}\); and \(s^{-m-l}\delta(a)s^{l}=s^{-m}\delta(a)\), \(s^{-m-l}\delta(b)s^{m}=s^{-l}\delta(b)\). Hence \(\tilde\delta(u+v)=\tilde\delta(u)+\tilde\delta(v)\).

Leibniz rule. \(uv=ab/s^{m+l}\), so
\(\qquad\tilde\delta(uv)=s^{-m-l}(\delta(a)b+a\delta(b))-(m+l)ab\,s^{-m-l-1}\delta(s)\)
\(\qquad =u\big[s^{-l}\delta(b)-l\,b\,s^{-l-1}\delta(s)\big]+v\big[s^{-m}\delta(a)-m\,a\,s^{-m-1}\delta(s)\big]=u\tilde\delta(v)+v\tilde\delta(u).\)

\(k\)-linearity. \(\tilde\delta\) is additive, and for \(\lambda\in k\), Leibniz gives \(\tilde\delta(\lambda u)=\tilde\delta((\lambda\cdot1)u)=\lambda\tilde\delta(u)+u\,\delta(\lambda\cdot1)=\lambda\tilde\delta(u)\), since \(\delta\) is a \(k\)-derivation, so \(\delta(\lambda\cdot1)=0\).

Uniqueness. If \(D':R\to M\) is a \(k\)-derivation with \(D'|_A=\delta\), then \(D'(a/s^{m})=D'(a\cdot s^{-m})=s^{-m}\delta(a)+a\,D'(s^{-m})\). Moreover \(0=D'(1)=D'(s^{m}s^{-m})=s^{m}D'(s^{-m})+s^{-m}\cdot m s^{m-1}\delta(s)\), so \(D'(s^{-m})=-m s^{-m-1}\delta(s)\). Hence \(D'=\tilde\delta\). \(\square\)

=== Step 2. Partial derivations on \(R\) and the vanishing criterion ===

2.1 (The polynomial module of differentials.) For every \(A\)-module \(M\), the map \(\mathrm{Der}_k(A,M)\to M^{n}\), \(D\mapsto(D(t_1),\dots,D(t_n))\), is a bijection. Injectivity: a \(k\)-derivation is \(k\)-linear and satisfies Leibniz, so \(D(\sum_e c_e t^{e})=\sum_e c_e\sum_{i}e_i t^{e-\epsilon_i}D(t_i)\) is forced. Surjectivity: given \((m_i)\in M^{n}\), the same formula defines a \(k\)-derivation. Hence \(\Omega^1_{A/k}\) is free with basis \(dt_i^{A}:=d_{A/k}(t_i)\), and
\(\qquad d_{A/k}(a)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{\partial a}{\partial t_i}\,dt_i^{A}.\)
In particular \(d_{A/k}(f)=0\iff\partial f/\partial t_i=0\) for all \(i\).

2.2 (Extensions.) For each \(i\), apply Lemma 1 with \(M=R\) and \(\delta=\partial/\partial t_i:A\to A\subseteq R\). We obtain a unique \(k\)-derivation \(\partial_i:R\to R\) with \(\partial_i|_A=\partial/\partial t_i\); explicitly \(\partial_i(a/s^{m})=s^{-m}\frac{\partial a}{\partial t_i}-m\,a\,s^{-m-1}\frac{\partial s}{\partial t_i}\).

2.3 (The identity \(\mathrm d(u)=\sum_i\partial_i(u)\,dt_i\).) Put \(dt_i:=\mathrm d(t_i)\in\Omega^1_{R/k}\). The map \(D_A:A\to\Omega^1_{R/k}\), \(D_A(a)=\sum_i(\partial a/\partial t_i)dt_i\), is a \(k\)-derivation (a \(k\)-linear combination, with coefficients \(dt_i\) in the \(R\)-module \(\Omega^1_{R/k}\), of the \(k\)-derivations \(\partial/\partial t_i\); equivalently it is the composite of \(d_{A/k}\) with the \(A\)-linear map \(\bigoplus_i A\,dt_i^{A}\to\Omega^1_{R/k}\), \(dt_i^{A}\mapsto dt_i\)). The map \(a\mapsto\mathrm d(a)\) is also a \(k\)-derivation \(A\to\Omega^1_{R/k}\). By the universal property of \(\Omega^1_{A/k}\) these two derivations correspond to \(A\)-linear maps \(\alpha,\beta:\Omega^1_{A/k}\to\Omega^1_{R/k}\) with \(\alpha(dt_i^{A})=\mathrm d(t_i)=\beta(dt_i^{A})\) for all \(i\); since the \(dt_i^{A}\) are a free basis (2.1), \(\alpha=\beta\) and therefore \(\mathrm d(a)=D_A(a)=\sum_i(\partial a/\partial t_i)dt_i\) for all \(a\in A\). By uniqueness in Lemma 1, \(\mathrm d(u)=\widetilde{D_A}(u)\) for all \(u\in R\). Using the explicit formula of Lemma 1 and the formulas of 2.2,
\(\qquad\widetilde{D_A}(a/s^{m})=s^{-m}D_A(a)-ma\,s^{-m-1}D_A(s)=\sum_i\Big[s^{-m}\tfrac{\partial a}{\partial t_i}-ma\,s^{-m-1}\tfrac{\partial s}{\partial t_i}\Big]dt_i=\sum_i\partial_i(a/s^{m})\,dt_i,\)\nso
\(\qquad\text{(\dag)}\qquad \mathrm d(u)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\partial_i(u)\,dt_i\quad\text{for all }u\in R.\)

2.4 (Linear independence of the \(dt_i\).) The map \(u\mapsto(\partial_1(u),\dots,\partial_n(u))\in R^{n}\) is a \(k\)-derivation (each component is one). By the universal property of \(\Omega^1_{R/k}\) there is a unique \(R\)-linear \(\Psi:\Omega^1_{R/k}\to R^{n}\) with \(\Psi(\mathrm d(u))=(\partial_1u,\dots,\partial_nu)\) for all \(u\). Then \(\Psi(dt_i)=\Psi(\mathrm d(t_i))=(\partial_j(t_i))_{j}=(\delta_{ji})_j=e_i\), because \(\partial_j|_A=\partial/\partial t_j\). Hence \(\sum_i r_i dt_i=0\) implies \(0=\Psi(\sum_i r_i dt_i)=\sum_i r_i e_i=(r_1,\dots,r_n)\), i.e. all \(r_i=0\).

2.5 (Criterion.) Combining (\dag) and 2.4:
\(\qquad\text{(\ddag)}\qquad \mathrm d(u)=0\iff\partial_i(u)=0\ \text{for every }i=1,\dots,n.\)

=== Step 3. \(\{u^{p}:u\in R\}\subseteq\ker\mathrm d\) ===

For \(u\in R\), the Leibniz rule gives \(\mathrm d(u^{p})=\sum_{j=1}^{p}u^{p-1}\mathrm d(u)=p\,u^{p-1}\mathrm d(u)=0\) since \(\mathrm{char}(k)=p\) and \(\mathrm d\) is \(k\)-linear (hence \(\mathbb Z\)-linear, so \(p\cdot x=0\) in the \(\mathbb Q\)? no: \(\Omega^1_{R/k}\) is an \(R\)-module, an additive group of characteristic \(p\), so \(p\,x=0\)). Thus every \(p\)-th power lies in \(\ker\mathrm d\).

=== Step 4. The polynomial case: \(\ker d_{A/k}=A^{p}\) ===

Write \(a=\sum_{e}c_e t^{e}\in A\) (finite sum over \(e=(e_1,\dots,e_n)\in\mathbb N^{n}\)). By 2.1 and the explicit derivative of a monomial,
\(\qquad\frac{\partial a}{\partial t_i}=\sum_{e:\,e_i\ge1} e_i\,c_e\, t^{e-\epsilon_i},\)\nand the monomials \(t^{e-\epsilon_i}\) occurring for distinct \(e\) are distinct (since \(e\mapsto e-\epsilon_i\) is injective). Hence \(\partial a/\partial t_i=0\) iff \(e_i c_e=0\) in \(k\) for every \(e\) with \(e_i\ge1\), i.e. iff \(c_e=0\) whenever \(p\nmid e_i\) (as \(e_i c_e=0\) in the field \(k\) of characteristic \(p\) iff \(p\mid e_i\) or \(c_e=0\)). By 2.1, \(d_{A/k}(a)=0\) iff this holds for every \(i\), i.e. iff \(c_e=0\) unless \(p\mid e_i\) for all \(i\). In that case, using \(k=k^{p}\) (0.3), choose \(b_e\in k\) with \(b_e^{p}=c_e\) for the finitely many surviving \(e\); then
\(\qquad a=\sum_{e\in p\mathbb N^{n}}c_e t^{e}=\sum_e b_e^{p}(t^{e/p})^{p}=\Big(\sum_e b_e t^{e/p}\Big)^{p}\in A^{p},\)\nby the Freshman's dream \((\sum_j x_j)^{p}=\sum_j x_j^{p}\) in the commutative ring \(A\). Conversely, every \(w^{p}\in A^{p}\) satisfies \(d_{A/k}(w^{p})=p\,w^{p-1}d_{A/k}(w)=0\). Hence \(\ker d_{A/k}=A^{p}\). Equivalently (2.1): \(\partial f/\partial t_i=0\) for all \(i\) iff \(f=f_0^{p}\) for some \(f_0\in A\).

=== Step 5. Divisibility lemma ===

Lemma 5. Let \(0\neq a\in A\) and \(i\in\{1,\dots,n\}\). If \(a\mid \partial a/\partial t_i\) in \(A\), then \(\partial a/\partial t_i=0\).

Proof. Put \(B=k[t_1,\dots,t_{i-1},t_{i+1},\dots,t_n]\), a domain, and view \(A=B[t_i]\). Write \(a=\sum_{j=0}^{J}g_j t_i^{j}\) with \(g_j\in B\), \(g_J\neq0\), so \(J=\deg_{t_i}a\). Suppose for contradiction that \(\partial a/\partial t_i\neq0\) and \(\partial a/\partial t_i=a\,g\) with \(g\in A\), \(g\neq0\). Since the derivative is nonzero, some \(j\) with \(p\nmid j\) has \(g_j\neq0\); let \(j'\) be the largest such \(j\). Then
\(\qquad\frac{\partial a}{\partial t_i}=\sum_{j\ge1,\;p\nmid j} j\,g_j\,t_i^{\,j-1},\)\nwhere the coefficient of \(t_i^{j'-1}\) is \(j'g_{j'}\neq0\) (the image of \(j'\) in \(k\) is nonzero because \(1\le j'\le p-1\) modulo \(p\), and \(g_{j'}\neq0\) in the domain \(B\)), while all terms with \(j>j'\) vanish by maximality of \(j'\). Hence \(\deg_{t_i}(\partial a/\partial t_i)=j'-1\). On the other hand, since \(B\) is a domain, degrees add in \(B[t_i]\): \(\deg_{t_i}(ag)=\deg_{t_i}(a)+\deg_{t_i}(g)=J+\deg_{t_i}(g)\ge J\ge j'>j'-1\), contradicting \(\partial a/\partial t_i=ag\). Therefore \(\partial a/\partial t_i=0\). \(\square\)

=== Step 6. \(\ker\mathrm d\subseteq\{u^{p}:u\in R\}\) ===

Let \(u\in R\) with \(\mathrm d(u)=0\).

Zero case. If \(u=0\), then \(u=0^{p}\) with \(0\in R\), and also \(\mathrm d(0)=0\) by additivity. Assume henceforth \(u\neq0\).

Reduced presentation. Choose \(b\in A\) and \(l\ge0\) with \(u=b/s^{l}\); then \(b\neq0\) by 0.2. For each irreducible \(\pi\in A\) (up to associates) set \(d=\prod_{\pi}\pi^{\min(v_\pi(b),\,l\,v_\pi(s))}\) (a finite product), and define
\(\qquad a:=b/d\in A\setminus\{0\},\qquad \sigma:=s^{l}/d\in A\setminus\{0\}.\)
Then in \(R\), \(u=a/\sigma\), because \((b/d)\,s^{l}=b\,(s^{l}/d)\) in \(A\). By construction \(v_\pi(a)=\max(v_\pi(b)-l\,v_\pi(s),0)\) and \(v_\pi(\sigma)=\max(l\,v_\pi(s)-v_\pi(b),0)\), so for each \(\pi\) at most one of \(v_\pi(a),v_\pi(\sigma)\) is nonzero: \(\gcd(a,\sigma)=1\) in the UFD \(A\). Also \(\sigma\mid s^{l}\) (as \(d\mid s^{l}\)), so by 0.4 \(\sigma\) is a unit of \(R\); and \(a\neq0\) since \(u\neq0\) and \(\sigma\) is a unit.

The key equation. By (\ddag), \(\partial_i(u)=0\) for every \(i\). Since \(\sigma\in R^\times\), the Leibniz rule in \(R\) gives \(0=\partial_i(1)=\partial_i(\sigma\sigma^{-1})=\sigma^{-1}\partial_i(\sigma)+\sigma\,\partial_i(\sigma^{-1})\), hence \(\partial_i(\sigma^{-1})=-\sigma^{-2}\partial_i(\sigma)\). Therefore
\(\qquad 0=\partial_i(a\sigma^{-1})=\sigma^{-1}\partial_i(a)-a\,\sigma^{-2}\partial_i(\sigma).\)
Multiplying by the unit \(\sigma^{2}\in R\): \(\sigma\,\partial_i(a)=a\,\partial_i(\sigma)\) in \(R\). Both sides lie in \(A\) (as \(a,\sigma\in A\) and \(\partial_i|_A=\partial/\partial t_i\) maps \(A\) to \(A\)), so by 0.2 the equality holds in \(A\):
\(\qquad\text{(\(*\))}\qquad \sigma\,\partial_i(a)=a\,\partial_i(\sigma)\quad\text{in }A,\ \text{for every }i.\)

Killing \(a\)'s derivatives. Fix \(i\). From \((*)\), \(a\mid\sigma\,\partial_i(a)\) in \(A\). Since \(A\) is a UFD and \(\gcd(a,\sigma)=1\), Euclid's lemma gives \(a\mid\partial_i(a)\) (comparing \(v_\pi\): \(v_\pi(a)>0\Rightarrow v_\pi(\sigma)=0\Rightarrow v_\pi(a)\le v_\pi(\partial_i a)\)). By Lemma 5, \(\partial_i(a)=0\). This holds for every \(i\), so by Step 4 there is \(0\neq a_0\in A\) with \(a=a_0^{p}\).

Killing \(\sigma\)'s derivatives. Substituting \(a=a_0^{p}\) into \((*)\): \(\sigma\,\partial_i(a_0^{p})=a_0^{p}\partial_i(\sigma)\) in \(A\). Since \(\partial_i(a_0^{p})=p\,a_0^{p-1}\partial_i(a_0)=0\) in \(A\) (characteristic \(p\); note we do not cancel anything, the left side is simply \(0\)), we get \(a_0^{p}\,\partial_i(\sigma)=0\). Now \(a_0\neq0\) and \(A\) is a domain, so \(a_0^{p}\neq0\); hence \(\partial_i(\sigma)=0\). This holds for every \(i\), so by Step 4 there is \(0\neq\sigma_0\in A\) with \(\sigma=\sigma_0^{p}\).

The \(p\)-th root lies in \(R\). We check \(\sigma_0\mid s^{l}\) by comparing valuations: for every irreducible \(\pi\), \(p\,v_\pi(\sigma_0)=v_\pi(\sigma)\le l\,v_\pi(s)\) (the inequality because \(\sigma\mid s^{l}\)), and since \(p\ge2\) this gives \(v_\pi(\sigma_0)\le l\,v_\pi(s)\). Hence \(\sigma_0\mid s^{l}\), so by 0.4 \(\sigma_0\in R^\times\), and \(a_0\sigma_0^{-1}\in R\).

Conclusion of the inclusion. In the commutative ring \(R\),
\(\qquad u=a\,\sigma^{-1}=a_0^{p}\,(\sigma_0^{p})^{-1}=a_0^{p}\sigma_0^{-p}=(a_0\sigma_0^{-1})^{p},\)\nwith \(a_0\sigma_0^{-1}\in R\). Thus \(u\) is a \(p\)-th power in \(R\).

=== Step 7. Conclusion ===

Step 3 gives \(\{u^{p}:u\in R\}\subseteq\ker(\mathrm d_{R/k})\) and Step 6 gives the reverse inclusion. Hence
\(\qquad\ker(\mathrm d_{R/k})=\{u^{p}:u\in R\},\)\nas claimed. \(\blacksquare\)

(Remarks on the points flagged previously: (i) the unit criterion 0.4 is proved and is used explicitly, together with \(\sigma\mid s^{l}\), before any computation with \(\sigma^{-1}\); (ii) the derivation \(\partial_i\) and the identity (\dag) are obtained from Lemma 1, whose proof verifies additivity by putting two elements over the common denominator \(s^{m+l}\), so no additivity is merely asserted; (iii) the case \(u=0\) is treated separately at the start of Step 6, so the factorisation/gcd construction is applied only to \(b\neq0\); (iv) membership of \(a_0\sigma_0^{-1}\) in \(R\) is proved by the valuation comparison \(v_\pi(\sigma_0)\le l\,v_\pi(s)\). The right-hand side is the set of \(p\)-th powers of elements of \(R\) itself, not \(S^{-1}(R^{p})\) or \(k[t_1^{p},\dots,t_n^{p}][1/s^{p}]\); and only perfectness of \(k\) (0.3) is used, not algebraic closedness.)

lemma_314.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(X\) be a smooth projective variety over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, and let \(j\ge 0\) be an integer. Fix a nonzero \(\xi\in\mathbb Q_\ell(j)\), let \(m\ge 1\), let \(Z_0\subseteq X_{\mathbb F_{q^m}}\) be a closed integral subscheme of pure codimension \(j\), let \(Z\subseteq X_k\) be the base change of \(Z_0\) to \(k\), and let \(\mathrm{cl}(Z)\in H^{2j}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) be the unique vector whose tensor with \(\xi\) is the \(\ell\)-adic cycle class of \(Z\) in \(H^{2j}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell(j))\). Then \(F^{m}(\mathrm{cl}(Z))=q^{mj}\,\mathrm{cl}(Z)\), where \(F=(\mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\) and \(\sigma(c)=c^q\).
lemma_314.proof:
PROOF OF lemma_314.

Notation fixed once and for all. q=p^a with p prime, k=\overline{F}_q, \sigma:k\to k, \sigma(c)=c^q, \ell\neq p prime, j\ge 0, 0\neq\xi\in\mathbb Q_\ell(j), m\ge 1, Q:=q^m=p^{am}. For a scheme W of finite type over \mathbb F_q we write W_k:=W\times_{\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_q}\operatorname{Spec}k and F_W:=(\mathrm{id}_{W_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*; by lemma_6a (eoinm/lemma_6a) F_W is a \mathbb Q_\ell-linear automorphism of H^i_{\acute et}(W_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) for every i, with inverse (\mathrm{id}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma^{-1})^*. All cohomology groups below are étale cohomology over k with \mathbb Q_\ell-coefficients unless a twist is written; H^i(W_k,\mathbb Q_\ell(j)):=H^i(W_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\mathbb Q_\ell(j).

PART 0. Two preliminary facts.

(0.1) Untwisting a Tate twist. \mathbb Q_\ell(j) is a one-dimensional \mathbb Q_\ell-vector space, so c\mapsto c\otimes\xi is a \mathbb Q_\ell-linear isomorphism H^{2j}(W_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\sim}H^{2j}(W_k,\mathbb Q_\ell(j)); hence the "unique vector" cl(Z) of the statement exists and is unique. As recorded in lemma_78, the arithmetic-Frobenius automorphism F_{W,*} of the twisted group induced by the Frobenius structures on W_k and on \mathbb Q_\ell(j) is F_W\otimes(q^{-j}\cdot\mathrm{id}); consequently, for every c\in H^{2j}(W_k,\mathbb Q_\ell),
   F_{W,*}(c\otimes\xi)=(F_Wc)\otimes q^{-j}\xi=q^{-j}\,(F_Wc\otimes\xi).
Thus fixedness in the twisted group is equivalent to the eigenvalue q^{j} in the untwisted group. All twisting in this proof is handled by this single equivalence, which we only invoke through lemma_78; every other group that appears is the strictly untwisted group with the strictly untwisted operator (\mathrm{id}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*.

(0.2) Formal properties of the cycle class map. We use the following standard functoriality of the \ell-adic cycle class map on smooth varieties over a field (it follows from the construction: for a closed immersion V\hookrightarrow W of pure codimension j with W smooth, cl_W([V]) is the image of 1\in H^0(V,\mathbb Q_\ell) under the purity/Gysin homomorphism H^0(V,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{2j}_V(W,\mathbb Q_\ell(j)), which is natural for cartesian squares of closed immersions, followed by the localisation map to H^{2j}(W,\mathbb Q_\ell(j)); additivity extends to cycles). If
   V' -> V
   |     |
   v     v
   W' -> W            (*)\nis a cartesian square of varieties over a field, with W,W' smooth, V,V' closed of pure codimension j, and W'\to W flat of relative dimension 0 (an open immersion, an isomorphism, or the base change by a field extension), then the pullback on cohomology carries cl_W([V]) to cl_{W'}([V']). Indeed flat pullback of the fundamental cycle [V] is the fundamental cycle of the flat pullback scheme V', and the Gysin homomorphism is cartesian-natural. If V'=\varnothing the pulled-back cycle is the zero cycle and the pulled-back class is 0 (the class lies in the image of H^{2j}_V(W)\to H^{2j}(W), and restriction to the open complement of V annihilates it by exactness of the localisation sequence of the pair). We also use compatibility with proper pushforward: for a proper morphism f:W\to W'' of smooth varieties, cl_{W''}(f_*z)=f_{\acute et,*}cl_W(z).

PART 1. Reduction to X smooth projective of pure dimension.

If X=\varnothing then X_{\mathbb F_{q^m}}=\varnothing contains no closed integral subscheme, so there is nothing to prove; assume X\neq\varnothing. X is of finite type over a field, hence noetherian. By the standard structure theorem for locally noetherian schemes, the connected components X_1,\dots,X_r of X exist, are open-and-closed subschemes, and r<\infty. (We deliberately do NOT argue that Frobenius permutes components: permutation gives only orbit-stability, not that a component descends; the open-and-closed property is what we need.) Each X_s is an \mathbb F_q-scheme via X_s\hookrightarrow X\to\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_q. The open immersion X_s\hookrightarrow X is étale, hence smooth, and X\to\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_q is smooth, so X_s\to\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_q is smooth. Being open AND closed, X_s\hookrightarrow X is also a closed immersion, so X_s\to\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_q is a composition of a closed immersion with the projective morphism X\to\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_q, hence projective. For a smooth morphism the function x\mapsto\dim_x(X_s/\mathbb F_q) is locally constant on X_s; since X_s is connected it is constant, so X_s is smooth projective of pure dimension d_s over \mathbb F_q.

Write S=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_q and T=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_{q^m}. Since X=\bigsqcup_s X_s as \mathbb F_q-schemes, base change gives X_{\mathbb F_{q^m}}=X\times_S T=\bigsqcup_s (X_s)_{\mathbb F_{q^m}}, a disjoint union of open-and-closed subschemes. Z_0 is integral, hence connected, so the continuous map |Z_0|\to\pi_0(|X_{\mathbb F_{q^m}}|) to the discrete set of components is constant; thus Z_0\subseteq (X_s)_{\mathbb F_{q^m}} for a unique index s. Fix it. Since (X_s)_{\mathbb F_{q^m}} is open-and-closed in X_{\mathbb F_{q^m}} and contains Z_0, the local rings of X_{\mathbb F_{q^m}} and of (X_s)_{\mathbb F_{q^m}} agree along Z_0, so Z_0 has pure codimension j in (X_s)_{\mathbb F_{q^m}} as well. (In particular j\le d_s; if j>d_s no such Z_0 exists and the statement is vacuous.)

Let \iota_t:(X_t)_k\hookrightarrow X_k be the open-and-closed immersion and r_t:=\iota_t^*. By lemma_13 (eoinm/lemma_13), \bigoplus_t r_t:H^{2j}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\sim}\bigoplus_t H^{2j}((X_t)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) is a \mathbb Q_\ell-linear isomorphism which is equivariant for the arithmetic Frobenius, i.e. it conjugates F_X to \bigoplus_t F_{X_t}.

The subscheme Z=Z_0\times_T\operatorname{Spec}k is contained in (X_s)_k\subseteq X_k (because Z_0\subseteq (X_s)_{\mathbb F_{q^m}} and (X_s)_{\mathbb F_{q^m}} is open-and-closed in X'). Applying the cartesian-square functoriality (0.2) to the square (Z\subset (X_s)_k)\to(Z\subset X_k) induced by the open immersion (X_s)_k\hookrightarrow X_k — over which Z is stable, so the fibre product is Z itself — we get r_s(cl_{X_k}(Z))=cl_{(X_s)_k}(Z). For t\neq s the fibre product Z\times_{X_k}(X_t)_k is empty (distinct components of X_k are disjoint, and base change preserves disjointness of the (X_t)_k), so the same functoriality gives r_t(cl_{X_k}(Z))=0.

Consequently, if we establish F_{X_s}^{\,m}\,cl_{(X_s)_k}(Z)=q^{mj}\,cl_{(X_s)_k}(Z), then by the F-equivariance of \bigoplus_t r_t,
  r_s(F_X^m cl_{X_k}(Z))=F_{X_s}^m r_s(cl_{X_k}(Z))=F_{X_s}^m cl_{(X_s)_k}(Z)=q^{mj}cl_{(X_s)_k}(Z)=q^{mj}r_s(cl_{X_k}(Z)),
  r_t(F_X^m cl_{X_k}(Z))=F_{X_t}^m(0)=0=q^{mj}r_t(cl_{X_k}(Z))\quad(t\neq s),\nand since \bigoplus_t r_t is injective, F_X^m cl_{X_k}(Z)=q^{mj}cl_{X_k}(Z). Hence, replacing X by X_s (which keeps Z_0, Z, \xi, m and j unchanged and preserves all hypotheses), we may and do assume from now on:
  X is smooth projective of pure dimension d over \mathbb F_q, and Z_0\subseteq X_{\mathbb F_{q^m}} is closed integral of pure codimension j.

PART 2. The base change X':=X_{\mathbb F_{q^m}} and the canonical identification of Frobenius with an m-th power.

Since \mathbb F_{q^m}/\mathbb F_q is finite and k is algebraic over \mathbb F_q and algebraically closed, k is an algebraic closure of \mathbb F_{q^m}; thus \overline{\mathbb F}_{q^m}=k and Q=q^m is a prime power. Put X':=X\times_S T=X_{\mathbb F_{q^m}}; it is smooth and projective over \mathbb F_{q^m} (both properties are stable under base change) and of pure dimension d (field extension preserves the dimensions of the irreducible components of a scheme of finite type).

Canonical identification of the geometric fibres. By ASSOCIATIVITY OF FIBRE PRODUCTS there is a canonical isomorphism of k-schemes
   \alpha:(X')_k:=X'\times_T U=(X\times_S T)\times_T U\ \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\ X\times_S U=:X_k\qquad(U=\operatorname{Spec}k),\ninduced by (X\times_S T)\times_T U\simeq X\times_S(T\times_T U)=X\times_S U. Explicitly, on T-points for a test k-algebra R, \alpha((x,t),u)=(x,u), with inverse (x,u)\mapsto(x,\pi(x),u) where \pi:X\to T is the structure morphism; the two composites are the identity by the universal property of the fibre product.
We stress (correcting the earlier error) that this isomorphism does NOT come from any assertion that \mathbb F_{q^m}\otimes_{\mathbb F_q}k is a field: for m>1 that tensor product is k^{m}, a product of m copies of k. The isomorphism \alpha is purely the associativity isomorphism of fibre products, valid for every m\ge1.

Define \theta:=\alpha^*:H^{2j}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\sim}H^{2j}((X')_k,\mathbb Q_\ell). Let \Phi:=(\mathrm{id}_{(X')_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma_Q)^* be the Q-power arithmetic Frobenius of H^{2j}((X')_k,\mathbb Q_\ell), \sigma_Q(c)=c^Q; \Phi is a \mathbb Q_\ell-linear automorphism by lemma_6a applied to the \mathbb F_{q^m}-scheme X'.

Claim. \theta\circ F_X^{m}=\Phi\circ\theta.
Proof of the claim. First, \sigma^m|_{\mathbb F_{q^m}}=\sigma_Q because \sigma^m(c)=c^{q^m}=c^{Q}. Consider the two endomorphisms of (X')_k=X\times_S T\times_T U, namely \mathrm{id}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma_Q (the Q-power Frobenius, taken over T) and the pullback of \mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma^m along \alpha. Both composites (X')_k\to X\times_S U are the morphism (x,t,u)\mapsto(x,\sigma^m(u)): for \alpha\circ(\mathrm{id}\times\sigma_Q) one gets (x,\sigma_Q(u))=(x,\sigma^m(u)), and for (\mathrm{id}\times\sigma^m)\circ\alpha one gets (x,\sigma^m(u)); these agree because \sigma^m and \sigma_Q coincide on k. (Note \sigma^m fixes \mathbb F_q pointwise since c^{q^m}=c for c\in\mathbb F_q, so both sides are well-defined morphisms into the fibre product over S.) Hence
   (\mathrm{id}\times\sigma_Q)^*\circ\alpha^*=\alpha^*\circ(\mathrm{id}\times\sigma^m)^*,   i.e.  \Phi\circ\theta=\theta\circ(\mathrm{id}\times\sigma^m)^*.
Second, \sigma is an \mathbb F_q-automorphism of k, so \mathrm{id}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma is an endomorphism of the \mathbb F_q-scheme X_k, and (\mathrm{id}\times\sigma)^m=\mathrm{id}\times\sigma^m as endomorphisms; by contravariance of pullback, ((\mathrm{id}\times\sigma)^m)^*=((\mathrm{id}\times\sigma)^*)^m, i.e. (\mathrm{id}\times\sigma^m)^*=F_X^m. Combining gives \Phi\circ\theta=\theta\circ F_X^m. \square

(Remark: the same identity is exactly the content of lemma_44 (eoinm/lemma_44) applied to X/\mathbb F_q and m: its canonical isomorphism H^n(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\simeq H^n((X_m)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) is \theta=\alpha^*, and it identifies the arithmetic Frobenius over \mathbb F_{q^m} with the m-th power of the arithmetic Frobenius over \mathbb F_q.)

PART 3. Compatibility of the cycle class with \alpha.

Let \gamma:=cl_{X_k}(Z)\otimes\xi\in H^{2j}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell(j)) (the geometric cycle class of Z on X_k; by definition of cl(Z) in the statement) and let \gamma_0:=cl_{X'}([Z_0])\in H^{2j}((X')_k,\mathbb Q_\ell(j)) be the cycle class of the codimension-j cycle [Z_0] on the \mathbb F_{q^m}-variety X'. Extend \theta to the twist by \theta_j:=\alpha^*\otimes\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb Q_\ell(j)}; since \alpha^* is \mathbb Q_\ell-linear and the Tate twist is a constant coefficient system, \theta_j(c\otimes\eta)=\theta(c)\otimes\eta for all \eta\in\mathbb Q_\ell(j).

Claim. \theta_j(\gamma)=\gamma_0.
Proof of the claim. By definition of Z as the base change of Z_0 to k, Z is the closed subscheme \alpha\big((Z_0)_k\big) of X_k where (Z_0)_k:=Z_0\times_T U, and \alpha restricts to an isomorphism of k-schemes \alpha|:(Z_0)_k\xrightarrow{\sim}Z. Thus we have a commutative diagram whose squares are cartesian (in fact the left square is an isomorphism and the outer square exhibits both as closed immersions)
   (Z_0)_k --i--> (X')_k
      |\simeq          |\simeq\alpha
      v                v
       Z  ---i'----->  X_k.
Both closed immersions i and i' have pure codimension j: i' does because Z is the base change of the codimension-j integral subscheme Z_0 by the flat morphism U\to T (flat base change preserves codimension in an equidimensional ambient scheme; equivalently, local rings are preserved under the flat extension), and i is its transport by \alpha. The class cl_{X_k}(Z) is the image of 1\in H^0(Z,\mathbb Q_\ell) under the Gysin map for i' followed by localisation; cl_{(X')_k}((Z_0)_k) is the image of 1\in H^0((Z_0)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) under the Gysin map for i followed by localisation. Naturality of the purity/Gysin homomorphism for the cartesian square above, together with the fact that \alpha| identifies the constant section 1 with the constant section 1, gives \alpha^*(cl_{X_k}(Z))=cl_{(X')_k}([(Z_0)_k]), provided the fundamental cycles correspond, i.e. provided (\alpha|)_*[(Z_0)_k]=[Z].
We verify the multiplicities. \mathbb F_{q^m} is perfect and Z_0 is integral, hence reduced and of finite type over \mathbb F_{q^m}; therefore Z_0 is geometrically reduced, so (Z_0)_k is reduced. A reduced noetherian scheme has length 1 at each of its generic points (the local ring at a generic point is reduced and artinian local, hence a field), so its fundamental cycle is the sum of its irreducible components with coefficient 1. The same holds for Z, and the isomorphism \alpha|:(Z_0)_k\xrightarrow{\sim}Z gives a bijection of irreducible component sets; hence (\alpha|)_*[(Z_0)_k]=[Z]. This proves \alpha^*(cl_{X_k}(Z))=cl_{(X')_k}([(Z_0)_k]).
It remains to identify cl_{(X')_k}([(Z_0)_k]) with cl_{X'}([Z_0]). Both are computed from the very same closed immersion i:(Z_0)_k\hookrightarrow(X')_k over the algebraically closed field k=\overline{\mathbb F}_{q^m}: by the definition of the cycle class map for a variety over a field, cl_{X'}([Z_0]) is precisely the Gysin class of the base-changed immersion (Z_0)_{\overline{\mathbb F}_{q^m}}=(Z_0)_k\hookrightarrow (X')_k=X'\times_{\mathbb F_{q^m}}\operatorname{Spec}k. Hence the two coincide. Therefore
   \theta_j(\gamma)=\theta_j(cl_{X_k}(Z)\otimes\xi)=\theta(cl_{X_k}(Z))\otimes\xi=\gamma_0, \quad\text{so also}\quad \gamma_0=c_0\otimes\xi\ \ \text{with}\ \ c_0:=\theta(cl_{X_k}(Z)). \quad\square

PART 4. Application of lemma_78 over \mathbb F_{q^m} and conclusion.

The data (X'/\mathbb F_{q^m},\ k=\overline{\mathbb F}_{q^m},\ \ell\neq p,\ Q=q^m,\ X'\ \text{smooth projective of pure dimension }d) satisfy the hypotheses of lemma_78 (eoinm/lemma_78), and [Z_0] is a codimension-j cycle on X' defined over \mathbb F_{q^m} (Z_0 is a closed integral subscheme of X' of pure codimension j, so its fundamental cycle is an effective codimension-j cycle on X'). Lemma_78 asserts that the automorphism F_{X',*} of H^{2j}((X')_k,\mathbb Q_\ell(j)) induced by the arithmetic Frobenius structures on (X')_k and on \mathbb Q_\ell(j) — on which the Frobenius acts as multiplication by Q^{-j}=q^{-mj} — fixes the class of z=[Z_0]:
   F_{X',*}(\gamma_0)=\gamma_0.
By the "equivalently" clause of lemma_78, applied with the prime power Q=q^m, with the same nonzero \xi\in\mathbb Q_\ell(j), and with the untwisted group H^{2j}((X')_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) carrying the untwisted operator \Phi=(\mathrm{id}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma_Q)^* (the operator of lemma_6a for X'/\mathbb F_{q^m}), the unique vector c_0 with \gamma_0=c_0\otimes\xi satisfies
   \Phi c_0=Q^{\,j}c_0=q^{mj}c_0.
For completeness we unfold the equivalence, using (0.1) with q replaced by Q: F_{X',*}(c_0\otimes\xi)=Q^{-j}(\Phi c_0\otimes\xi); equality with c_0\otimes\xi, followed by tensoring the identity \Phi c_0\otimes\xi=Q^{j}(c_0\otimes\xi) with \xi^{-1} (i.e. applying the inverse of c\mapsto c\otimes\xi), gives \Phi c_0=Q^{j}c_0.

Now combine the three displayed identities. By Part 3, c_0=\theta(cl_{X_k}(Z)). By the Claim of Part 2, \theta(F_X^m cl_{X_k}(Z))=\Phi(\theta(cl_{X_k}(Z)))=\Phi c_0. Hence
   \theta\big(F_X^m cl(Z)-q^{mj}cl(Z)\big)=\Phi c_0-q^{mj}c_0=0,\nand \theta is an isomorphism, so F_X^m cl(Z)=q^{mj}cl(Z) in H^{2j}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell).

Finally, transporting back along the F-equivariant decomposition of Part 1 (the argument given there) yields the same eigenvalue identity for the original X, which completes the proof for general smooth projective X.

PART 5. Edge cases and remarks.
(i) j=0. Then q^{mj}=1 and the statement asserts F^m-invariance of cl(Z). The proof above applies verbatim: a codimension-0 cycle on X_{\mathbb F_{q^m}} is a formal sum of irreducible components of X_{\mathbb F_{q^m}}, so an integral Z_0 of codimension 0 is an irreducible component (X_{\mathbb F_{q^m}} is smooth, hence regular, hence its irreducible components are open-and-closed and integral), Z is the corresponding reduced union of components of X_k, cl(Z)\in H^0(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) is its characteristic function, and lemma_78 with j=0 gives \Phi c_0=c_0. There is no separate case p=0: p is prime by hypothesis.
(ii) X=\varnothing or j>\dim X: no closed integral subscheme Z_0 of pure codimension j exists, so the assertion is vacuous.
(iii) Independence of \xi: if \xi'=\lambda\xi with \lambda\in\mathbb Q_\ell^{\times}, the corresponding vector is cl'(Z)=\lambda^{-1}cl(Z), and the identity F^mcl'(Z)=q^{mj}cl'(Z) is equivalent to the one proved. The eigenvalue q^{mj} does not depend on the choice of \xi.
(iv) Throughout, the group H^{2j}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) and the operator F were used strictly UNTWISTED, exactly as in the statement; the only place a twist enters is lemma_78 and its stated equivalence, which converts fixedness in H^{2j}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell(j)) into the eigenvalue q^{mj} in the untwisted group. This is the correct normalisation: e.g. for X=\mathbb P^1_{\mathbb F_q}, j=1, m=1 and Z_0 a rational point, the untwisted class c satisfies Fc=qc, not Fc=c.

lemma_320.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(X\) be a proper scheme over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, and let \(n\ge0\) and \(m\ge1\) be integers. Write \(F_1=(\mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\) and \(F_m=(\mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma^{m})^*\), \(\sigma(c)=c^q\), for the \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear automorphisms of \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) induced by the \(q\)-power and \(q^m\)-power arithmetic Frobenius. Then \(F_1\) is semisimple on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) if and only if \(F_m\) is.
lemma_320.proof:
Fix throughout a prime power q = p^a, a proper scheme X over F_q, k = \overline{F}_q, a prime \ell \neq p, integers n \ge 0 and m \ge 1, and write V := H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k, \mathbb Q_\ell) and \sigma : k \to k, \sigma(c) = c^q.

Step 1 (The two Frobenius morphisms and the relation F_m = F_1^m).
Since \sigma fixes \mathbb F_q pointwise, Spec\,\sigma : Spec\,k \to Spec\,k is a morphism over Spec\,\mathbb F_q, hence
\[\Phi_1 := \mathrm{id}_{X} \times_{\mathrm{Spec}\,\mathbb F_q} \mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma \; : \; X_k \longrightarrow X_k\]\nis a well-defined morphism of schemes, and likewise Spec\,\sigma^{r} is a morphism over Spec\,\mathbb F_q for every r \ge 1, giving \Phi_r := \mathrm{id}_X \times \mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma^r : X_k \to X_k. (This is exactly the operator denoted (\mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma)^* resp. (\mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma^m)^* in the statement, i.e. F_1 = \Phi_1^* and F_m = \Phi_m^*.)
The composition of product morphisms is the product of the compositions, and \sigma^r = \sigma \circ \cdots \circ \sigma (r times); therefore
\[\Phi_1^{\,r} := \underbrace{\Phi_1 \circ \cdots \circ \Phi_1}_{r} = \mathrm{id}_X \times \mathrm{Spec}(\sigma^{r}) = \Phi_r .\]
Indeed, on underlying topological spaces both maps send (x, \mathfrak p) to (x, \sigma^{-r}(\mathfrak p)), and on structure sheaves both act on the k-factor by \sigma^r and on the X-factor as the identity; hence they coincide as morphisms of schemes.
Étale pullback is contravariant and functorial: for morphisms f, g of schemes one has (g \circ f)^* = f^* \circ g^* on étale cohomology with \mathbb Q_\ell-coefficients, and (\mathrm{id})^* = \mathrm{id}. Applying this with f = g = \Phi_1 repeatedly gives
\[F_m \;=\; \Phi_m^* \;=\; (\Phi_1^{\,m})^* \;=\; (\Phi_1^*)^{m} \;=\; F_1^{\,m}\tag{1}\]\nas endomorphisms of V. (Concretely: (\Phi_1^{\,m})^* = (\Phi_1^{\,m-1}\circ\Phi_1)^* = \Phi_1^*\circ(\Phi_1^{\,m-1})^*, and induction on m yields the claim.)

Step 2 (Invertibility).
By lemma_6a of eoinm, applied to the \mathbb F_q-scheme X, the pullback F_1 = (\mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma)^* is a \mathbb Q_\ell-linear automorphism of V (its inverse being the geometric Frobenius (\mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma^{-1})^*). In particular F_1 \in \mathrm{GL}(V), and by (1) so is F_m = F_1^{\,m}.

Step 3 (Reduction to linear algebra over an algebraically closed field).
By lemma_5 of eoinm, for a \mathbb Q_\ell-linear operator on a \mathbb Q_\ell-vector space, being semisimple is equivalent to its base change to \overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell being diagonalizable; we use this as the definition of "semisimple" for F_1 and F_m. Put K := \overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell, \bar V := V \otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell} K, and T := F_1 \otimes_K \mathrm{id}_{\bar V} \in \mathrm{GL}(\bar V). Base change is compatible with powers, since (A\otimes 1)\circ(B\otimes 1) = (A\circ B)\otimes 1 for endomorphisms A, B of V; hence by (1)
\[T^{m} \;=\; (F_1\otimes 1)^{m} \;=\; F_1^{\,m}\otimes 1 \;=\; F_m\otimes 1 .\tag{2}\]
Thus the assertion "F_1 semisimple \Leftrightarrow F_m semisimple" is precisely the assertion, for the invertible K-linear operator T on the K-vector space \bar V with K algebraically closed of characteristic 0, that T is diagonalizable if and only if T^m is diagonalizable. (No finiteness of \dim_{\mathbb Q_\ell} V is needed; the argument below works in arbitrary dimension.)

Step 4 ((\Rightarrow) direction of the linear-algebra statement).
Assume T is diagonalizable: \bar V has a basis B of eigenvectors of T, say T e = \alpha_e e with \alpha_e \in K. Then T^{m} e = \alpha_e^{m} e for every e \in B, so B is also a basis of eigenvectors of T^m; hence T^m is diagonalizable.

Step 5 ((\Leftarrow) direction of the linear-algebra statement).
Assume T^m is diagonalizable. Then \bar V possesses a basis of eigenvectors of T^m, and consequently
\[\bar V \;=\; \bigoplus_{\lambda \in \Lambda} \bar V_\lambda, \qquad \bar V_\lambda := \ker(T^{m} - \lambda\,\mathrm{id}),\]\nwhere \Lambda := \{\lambda \in K^{\times} : \bar V_\lambda \neq 0\} is the set of eigenvalues of T^m; the equality holds because every vector is a finite linear combination of basis eigenvectors, and \Lambda \subset K^{\times} because T^m is invertible (T \in \mathrm{GL}(\bar V) implies T^m \in \mathrm{GL}(\bar V), so 0 is not an eigenvalue).

(a) Each \bar V_\lambda is T-stable: if v \in \bar V_\lambda then (T^m - \lambda)Tv = T(T^m v - \lambda v) = T(0) = 0, using that T commutes with every polynomial in T^m and is K-linear.

(b) Fix \lambda \in \Lambda and choose \mu \in K^{\times} with \mu^{m} = \lambda (possible since K is algebraically closed and \lambda \neq 0). Define S := \mu^{-1} T|_{\bar V_\lambda} \in \mathrm{End}_K(\bar V_\lambda). For v \in \bar V_\lambda we have T^{m}v = \lambda v, hence S^{m} v = \mu^{-m}\lambda v = v; that is, S^{m} = \mathrm{id}_{\bar V_\lambda}.

(c) S is diagonalizable. Let v \in \bar V_\lambda be arbitrary and consider the S-cyclic subspace W := \mathrm{span}_K\{S^{j}v : j \ge 0\}. Since S^{m} = \mathrm{id}, every S^{j}v with j \ge m equals S^{j \bmod m}v, so W = \mathrm{span}_K\{v, Sv, \dots, S^{m-1}v\} is finite dimensional, and it is S-stable because S(S^{m-1}v) = S^{m}v = v \in W. The operator S|_W therefore satisfies the polynomial X^{m} - 1 \in K[X]. Over the characteristic-zero field K, X^{m} - 1 = \prod_{\zeta \in \mu_m(K)} (X - \zeta) is a product of m \emph{distinct} linear factors: the m-th roots of unity in K are pairwise distinct because X^{m}-1 has no repeated roots (its derivative mX^{m-1} does not vanish at any root \zeta \neq 0, as \mathrm{char}\,K = 0). Hence the minimal polynomial of S|_W, which divides X^{m}-1, is a product of distinct linear factors, so S|_W is diagonalizable. Thus v = \sum_{\zeta^{m}=1} v_\zeta is a finite sum of eigenvectors of S|_W, hence of S, with S v_\zeta = \zeta v_\zeta. As v was arbitrary, \bar V_\lambda is spanned by eigenvectors of S, i.e. S is diagonalizable.

(d) Since T|_{\bar V_\lambda} = \mu S, the same eigenbasis diagonalises T|_{\bar V_\lambda} (with eigenvalues \mu\zeta). Taking the union over \lambda \in \Lambda of the eigenbases of the T-stable summands \bar V_\lambda gives a basis of \bar V consisting of eigenvectors of T. Hence T is diagonalizable.

This completes the proof of the linear-algebra equivalence.

Step 6 (Conclusion).
Applying Step 4 with T = F_1 \otimes 1 shows: if F_1 is semisimple on V then T^m = F_m \otimes 1 (by (2)) is diagonalizable, i.e. F_m is semisimple on V. Applying Step 5 shows the converse: if F_m is semisimple, i.e. T^m is diagonalizable, then T = F_1 \otimes 1 is diagonalizable, i.e. F_1 is semisimple. (For m = 1 the two operators coincide and the equivalence is tautological, which is also covered by the argument above.) This is exactly the required statement.

Remark. The proof used only (i) that F_1 is an invertible \mathbb Q_\ell-linear operator on H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) — supplied by lemma_6a, valid for every \mathbb F_q-scheme, hence in particular for proper X — and (ii) the identity F_m = F_1^{\,m}, which is formal from \sigma^{m} = \sigma^{\circ m} and functoriality of étale pullback. Properness of X is not used by the argument; it guarantees in the usual situations that the groups are finite dimensional, but the equivalence holds for arbitrary \mathbb Q_\ell-vector spaces.

lemma_324.statement: Let \(\ell\) be a prime, let \(c\in\mathbb Q_\ell^{\times}\), let \(V\) and \(W\) be finite-dimensional \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-vector spaces, let \(\langle-,-\rangle:V\times W\to\mathbb Q_\ell\) be a perfect bilinear pairing, and let \(T_V\in\mathrm{GL}(V)\) and \(T_W\in\mathrm{GL}(W)\) satisfy \(\langle T_Vv,\,T_Ww\rangle=c\,\langle v,w\rangle\) for all \(v\in V\), \(w\in W\). Then the base change of \(T_V\) to \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\) is diagonalizable if and only if the base change of \(T_W\) to \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\) is diagonalizable.
lemma_324.proof:
We prove the statement by reducing to linear algebra over the algebraically closed field K := \overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell, and then showing that T_W is, up to the non-zero scalar c and a change of basis, the contragredient of T_V^{-1}.

STEP 0 (Base change of all the data to K). Write K = \overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell and set V_K := V \otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell} K, W_K := W \otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell} K. Define a K-bilinear pairing
\[ \langle -, - \rangle_K : V_K \times W_K \to K, \qquad \langle v\otimes \alpha,\, w\otimes \beta\rangle_K := \alpha\beta\,\langle v,w\rangle, \]
extended K-bilinearly. This pairing is perfect: by perfectness of \langle-,-\rangle the map W \to V^{\vee},\ w\mapsto\langle -,w\rangle is a \mathbb Q_\ell-linear isomorphism, so if (v_1,\dots,v_n) is any \mathbb Q_\ell-basis of V, the dual basis (v_1^{\vee},\dots,v_n^{\vee}) of V^{\vee} has unique preimages w_1,\dots,w_n\in W, and (w_1,\dots,w_n) is a \mathbb Q_\ell-basis of W with \langle v_i,w_j\rangle = \delta_{ij}. Since K is free (hence flat) over \mathbb Q_\ell, the families (v_i\otimes 1) and (w_j\otimes 1) are K-bases of V_K and W_K, and the Gram matrix of \langle-,-\rangle_K in these bases is the identity matrix; hence \langle-,-\rangle_K is perfect. In particular \dim_K V_K = \dim_K W_K = n.

The operators T_V, T_W extend to K-linear automorphisms \mathcal T_V := T_V\otimes \mathrm{Id}_K of V_K and \mathcal T_W := T_W\otimes \mathrm{Id}_K of W_K (automorphisms because T_V,T_W\in\mathrm{GL}). By "the base change of T_V to K" we mean exactly \mathcal T_V, so the lemma asserts: \mathcal T_V is diagonalizable over K iff \mathcal T_W is diagonalizable over K. The relation is preserved by base change: for pure tensors, \langle \mathcal T_V(v\otimes\alpha), \mathcal T_W(w\otimes\beta)\rangle_K = \alpha\beta\langle T_Vv,T_Ww\rangle = c\,\alpha\beta\langle v,w\rangle = c\,\langle v\otimes\alpha, w\otimes\beta\rangle_K, and both sides are K-bilinear, so
\[ \langle \mathcal T_V v, \mathcal T_W w\rangle_K = c\,\langle v,w\rangle_K \qquad\text{for all } v\in V_K,\ w\in W_K, \tag{1}\]
where c\in\mathbb Q_\ell^{\times}\subset K^{\times} is non-zero. From now on we drop the subscript K and work over the algebraically closed field K with a perfect pairing satisfying (1).

STEP 1 (Degenerate case). If n = 0 then V = W = 0 and both T_V, T_W are the identity of the zero space, which is diagonalizable (the empty basis is a basis of eigenvectors). Hence the equivalence holds trivially. Assume n \ge 1 from now on; in particular V and W are non-zero.

STEP 2 (The intertwining identity). Define the K-linear map
\[ \varphi : W \longrightarrow V^{\vee}, \qquad \varphi(w) := \langle -, w\rangle_K . \]
Because the pairing is perfect, \varphi is a K-linear isomorphism. Let S^{*} : V^{\vee}\to V^{\vee} denote the contragredient (transpose) of S\in\mathrm{End}_K(V), defined by S^{*}(f) := f\circ S, i.e. (S^{*}f)(v) = f(Sv).

We claim
\[ \varphi\circ \mathcal T_W \;=\; c\,(\mathcal T_V^{-1})^{*}\circ\varphi . \tag{2}\]
Indeed, fix w\in W and v\in V. Applying (1) with v replaced by \mathcal T_V^{-1}v gives
\[ \langle v, \mathcal T_W w\rangle_K \;=\; \langle \mathcal T_V(\mathcal T_V^{-1}v),\ \mathcal T_W w\rangle_K \;=\; c\,\langle \mathcal T_V^{-1}v,\, w\rangle_K . \]
Evaluating the left-hand side and the right-hand side as functionals in v:
\[ (\varphi(\mathcal T_W w))(v) = \langle v,\mathcal T_W w\rangle_K = c\,\langle \mathcal T_V^{-1}v, w\rangle_K = c\,(\varphi(w))(\mathcal T_V^{-1}v) = c\,\bigl((\mathcal T_V^{-1})^{*}\varphi(w)\bigr)(v), \]
which proves (2) since two functionals agreeing on every v are equal. As \varphi is an isomorphism, (2) is equivalent to
\[ \mathcal T_W \;=\; c\;\varphi^{-1}\circ (\mathcal T_V^{-1})^{*}\circ\varphi . \tag{3}\]

STEP 3 (Three elementary facts about diagonalizability over a field). We record and prove the three operations used in (3).

(3a) Inversion. For A\in\mathrm{GL}(U) with U a finite-dimensional K-vector space, A is diagonalizable iff A^{-1} is.
